articles.title: Russian-Indian BrahMos missile is getting future-ready
articles.body:
Russian-Indian BrahMos missile is getting future-ready
The BrahMos corporation is working to add more destructive power and reach to its namesake supersonic cruise missile, following its spectacular combat successes last year.
The operational and functional parameters of the missile are being upgraded, and new versions are in the works, the CEO and managing director of the joint venture between India and Russia, Jaiteerth Joshi, told local media recently.
Named after the Brahmaputra and Moskva rivers, the BrahMos is engineered for high-precision, long-range strikes. The missile offers militaries the versatility to engage threats using land, sea, and underwater platforms.
BrahMos earned its stripes last year when the Indian and Pakistani militaries briefly clashed with missiles and drones, following a terrorist attack on civilians in India’s Jammu and Kashmir state.
As the two militaries tested each other with drones, India fired BrahMos missiles to strike hardened high-value targets, including hangars reportedly housing Pakistan’s US-made F-16 fighter jets.
India has said there was not a single interception of the BrahMos during the clashes, dubbed Operation Sindoor, and buyer interest has risen since.
BrahMos Aerospace is a joint venture between India’s DRDO and Russia’s NPO Mashinostroyeniya.
BrahMos’ trajectory into the future
BrahMos started as a land-launched cruise missile, but its developers have worked to give it more flexibility and lethality as battlefield needs evolved and expanded.
The missile, which flies at nearly three times the speed of sound and carries a 200 to 300 kg warhead, had an initial range of 290 km but continuous upgrades have extended its reach.
In 2023, the Indian Air Force (IAF) successfully tested a version with a 450 km range. Mated to the Su-30MKI fighter, this variant, called the BrahMos-A, offers the IAF a standoff precision strike capability that few air forces in the world can match.
There is also a Block III land-attack variant, which can fly very low and approach targets from unexpected angles – dodging any defenses the enemy may try to throw at it.
The BrahMos corporation is working on a long and ambitious list of upgrades. At the top of the current development efforts sits a lighter, air-launched variant.
Christened the BrahMos-NG, it can be flown on the IAF’s other fighter jets, including the domestically produced Tejas light combat aircraft. The Su-30MKI will be able to sortie armed with three of these missiles.
The BrahMos-NG will feature higher domestically-produced content and advanced materials. The Indo-Russian joint venture expects to unveil this prototype by 2027-28.
The BrahMos corporation is also working on a very long-range missile. This version would be able to strike targets up to 1,500 km away, far more than the 290 km range of the original missile unveiled in the early 2000s.
This long-range version is at the conceptual stage, and the company is discussing further upgrades with its Russian joint venture partner. Joshi has told Indian media outlets in recent interviews that the range-extension program will proceed in phases, with test firings from land, sea, and air to validate the missile’s operational capabilities.
Also, on the missile maker’s drawing board is a hypersonic version – the new frontier of modern warfare – currently called BrahMos II.
The concept aims to integrate advanced technologies, state-of-the-art design, and smart materials to field a hypersonic futuristic weapon that will dominate fast-evolving battlefield technology.
BrahMos II will have an “air-breathing” scramjet engine that would boost it to a top speed of Mach 5.
BrahMos is seeing high global interest
The missile has already been sold to multiple countries, and many others have shown an interest in buying it.
One of the first foreign customers of the Indo-Russian missile was the Philippines, with Manila signing a $375 million contract in 2022. The first batch of BrahMos missiles was delivered to the country in April 2024, and the second in April 2025.
In June this year, India confirmed it had a deal with Vietnam to supply the missiles.
Indonesia, which has also evinced interest, has moved forward with procurement plans.
In addition, over a dozen nations including Malaysia, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Chile, and South Africa have evaluated or expressed a formal interest in the BrahMos missile system.
BrahMos is gearing up for a demand surge
The BrahMos project is a trailblazer in India’s defense industry. It broke the shackles of excessive bureaucratic controls that were once the hallmark of Indian state-owned defense corporations that had forced the country to remain a major arms importer.
Effective management and the synergizing of commercial viability, strike capabilities, and indigenization have helped the missile become the battlefield success it is, whie making inroads into the global arms market.
With a burgeoning order book, BrahMos corporation is prioritizing the fulfillment of orders received from the Indian armed forces, for whom the missile is a primary strike weapon. India recently contracted for more BrahMos launchers and fire-control systems, so more of its warships can be armed with the missile.
The missile maker now has production facilities in four Indian cities: Hyderabad, Nagpur, Pilani and Lucknow. Research and development clusters, nicknamed ‘tech-bricks’ have been set up to work on niche technologies for the next generation missiles.
The supply chain is being expanded to make it more robust and resilient – and to meet an expected surge in demand. For this, the company will expand the industry partners for each system and subsystem to up to 45, from the current one or two partners.
India’s arms export ambitions ride on BrahMos
New Delhi is gradually setting its sights to make a complete transformation from being one of the biggest arms importers to a major defense exporter.
It also simultaneously wants to see more domestically produced components and technology being used in its products. Indian defense exports registered an impressive 67% annual growth to reach $4 billion in the financial year ended March.
The federal government’s annual defense production target is $31 billion by 2029, of which defense exports are pegged at $5.5 billion.
BrahMos will be key to New Delhi’s ambitious goals to emerge as a major global arms exporter.

articles.title: France to field twelve SAMP/T NG air defence units
articles.body:
France has ordered four additional SAMP/T NG firing units, taking its total order for the ground-based air and missile defence system to twelve, according to eurosam.
The Organisation for Joint Armament Cooperation, known as OCCAR, placed the contract on behalf of France with eurosam, the Franco-Italian grouping formed by MBDA France, MBDA Italy and Thales. The units will be delivered to the French Air and Space Force in a multi-layer configuration combining Aster and MICA VL missiles.
The company said: “This order is an additional step towards the renewal of the European Long-Range Air and Missile Defence ground capabilities, following the SAMP/T NG development launched in 2021.”
It added: “OCCAR-EA, eurosam and its members, MBDA and Thales will continue to lead the way in state of the art and sovereign air and Missile defence systems for the benefit of European defence. These advanced air defence systems are crucial in the current global context to respond to increasingly challenging threats.”
A SAMP/T NG firing unit holds up to forty-eight Aster missiles ready to fire, carried across up to six launcher modules of eight rounds each, alongside a multi-function radar and identification module able to detect and identify targets beyond 350km, and an engagement module. The whole system is mobile and eurosam says it can be operational in under thirty minutes, offering 360-degree coverage and engaging targets beyond 150km.
The system is designed around the Aster 30 B1 and the newer Aster B1NT. The B1NT uses a Ka-band seeker and new interception algorithms to give what the company describes as a hit-to-kill capability against short and medium range ballistic missiles, low manoeuvring targets and hypersonic missiles.
Britain has a stake in the wider programme, since the United Kingdom is a participant in the FSAF-PAAMS arrangement that OCCAR manages, and the fourteenth amendment to that contract, signed in Paris in January 2024, covered supplementary procurement of equipment allowing Britain to carry out mid-life upgrades to its own Aster missiles. Aster is the weapon carried by the Royal Navy’s Type 45 destroyers as part of the Sea Viper system, which HMS Diamond used against Houthi missiles and drones in the Red Sea.
France and Italy have supplied SAMP/T systems to Ukraine, where the type has engaged Russian ballistic missiles.
The order lands while Britain has no ground-based long-range air defence system assigned to the defence of the United Kingdom. Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, confirmed this week that a further £790 million will be invested in homeland integrated air and missile defence, covering enhanced command and control, improved sensing and radar systems, counter-drone capabilities and more effective layered defences.
The Defence Committee reported yesterday that anti-strike capabilities for shooting down ballistic, hypersonic and cruise missiles and drones are among the capabilities European NATO members lack in sufficient numbers, and that replacing American military capabilities with European weapons has been costed by the Kiel Institute at an extra €50 billion each year over the next decade.
Sky Sabre gives the British Army a medium range ground-based system, currently deployed in Poland and the Falkland Islands. This publication has reported on continuing work on the potential of British destroyers in the ballistic missile defence role and on when those destroyers will receive their missile upgrades.

articles.title: Poroshenko announces transfer of five Ai-Petri systems to defend Kyiv
articles.body:
Petro Poroshenko, a member of the Ukrainian Parliament and leader of the European Solidarity party, handed over five Ai-Petri data transmission and electronic warfare systems to strengthen Kyiv's defense against air attacks by Russian occupiers.
"Today we are handing over five systems, manufactured with funds from a grant from the city of Kyiv, to the leadership of the Ground Forces and other units. I thank Kyiv community and Kyiv City Council for this cooperation. All of them will help defend the capital's airspace," Poroshenko said on Facebook on Friday.
According to him, since late September and early October, the enemy has been employing new tactics for which Ukraine was not entirely prepared: it is making massive use of Shahed drones and new Kometa multi-channel antennas, which significantly complicate the operation of Ukrainian electronic warfare and air defense systems.
"This requires a concentrated effort, constant modernization, and technological improvements; it forces us to switch to three-shift operations and relocate production, particularly to underground workshops. We are modernizing not only our countermeasures against technical reconnaissance but also our electronic intelligence capabilities: direction-finding equipment, new high-frequency amplifiers, and transmitters. When used correctly, they disrupt network communications and blind attack systems," Poroshenko said.
As previously reported, MP and leader of the European Solidarity party Petro Poroshenko has invested over UAH 200 million since the autumn of 2023 in the production of Ai-Petri SV systems, which have successfully passed testing and are in use by the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Each system includes the counter-surveillance device itself, a pickup truck, a charging station, a generator, and the necessary electronics. In March 2025, Poroshenko announced a contract with the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, and on June 29 of that year, he announced the start of cooperation with the command of the Ukrainian Ground Forces regarding the supply of these systems to the military. On September 9, 2026, the Ai-Petri counter-surveillance system was unveiled for the first time at the MSPO 2026 security and defense technology exhibition, held in Kielce, Poland.
As reported, following a massive Russian strike on Kyiv on the night of Thursday, October 22, damage was recorded in six of the capital's ten administrative districts. One fatality and 24 injuries were reported, 16 of whom were hospitalized.
According to the Air Force, Russian occupiers launched a massive combined strike against Ukraine overnight, using Iskander-M, S-400, Zircon, and Onyx missiles, as well as 210 attack UAVs and decoy drones. Kyiv was the main target of the attack. As of 09:00, air defenses had shot down and neutralized 181 enemy UAVs (including 87 jet-powered ones), but strikes were recorded at 32 locations, and debris was found at eight locations. Serhiy "Flash" Beskrestnov, an advisor to the President of Ukraine on defense technologies, said the occupiers used an Iskander ballistic missile with a cluster warhead to strike the center of Kyiv.
On Thursday night, air defense forces shot down and neutralized via electronic warfare 140 out of 176 drones of various types that Russian troops had used to attack Ukraine.

articles.title: Iran says US military not allowed to enter Gulf
articles.body:
- Iran said on Saturday that US military ships would never be allowed to enter the Gulf "under any circumstances" and that President Donald Trump will "take that dream to his grave".
- Saudi forces launched deadly airstrikes on Yemen's Houthi-controlled Sanaa governorate on Saturday, media belonging to the Iran-backed group said, while also reporting around 20 strikes on Mocha.
- A Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said it destroyed two ballistic missiles firedby the Iran-aligned group towards Taif and Yanbu on Saturday, as fighting between the sides continued.
- Israel's military launched an operation in the occupied West Bank on Friday, it said, that would last several days and include searches and building demolitions, after gunmen killed two soldiers days ahead of Israeli elections in which security has been a key focus.
Turkey to tell Yemen Houthi attacks 'unacceptable'
Turkey's foreign minister will tell his Yemeni counterpart on Saturday that Houthi attacks on civilians are "unacceptable" and express hope the conflict can be resolved through dialogue, a Turkish foreign ministry source said.
Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan is due to meet Yemen's Afrah al-Zouba in Istanbul, a day after hosting talks with senior European and regional diplomats.
The Houthis have been at war since 2014 with Yemen's internationally recognised government.
Following an uneasy four-year truce, fighting reignited in July, months into the US-Iran conflict that has plunged the wider region into crisis.
Iranian President Massoud Pezeshkian will meet his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin in Moscow next week, Iranian media reported.
Pezeshkian is due to visit Russia for a meeting of gas-exporting countries.
Russia and Iran, two of the most sanctioned nations on earth, have grown closer together in the years since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
"The Iranian president will visit Moscow to attend the summit of gas-exporting countries that will take place on Tuesday, October 27," the Tasnim news agency reported, citing Tehran's ambassador to the country, Kazem Jalali.
The two leaders will discuss economic cooperation as well as "questions of geopolitics", Jalali was quoted as saying.
Saudi-led coalition says it destroyed Houthi missiles
A Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said it destroyed two ballistic missiles firedby the Iran-aligned group towards Taif and Yanbu on Saturday, as fighting between the sides continued.
Saudi Arabia's Civil Defence briefly issued alerts on Saturday warning of potential danger in Taif and Yanbu, as well as the holy city of Mecca and its second-largest city, Jeddah.
The service issued notices around 10 minutes later saying the danger had passed.
Saudi civil defence issues 'potential danger' warning
Saudi Arabia's civil defence agency broadcast warnings of "potential danger" for four of its western provinces, including that of Mecca, home to Islam's holiest city, on Friday, without saying why.
The alerts, which also covered the major Red Sea city of Jeddah, nearby Taif and the coastal oil hub of Yanbu, were all rescinded minutes later.
Residents were instructed to "proceed to the nearest safe place" by the agency. The agency also repeated a legal warning against sharing images or information related to "countering missiles and drones".
Netanyahu says Palestinian Authority in for 'big surprise'
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that the Palestinian Authority was in for a "big surprise" after he ordered a major military operation in response to an attack on soldiers in the West Bank.
Netanyahu, days ahead of elections, declined to answer directly when he was asked if he would dismantle the Palestinian Authority but said he favoured "ruse and surprise".
"We transformed the Middle East. I said that we would change things and we have," Netanyahu told i24News in an interview conducted late Friday.
"There is a very big surprise for the Palestinian Authority as well."
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said on Saturday it had intercepted a ballistic missile launched towards Riyadh by the Iran-backed group.
Two explosions rang out in Riyadh early Saturday, an AFP journalist in the Saudi capital said, as the Houthis keep up strikes on the kingdom.
An early warning system was activated to alert residents to a potential threat, the Saudi civil defence said.
"Air defences intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthi terrorist militia toward Riyadh," coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki posted on X.
Iran said on Saturday that US military ships would never be allowed to enter the Gulf "under any circumstances" and that President Donald Trump would "take that dream to his grave".
The remarks came amid mounting US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran, as US ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack warned that Washington could "absolutely" strike Iran as soon as this weakened.
"We will not allow US military ships in the Persian Gulf under any circumstances and at any time," said Iran's armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi, according to Iranian state television.
"The US president must dream of seeing the armed forces enter the Persian Gulf. He will take that dream to his grave."

articles.title: Ukraine receives only 24 Patriot missiles from USA over past three months - Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that Ukraine has received only 24 interceptor missiles for its U.S.-made Patriot air defense systems over the last three months—a quantity far short of what is actually needed.
In an interview with ABC News on Friday, he noted that 30 ballistic missiles were fired at Kyiv just this past Thursday evening.
According to Zelenskyy’s estimates, Ukraine requires an average of 350 Patriot interceptor missiles per month.
Asked if he believes Putin requested that Trump to turn off intelligence-sharing between the U.S. and Ukraine, Zelenskyy responded, "I don't know. I hope, I trust and I hope God bless. No."
The President of Ukraine noted that he does not feel betrayed by the United States, but expressed regret over the lack of American aid. "I feel what I feel. It's not supportive," Zelenskyy said.
He emphasized that he is grateful for the partnership in the war against the Russian Federation, but suggested that, at times, he may not be as "polite" as other partners expect him to be. "Of course I'm a normal person, I'm just human, maybe not such a big humanitarian as Putin, of course … Like between friends, like in the family, you have to be honest, not to play games. I don't play games with Trump. This is my difference between me and Putin. I don't play with him any games. I'm direct, honest," Zelenskyy said.
The Ukrainian head of state believes that this is Trump’s personal decision “to be friends with Putin or not," but suggested that “they're in quite very good relations.”
Zelenskyy stated that the Ukrainian side is "ready to stop this war as quick as possible," but noted that the Russian Federation currently controls more than 19% of Ukrainian territory, and that Ukraine is not prepared to cede any further territory for the sake of ending the war.
As earlier reported, by June 2025, the U.S. military will likely have used up to two-thirds of its stockpile of missile-defense interceptors, even as American defense companies ramp up production. Specifically, Lockheed Martin is working to increase its annual production capacity for advanced PAC-3 interceptors, used in Patriot missile systems, from approximately 600 to 2,000 units. According to Bloomberg, the shortage in missile stockpiles has already affected supplies to other U.S. allies.
German authorities are seeking permission from the USA to assemble an advanced version of the Patriot interceptor missiles at facilities in Germany, stated German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius.
Zelenskyy has stated that Ukraine is not the top priority for suppliers of American PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles for Patriot air defense systems, as the majority of these have long been directed to the Middle East. According to the president, Ukraine is also working with European and other nations around the world to secure additional missile supplies to protect its population.
According to him, Ukraine received 675 missiles throughout 2023, and 364 in 2025—yet the number of Russian missile strikes has increased during this period. For 2026, the delivery of 264 PAC-3 and PAC-2 missiles was planned. The PAC-3 missiles are supplied by the United States through the PURL program. "All our partners—both Americans and Europeans—are aware of the sums they are contributing and know exactly how many missiles they are providing us. There are also separate bilateral agreements with various European nations and countries in the Middle East. But, unfortunately, you can see a downward trend, and this depends primarily on the American side," Zelenskyy stated in August of this year.
On October 21, Ukrainian Minister of Defence Yevhen Khmara and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Mykhailo Drapaty met with a delegation from the American defence company Lockheed Martin, led by Orlando Sanchez Jr., President of Lockheed Martin Aeronautics. The discussions focused on the importance of stable arms supplies and future cooperation. In particular, the parties addressed increasing the delivery of PAC-3 interceptor missiles to counter the threat of strikes by Russian ballistic missiles.

articles.title: US lawmakers urge Pentagon to expand Starshield contract for Ukraine
articles.body:
US lawmakers urge Pentagon to expand Starshield contract for Ukraine
Members of the US Congress have called on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the Pentagon to expand its contract under the Starshield programme and restore Ukraine's access to Starlink and Starshield satellite communications following recent disruptions.
Source: a letter from US lawmakers
Details: In a bipartisan, bicameral appeal, US lawmakers insist that services be restored without speed restrictions to ensure Ukraine has the technical capabilities it needs.
Quote: "Ukrainian forces depend on these services for command and control, intelligence sharing, battlefield communications, and the operation of unmanned systems. Any degradation in service, including reduced connection speeds, restricted geographic coverage, or interruptions in access, undermines Ukraine's military effectiveness and provides Russian forces with an operational advantage that will extend the conflict and put more civilians in harm's way."
Details: The lawmakers urged the US Department of Defense to maintain the coverage Ukraine needs to conduct legitimate military operations, including over Russian territory, and to ensure that the transition from the commercial Starlink service to the government-run Starshield programme takes place without any interruption to service.
"Decisions regarding service availability, coverage, and performance should not be left solely to the discretion of a private provider when they have direct consequences for Ukraine's ability to defend itself," the lawmakers added.
They also called on the Department of Defense to consider using its powers under the relevant provision of the Defense Production Act, which allows the federal government to require companies to prioritise government orders.
"The United States and Europe have made significant investments in Ukraine's defence because of how a Russian victory would put our security at risk. Those investments should not be undermined by preventable disruptions to the communications infrastructure on which Ukrainian forces depend," the lawmakers concluded.
Previously: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed on 23 October that speed restrictions for Starlink satellite communications terminals in Ukraine remain in force.
The New York Times reported that US senators had warned the White House they would withhold votes on nominees until President Donald Trump's administration ensured the restoration of the communications capabilities used by Ukrainian troops.
A bipartisan group of nearly 20 members of the US House of Representatives called on Trump to ask Elon Musk to give Ukraine access to Starlink systems to target missile launchers on Russian territory.
US Democratic Senator Chris Coons had previously contacted Elon Musk's SpaceX, asking the company to explain who had decided to restrict Starlink's operation in Ukraine and why.
Background:
- The Wall Street Journal reported that Elon Musk had ordered Starlink services to be slowed down. It is unclear to what extent Trump was involved in discussions about the slowdown.
- US Republican Senator Thom Tillis is seeking an investigation into the Pentagon's actions with regard to problems with Starlink satellite communications systems encountered by the Ukrainian Armed Forces.
- US House of Representatives member Joe Wilson and nearly two dozen of his colleagues prepared a letter calling for Ukraine to be permitted to use Starlink for strikes on launch sites within Russian territory.
- The Wall Street Journal, citing US and Ukrainian officials familiar with the matter, reported that Trump had called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on the military version of Starlink in Ukraine.
- On the evening of 22 October, Trump said Musk had already lifted speed restrictions on the military version of Starlink in Ukraine but declined to say whether he had personally called him about the issue.
- Ukraine's Defence Ministry said it was recording disruptions to Starlink and Starshield services on the line of contact.

articles.title: Polish FM refutes Musk’s claim that Ukrainian elites profiting from US aid to Ukraine
articles.body:
Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski has refuted a claim by SpaceX CEO Elon Musk that Ukrainian elites are allegedly enriching themselves through the multi-billion-dollar aid provided by U.S. taxpayers. Sikorski pointed out that the USA ceased funding for Kyiv last year, and that purchases of American weaponry are now being financed by European states.
“No, Elon, the U.S. stopped funding Ukraine last year. In fact, U.S. companies make money on American weapons for which we Europeans pay. The more you meddle in our politics and the more you play politics with your products, the more you damage your brand,” the minister said on X.
Meanwhile, Musk posted on the social media platform X, highlighting a significant disparity in motives between Ukraine’s elites and its ordinary citizens. He alleged that those in power have enriched themselves through hundreds of billions of dollars in foreign aid, even as the general population is being mobilized for the military. The American billionaire further suggested that a portion of U.S. taxpayer funds may be finding its way back—via money-laundering schemes—to finance political campaigns within the United States, which he posited as an explanation for why certain American politicians continue to support Ukraine.
At the same time, ABC News chief international correspondent James Longman reported on X, citing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, that the current performance of Starlink terminals remains insufficient to support the operation of Ukrainian defense drones. According to the journalist, the United States has provided Ukraine with only 24 interceptor missiles for Patriot air defense systems over the past three months, whereas Russian forces launched 80 ballistic missiles into Ukrainian territory in the last week alone.

articles.title: Germany in talks with Ukraine to purchase Bars jet-powered drones – Bloomberg, photo
articles.body:
Germany in talks with Ukraine to purchase Bars jet-powered drones – Bloomberg, photo
Germany plans to replenish its stockpile of precision-guided weapons with several thousand missiles from European arms manufacturers. In particular, the country is in talks with Ukraine regarding Bars jet-powered drones.
Source: Bloomberg
Details: According to Bloomberg, the Ukrainian jet-powered UAVs are among four main options being considered by the German Defence Ministry. In addition to Bars, Germany is discussing a contract worth more than €1 billion to purchase Anthem ground-launched cruise missiles from US company Covenant.
Germany is also considering Ruta missiles from the Dutch company Destinus, which have been used in Ukraine, and the HS1 high-speed missile being developed by German-British defence start-up Hypersonica, the financial news agency's sources said.
"They are also in talks with Ukraine to co-produce and acquire the Bars cruise missile, whose manufacturer has not been made public, people familiar with the negotiations said," Bloomberg reported.
The Bars jet-powered drone has a strike range of up to 1,000 km and can carry a warhead weighing up to 60 kg. The UAV can reach speeds of more than 700 km/h. Bars operates as a modular platform which, depending on its fuel load and warhead weight, can be used for long-range and mid-range strikes as well as strikes near the front line.
The manufacturer of Bars drones is capable of producing around 600 jet-powered drones per month. The company is also working on upgrading the drone to the Bars 2.0 version.
Background: Earlier, Ukrainska Pravda reported that Ukraine and Germany signed an agreement in July 2026 on the joint production of Bars UAVs. During the first stage of the project, Germany will finance drone production, with all the systems produced to be supplied to Ukraine's defence forces.

articles.title: UK-France deepen nuclear defence ties in first joint exercise
articles.body:
UK-France deepen nuclear defence ties in first joint exercise
UK deepens nuclear defence ties with France in historic first joint air exercise as RAF Typhoon fighters join French Rafale jets in a French nuclear exercise.
- For the first time, RAF Typhoon fighters have taken part in a French nuclear air exercise, flying alongside French Rafale in a show of allied strength.
- Exercise “Rummy” marks a major step forward in UK-France defence cooperation under the Northwood Declaration.
- This partnership is vital to protecting the UK and deterring threats in an increasingly complex security environment.
The UK’s defences are being strengthened as RAF Typhoon fighters join French Rafale jets in a French nuclear exercise for the first time.
Exercise “Rummy” saw British and French forces operate side by side over the Mediterranean, demonstrating the readiness and capability that help deter threats and keep the UK safe.
Launching from Saint-Dizier Air Base in France, French Rafale simulated a nuclear strike mission, escorted by RAF Typhoons.
Conducted under robust safety and security arrangements, the exercise did not involve nuclear weapons. The exercise focused on improving how our forces work together, ensuring that if the UK faces a serious threat, our military can respond quickly and effectively alongside our closest European ally.
This exercise shows the UK’s commitment to standing united against any threat, strengthening deterrence and protecting peace and security alongside European Allies to protect national security. As close NATO Allies and European nuclear powers, the UK and France play a vital role in the security of the Euro-Atlantic region.
The exercise complements the work the UK is doing to invest £63 billion over the next four years to strengthen the UK’s nuclear deterrent, funding Dreadnought and SSN-AUKUS submarines, a new warhead and other vital nuclear work. The UK will also buy 12 F-35A aircraft and join NATO’s nuclear mission, delivering a more European NATO and reinforcing the UK’s contribution to collective defence.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said:
  This exercise marks a new chapter in the defence nuclear relationship between the United Kingdom and France.
As Europe’s nuclear powers, we have a shared responsibility to contribute to the security and stability of the Euro-Atlantic region. This exercise demonstrates the depth of our partnership, the credibility of our deterrents and our determination to stand together in the face of emerging threats.
In an increasingly dangerous world, our adversaries should be in no doubt: the UK and France remain united in our commitment to European security and to maintaining the deterrence that has helped preserve peace for generations.
Minister of the Armed Forces and Veterans Catherine Vautrin said:
  Having independent nuclear forces does not exclude coordination. Our nuclear cooperation with the United Kingdom keeps deepening: on Tuesday night, UK Typhoons participated for the very first time to a French nuclear exercise alongside Rafales.
Through coordination, our nuclear forces demonstrate that they can contribute even more significantly to the overall security of the Alliance and to the peace and stability of the Euro Atlantic area.
Exercise “Rummy” represents a key milestone in the UK-France nuclear partnership and the programme of cooperation agreed under the Northwood Declaration.
Demonstrating the commitment of both nations to jointly deter common threats, the exercise showcases the depth of their bilateral nuclear defence relationship and proves that British and French forces are ready and able to operate together to protect shared interests and contribute to collective security in a period of heightened global instability.
The UK and France are close defence allies, underpinned by the refreshed Lancaster House Agreement between our two nations, expanding our joint deployable force, boosting our nuclear cooperation and developing the next generation of high-tech weapons.
Notes to Editors:
- Operation Rummy took place from 20-21 October 2026.
- Both the UK and France and retain sovereign, independent nuclear forces and national decision making.

articles.title: Ukraine continues to receive intelligence from CIA, despite strained relations between Trump and Zelenskyy – media
articles.body:
The U.S. intelligence community continues to assist Ukraine in defending itself against Russian aggression—notably by providing early warnings of incoming missiles and drones—even as relations between President Donald Trump and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy remain poor, reports The Atlantic.
Citing an unnamed high-ranking officer who frequently visits Ukraine, the publication notes that the CIA plays a leading role among American personnel in the country. The source also remarked that, with the CIA’s help, Ukrainians have become very adept at carrying out strikes against Russia.
Another intelligence official based in the Baltic states, who works closely with the USA to counter Russian influence, told the publication that CIA operations are currently much more aggressive than they were during the administration of former President Joe Biden, though you would never know it from Trump’s rhetoric.
“The administration’s policy is deeply conflicted, and perhaps no one understands that better than John Ratcliffe, the director of the Central Intelligence Agency. He has a foot in two worlds: advising a president who’s continuously at odds with Ukraine’s leadership, and running an agency that’s essential to Ukraine’s war for survival … ,” the article says.
Ukrainians do not view Ratcliffe as their defender. They know that he works for an unpredictable boss and that, should Trump carry out his recent threat to cut off intelligence support unless Ukraine stops attacking Russian oil refineries, Ratcliffe will follow that order, The Atlantic added.
Sources familiar with the matter describe Ratcliffe as someone who clearly understands the threat that the Russian Federation poses not only to Ukraine but also to the United States and its allies. The same can be said of U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, both of whom have now aligned themselves with Trump’s rhetoric.
According to the report, the CIA Director has likely advised Ukrainian President Zelenskyy on how to engage with Trump.
Commenting on disruptions to the Starlink satellite network and American early-warning systems, the publication notes that the USA has not yet officially cut off the flow of intelligence, though Trump could take such measures at any moment. The ezine says that should Trump decide to do so, those who have worked with Ratcliffe say he would not attempt to persuade the president to change his mind even despite concerns within CIA headquarters.

articles.title: Russian Iskander parts plant likely hit by cruise missiles
articles.body:
A missile strike likely hit the Proton plant in the Russian city of Orel, a manufacturer of optoelectronic equipment whose components are used in Russia’s Iskander-M ballistic missiles, Pantsir-S1 air defense systems and Kh-71 cruise missiles, according to the monitoring channel Exilenova+.
Local authorities declared an aviation and missile danger alert in Orel during the attack. Information on the extent of the damage at the plant is still being clarified, and the type of weapon used and the exact time of the strike have not yet been confirmed.
The joint-stock company Proton is part of Russia’s defense industry supply chain and produces optoelectronic equipment and components for military use. Its products include diode modules, switch-inverters and electronic components for onboard weapon systems, which are supplied for the production of the 9M723 missiles of the Iskander-M short-range ballistic missile system, the S-71 Kover air-launched cruise missile and the Pantsir-S1, a truck-mounted system that combines anti-aircraft missiles and rapid-fire cannons to shoot down aircraft, drones and cruise missiles.
The Iskander-M is one of Russia’s main weapons for long-range strikes against Ukraine, firing ballistic missiles with a range of up to 500 km (310 miles). The S-71 Kover belongs to a family of newer Russian air-launched cruise missiles, and Ukrainian military intelligence has previously identified the same R500 turbojet engine in the S-71K Kover and the new Filin ground-launched cruise missile, which Russia began using against Ukraine in late summer 2026.
Orel, the capital of Russia’s Orel region about 160 km (100 miles) from the Ukrainian border, has been the target of repeated long-range strikes. On Oct. 31, 2025, the Ukrainian Navy said it hit the city’s thermal power plant with Neptune cruise missiles, and in May 2025 drones struck the Bolkhov semiconductor plant in the same region, which produces components used by Russia’s defense industry.
Ukraine has increasingly targeted Russian plants that build missiles and their components. In August 2026, Ukrainian Flamingo cruise missiles hit the Progress Rocket and Space Center in Samara, and earlier this month the Ukrainian General Staff confirmed a strike on the Redkino Experimental Plant in Tver region, which produces components for cruise missile fuel.

articles.title: Saudi-led coalition intercepts missiles, drones as Houthis report Saudi airstrikes
articles.body:
RIYADH/SANAA, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- The Saudi-led coalition said Friday that it had intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles and two drones launched by Yemen's Houthi group toward Saudi Arabia, while Houthi-run al-Masirah TV reported Saudi warplanes carried out a series of airstrikes on Houthi-held areas in Yemen.
Coalition spokesman Turki Al-Maliki said in the afternoon on X that Saudi air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis toward Khamis Mushait in the southwest.
Earlier in the day, the coalition said it intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis toward the Saudi capital, Riyadh, as well as two Houthi drones toward the southern region.
Houthi-run al-Masirah TV on Friday reported continued Saudi airstrikes on Houthi-controlled areas, saying three people were killed and nine others injured near the Houthi-held Yemeni capital, Sanaa.
The broadcaster said the casualties occurred when airstrikes "hit a house" in Nihm district, northeast of Sanaa. Citing a local Houthi security official, it said all 12 victims were members of the same family.
Airstrikes were also reported in the northern province of Saada, the western Red Sea province of Hodeidah, and areas in the southwestern province of Taiz, including the port city of Mocha, reported al-Masirah.
The broadcaster also cited a Houthi military source as saying Saudi aircraft struck a lighthouse on Mayyun Island in the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
There was no immediate comment from the Saudi-led coalition and the casualties could not be independently verified.
The exchange of strikes came amid an escalation in the conflict, with Saudi warplanes carrying out strikes deep inside Houthi-held territory and the Houthis launching repeated missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of the country's north, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene the following year in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government. ■

articles.title: Key dates in the latest slump in US-Ukrainian ties
articles.body:
Key dates in the latest slump in US-Ukrainian ties
Oct 24 - After warmer relations between US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy over the summer, ties have soured in recent weeks, sparking worries of a deeper break between the United States and Ukraine.
Here is a timeline of the main developments:
September 13
Trump calls on Zelenskiy to stop targeting Russian diesel infrastructure.
September 21
Trump, in a call, presses Zelenskiy to halt the strikes, the Financial Times reports.
October 3
Zelenskiy appears to defy Trump, saying Ukraine will double down on attacking Russian refineries.
October 9
US and Ukrainian officials meet in Miami. Sources tell Reuters that Trump's envoys struck a tough tone with Ukraine, saying the US was frustrated with Ukraine's continued strikes on Russian energy targets.
Trump says Russia has agreed to supply diesel to global markets, and his administration temporarily lifts sanctions on Russian fuel. Zelenskiy calls the move "weak."
October 10
Trump says that "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president" amid continued strikes on refineries.
October 11
Trump says Ukraine and Russia have agreed to an "energy ceasefire" but neither Ukraine nor Russia confirms that they have agreed to it. Mutual strikes continue.
October 13
Russia launches two missile strikes in 24 hours without warnings from allies, Zelenskiy says. But Trump says the US is still sharing intelligence with Ukraine.
October 14
Ukraine says Elon Musk's SpaceX has restricted Starlink services, hampering attack and air defense drone missions.
October 15
The order to limit satellite usage came from inside the White House, Reuters reports.
October 16
Ukraine's resumption of strikes on Russian refineries is a "disgrace," Trump says.
Zelenskiy welcomes the prospect of a greater role in talks for European allies he calls "real leaders."
Trump says he is waiving the application of certain sanctions, restrictions and duties on Russia, citing the US national interest.
October 17
Zelenskiy says Trump's move is "wrong."
October 19
Trump says Zelenskiy should "get somebody else to negotiate" an end to the war.
Zelenskiy says US decisions, including delays in arms shipments and restrictions on intelligence sharing, are "hard to explain."
The Kremlin says Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping could hold a three-way meeting. Ukraine says such a gathering could only prolong the war.
October 20
Trump calls on Ukraine to end the war and suggests Russia has the upper hand.
Zelenskiy says Ukraine is grateful that US intelligence and early warnings about Russian ballistic attacks were restored.
US envoy Steve Witkoff holds what a US official calls "constructive" talks with Zelenskiy in Norway.
October 21
During a visit by Witkoff, Russia frees Stephen Hubbard, a retired US schoolteacher in custody since 2022. Trump says he had asked Putin for the release.
October 22
Russia launches 21 ballistic missiles at Kyiv, authorities report. Zelenskiy says the attack shows Witkoff's talks with Putin had no effect. REUTERS

articles.title: Iran’s new military doctrine is designed to make victory meaningless
articles.body:
Iran’s latest military doctrine rests on a dangerous proposition: a country does not have to defeat a superior enemy on the battlefield to deny it a meaningful victory. By threatening broader retaliation, expanding the geography of conflict and exploiting vulnerabilities in regional trade, Tehran is attempting to make the political rewards of military action increasingly difficult to secure.
On Oct. 21, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) announced that Iran’s military doctrine would move beyond retaliatory strikes towards offensive and asymmetric operations.
The declaration reinforced earlier statements by Iranian military officials that the country was shifting away from a predominantly defensive posture.
Although official announcements do not establish how comprehensively this change has been implemented, they reveal the direction in which Tehran wants its adversaries to believe its strategy is moving.
The distinction matters because military superiority and strategic success are not interchangeable. Washington and Israel may destroy military facilities, disrupt command structures and degrade Iran’s weapons production. Yet these achievements cannot, by themselves, guarantee political compliance, regional stability or a durable settlement.
Iran’s objective, therefore, is not necessarily to win a conventional war against the United States. Rather, it is to deny Washington the ability to translate battlefield superiority into a political outcome that Tehran considers unacceptable.
This strategy could raise the costs of another attack, but it could also deepen the insecurity that makes another war possible. The central question is no longer simply who can inflict greater damage. It is whether either side can turn military force into a political settlement that lasts.
What It Means to Win a War
Iran’s strategic predicament is straightforward. Its conventional air power and technological capabilities cannot match those of the United States and Israel. A strategy built around symmetrical warfare would leave Tehran vulnerable to sustained aerial attacks, precision strikes and the systematic destruction of military infrastructure. Its response has consequently relied on a different calculation: if it cannot prevent an adversary from striking, it can make the consequences of that strike more costly and unpredictable.
Missiles, drones, dispersed launch systems and decentralised command structures are central to this approach. Rather than depending exclusively on the survival of major military installations, Iran can seek to preserve enough capacity to retaliate after suffering substantial damage. Its longstanding emphasis on asymmetric warfare also allows it to exploit the difference between the relatively low cost of some offensive systems and the expense of intercepting them.
The strategic logic extends beyond weapons. Iran can threaten military facilities, shipping routes and economic infrastructure across a wider regional theatre.
A conflict that begins with strikes on Iranian territory could therefore create security and economic consequences for states that are not directly involved in the initial attack.
The threat of escalation becomes part of Iran’s deterrent, even before every threatened operation is carried out.
This is a strategy of strategic denial. Its purpose is not necessarily to defeat an opponent in every engagement but to prevent that opponent from achieving its political objectives at an acceptable cost. If Washington seeks to eliminate a military threat, compel Iranian concessions or reshape Tehran’s regional behaviour, the relevant measure of success is not simply the number of targets destroyed. It is whether the intended political outcome follows.
Yet strategic denial should not be confused with victory. A state that survives an attack may still lose military capacity, economic resources and diplomatic leverage. Iran’s ability to impose costs does not automatically give it the ability to dictate the terms of a settlement. Its doctrine may complicate an adversary’s calculations without resolving the underlying imbalance of power.
Beyond Iran’s Borders
The most consequential feature of Iran’s approach is its potential to widen the conflict geographically. Tehran does not need to confine its response to the immediate battlefield if it believes that pressure on regional infrastructure and international commerce can influence an adversary’s decisions. This creates a direct connection between military strategy and the global economy.
The Strait of Hormuz illustrates the problem. The US Energy Information Administration estimated that roughly 20 million barrels of oil per day passed through the strait in 2024, equivalent to about one-fifth of global petroleum liquids consumption. The route is also critical to international liquefied natural gas trade.
Any sustained disruption could increase energy prices, raise shipping and insurance costs, and intensify inflationary pressure across economies far beyond the Middle East.
For Iran, the strategic attraction is clear. A threat to a vital maritime chokepoint can make the consequences of military escalation visible to governments, businesses and consumers around the world. The resulting economic pressure may complicate the calculations of states supporting military action against Tehran. It also forces regional governments to consider whether hosting foreign military forces could expose their own economies to retaliation.
But this leverage has limits. Disrupting the Strait of Hormuz would also damage Iran’s interests, aggravate economic hardship and alienate states that might otherwise favour diplomacy. Other countries could respond by strengthening maritime coalitions, expanding alternative supply arrangements or increasing military pressure on Iran. A tactic designed to internationalise the cost of war could therefore internationalise the opposition to Tehran.
Nor does economic pain necessarily translate into political concessions. Governments may absorb substantial costs if they believe their security or credibility is at stake. The assumption that higher energy prices or disrupted trade will compel Washington to retreat is no more reliable than the assumption that military strikes will automatically force Tehran to comply.
Iran’s widening battlefield is thus both a source of leverage and a mechanism of escalation. It raises the stakes for all parties, but it also increases the number of actors with reasons to intervene. The more regional commerce becomes an instrument of coercion, the harder it becomes to separate military confrontation from the wider economic order.
Why Strategic Denial Is Not the Same as Victory
Iran’s doctrine may be designed to make an adversary’s victory elusive, but it cannot guarantee that Tehran will emerge in a stronger position. The strategy depends on the credibility of its threats, the survival of enough military capability to carry them out and the willingness of its opponents to consider the potential costs before acting. Each condition can change during a conflict.
A sustained campaign could weaken Iran’s missile infrastructure, reduce its stockpiles and disrupt the command systems needed to coordinate retaliation. Regional partners could also become less willing or less capable of supporting Tehran if the costs of confrontation rise. Meanwhile, attacks on neighbouring states or commercial shipping could encourage closer security cooperation between Gulf governments, Washington and other external powers.
There is also a fundamental political problem. A doctrine built around imposing unacceptable costs can deter an adversary, but it can also reinforce the adversary’s belief that Iran must be contained through stronger military pressure.
If every attack is answered by a wider threat and every response produces another escalation, the logic of deterrence risks becoming a cycle of mutual insecurity.
This is where Iran’s strategic calculation becomes especially precarious. Preventing an opponent from claiming victory is a negative objective. It can obstruct an adversary’s plans, but it does not establish a stable political order or secure long-term economic recovery. For Tehran, a meaningful strategic outcome would require more than surviving a confrontation. It would require preserving national security, reducing the risk of renewed war and creating conditions in which economic reconstruction becomes possible.
The same distinction applies to Washington and Israel. Tactical success may weaken Iran’s military capabilities, but it cannot by itself resolve the political disputes that sustain the confrontation. If military action leaves both sides convinced that the other remains an intolerable threat, battlefield gains may simply postpone the next round of conflict.
A more durable outcome requires a credible path from deterrence to diplomacy. Crisis communication channels, arrangements to protect commercial shipping and verifiable agreements on the issues driving confrontation would not eliminate the rivalry. They could, however, reduce the risk that a local incident triggers a broader regional war. Such mechanisms matter precisely because neither side can reliably control every consequence of escalation.
Iran’s new doctrine should therefore be understood not as proof that Tehran can defeat a militarily superior opponent, but as an effort to make the exercise of that superiority politically and economically costly. Its success will depend on whether the threat of retaliation changes adversarial behaviour without provoking a response that leaves Iran more isolated and vulnerable.
Ultimately, the measure of success is not whether an adversary can be prevented from claiming victory. It is whether either side can achieve a political settlement that remains viable after the guns fall silent.
A doctrine that makes victory elusive may deter aggression. Without a credible path to peace, however, it can also make the next war harder to avoid.

articles.title: Ukraine sanctions Russian arms suppliers as Moscow ramps up attacks
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky imposed new sanctions on Russian citizens and companies helping produce ballistic missiles, aircraft, armored vehicles, and drones, the President’s Office announced on Oct. 24.
Included in the first sanctions list are 51 Russian citizens and 44 businesses producing and supplying raw materials, equipment, and tools used in long-range weapons like Iskander, Kalibr, Kh-101, and Kinzhal missiles.
A second sanctions list targets 32 Russian citizens and 35 companies involved in the production and supply chains of equipment and components used in Russia’s military-industrial complex.
"We are systematically identifying and imposing sanctions on enterprises involved in producing Russian ballistic missiles and other weapons. We are working to extend these sanctions to other jurisdictions," said Ukraine’s sanctions chief, Vladyslav Vlasiuk.
"Together, these measures should significantly weaken the Russian military-industrial complex's ability to produce weapons."
In particular, Ukraine targeted Russia's RUSAL Group, a key company involved in the production of military aircraft, armored vehicles, missile weapons, and drones. The company imported 150 million rubles ($1.8 million) worth of aluminum oxide between April 2024 and March 2025, which supplied Russia's military-industrial complex, the President's Office said.
The sanctions come as Russia ramps up its production of missiles and drones. Ukrainian intelligence (HUR) told Ukrainian media earlier this week that Russia produces some 10,000 drones per month and is currently stockpiling 700 ballistic missiles.
As Russia scales up arms production, attacks on Ukrainian cities, particularly Kyiv, have reached unprecedented levels. Civilian casualties are currently at levels not seen in over four years.
Last month, Russia killed at least 328 civilians and injured 2,105 — the deadliest September since the start of the full-scale invasion, and 85% higher than September 2025, the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine reported on Oct. 15.

articles.title: Xi’s Military Purges Make US Deterrence More Urgent
articles.body:
China’s top military command has been almost emptied out. Of the seven members chosen for the Central Military Commission in 2022, only Xi Jinping and one general remain active. Days before Xi met U.S. President Donlald Trump in Washington last month, Beijing formally expelled Gen. Zhang Youxia, Xi’s longtime ally and former top military deputy, and Gen. Liu Zhenli, the former chief of the Joint Staff Department.
We do not know why Xi is doing this or what he intends to do next. But the purge has further strengthened his hand over the military. Reuters reported that analysts see Xi’s grip on the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) as strengthened by the removal of senior commanders and their protégés even as the upheaval weakens near-term readiness. If Xi chooses to invade Taiwan, impose a blockade, or undertake another act of military aggression in the region, more of that decision now rests with him. We do not know whether he will. That freer hand adds risk.
The scale of the purge is extraordinary. The Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) found that 41 of the 47 officers who held three-star rank in 2022 or were promoted afterward had been purged or potentially purged. Of the 35 three-star generals and admirals Xi promoted beginning in 2020, 32 had been investigated and 29 had been purged or potentially purged. Across the PLA, roughly 52 percent of senior leadership positions have been affected.
CSIS concluded that vacant posts and less experienced officers would complicate large-scale operations against Taiwan, including a blockade or amphibious assault. But we should not assume those complications will last. Taiwan’s defense ministry has warned of “rising unpredictability” in Chinese decision-making amid the purge. With this much upheaval in Beijing and more authority concentrated in Xi’s hands, steady, credible deterrence from Washington matters even more. Beijing should have no reason to believe an invasion, blockade or other act of aggression against Taiwan could succeed.
That means three things.
First, we should not answer upheaval in Beijing by creating upheaval at the Pentagon. One of America’s greatest military advantages is our professional officer corps, whose duty is to the constitution rather than a ruling party. Yet in 2025, Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth removed Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. C.Q. Brown along with five other senior generals and admirals. In April, Hegseth abruptly removed Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George with more than a year remaining in his term while American forces were fighting in the Middle East. The Pentagon gave no public reason, and Reuters noted that removing a service chief during wartime is “extremely rare.” Experienced commanders who are prepared to give presidents unwelcome advice make our military stronger.
Second, our military resources have to match our priorities. The Iran war is draining weapons that matter for deterrence in the Indo-Pacific. In September, the Congressional Budget Office estimated that the war had cost the Defense Department about $38 billion through August 1, with another month costing $2 billion to $3 billion depending on the intensity of fighting. More importantly, CBO found that heavy use of missile-defense interceptors will leave U.S. inventories reduced for several years and warned that the shortfall would be especially problematic in a conflict with China over Taiwan. If we are serious about the CCP as our foremost long-term strategic challenge, we should end the Iran war and rebuild depleted stockpiles, immediately.
Third, deterrence requires communication as well as strength. After air and maritime safety talks in May, U.S. and Chinese military representatives agreed that better communication could reduce miscalculations and the risk of unsafe encounters. With this much turnover at the top of the PLA, those channels matter even more.
We do not know Xi’s objectives. We know he has strengthened his own hand amid the uncertainty created by his purge of the military. Without any meaningful check on his power, Xi has a freer hand to pursue potentially more aggressive military decisions, adding risk to our relationship with the CCP.
Our job is not to guess Xi’s next move. It is to make sure Washington remains steady, with experienced military leadership, the weapons and forces needed to deter aggression, strong alliances, and reliable communication to keep a crisis from becoming a war.

articles.title: US senators threaten to block Trump's nominees over Starlink restrictions in Ukraine – NYT
articles.body:
US senators threaten to block Trump's nominees over Starlink restrictions in Ukraine – NYT
US senators have warned the White House they will withhold their votes to confirm nominees until US President Donald Trump's administration secures the restoration of communications systems used by Ukrainian forces, The New York Times reports.
Source: The New York Times, citing sources
Details: According to three people familiar with the discussions, Republicans and Democrats in the Senate have told senior White House officials that they will block confirmation of Trump's nominees awaiting congressional approval until the administration restores critically important satellite communications capabilities used by the Ukrainian military.
The move, disclosed to the NYT by sources speaking on condition of anonymity because it has not yet been officially announced, will intensify bipartisan tensions over the White House's ever-more conciliatory approach towards Russia.
This will take place during the remaining congressional session scheduled for after the midterm elections, when Republicans are expected to try to confirm dozens of Trump's nominees before the current Congress's term ends.
The stance highlights growing divisions between the White House and Congress over Russia, with even senior Republicans showing increasing willingness to challenge Trump's policy positions. It also points to a possible shift after the midterm elections, when control of Congress could pass to the Democrats and lawmakers from both parties may be more resolute in using their leverage and oversight powers on the issue.
Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick, a Republican from Pennsylvania who is fighting to retain his seat in a highly contested district, has threatened to seek the dismissal of US officials responsible for the network disruptions as well as cuts to their departments' budgets. He said he doubts the problems were accidental.
A US Senate staff member told the NYT on condition of anonymity that the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations had approved several shipments of critical air defence interceptors that had still not been delivered to Ukraine, raising concerns about delays in aid already authorised by Congress.
Staff are also considering launching investigations into SpaceX in connection with the satellite disruptions and have asked companies involved in Russian diesel fuel transactions to retain documents in the event of possible congressional investigations, the source added.
Previously: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed on 23 October that speed restrictions for Starlink satellite communications terminals in Ukraine remain in force.
A bipartisan group of nearly 20 members of the US House of Representatives called on President Donald Trump to ask Elon Musk to give Ukraine access to Starlink systems to target missile launchers on Russian territory.
US Democratic Senator Chris Coons had previously contacted Elon Musk's SpaceX, asking the company to explain who had decided to restrict Starlink's operation in Ukraine and why.
Background:
- The Wall Street Journal reported that Elon Musk had ordered Starlink services to be slowed down. It is unclear to what extent Trump was involved in discussions about the slowdown.
- US Republican Senator Thom Tillis is seeking an investigation into the Pentagon's actions with regard to problems with Starlink satellite communications systems encountered by the Ukrainian Armed Forces.
- US House of Representatives member Joe Wilson and nearly two dozen of his colleagues prepared a letter calling for Ukraine to be permitted to use Starlink for strikes on launch sites within Russian territory.
- The Wall Street Journal, citing US and Ukrainian officials familiar with the matter, reported that Trump had called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on the military version of Starlink in Ukraine.
- On the evening of 22 October, Trump said Musk had already lifted speed restrictions on the military version of Starlink in Ukraine but declined to say whether he had personally called him about the issue.
- Ukraine's Defence Ministry said it was recording disruptions to Starlink and Starshield services on the line of contact.
