articles.title: Are Israel's drones signalling a new escalation with Hezbollah?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Are Israel's drones over Beirut signalling a coming escalation with Hezbollah?
Reports of increased Israeli drone activity over Beirut and its southern suburbs have raised questions about whether Israel is preparing for a new escalation against Hezbollah.
But while the flights have become more conspicuous in recent days, analysts told The New Arab that their presence alone does not establish that a wider offensive is imminent.
A report by local Lebanese news outlet Lebanon Files said Israeli reconnaissance flights had "returned" to Beirut and Mount Lebanon’s airspace. However, there is no publicly available evidence establishing that the flights had stopped before recently becoming more noticeable.
Israeli drones have continued to be reported over Beirut and its southern suburbs in recent months, including in reports published in September and footage circulated this week.
The question, therefore, is not simply whether the drones are present, but whether there has been a meaningful change in the frequency, duration or scope of their operations.
Surveillance and pressure on Hezbollah
Elijah J. Magnier, a veteran war correspondent and political analyst, told The New Arab that the activity should be taken seriously, while cautioning against treating visible drone flights as evidence of an imminent attack.
"Local reporting today documented a drone flying at low altitude over the southern suburbs. That establishes a visible presence; it does not, by itself, establish a sustained increase in surveillance or an imminent offensive," he said in comments to The New Arab on 21 October.
Magnier said Israeli drone flights could serve several purposes at once, including gathering intelligence, updating potential targets, monitoring movements and exerting psychological pressure on residents. A conspicuous presence over the capital can also serve as a reminder of Israel’s ability to strike south of Beirut.
If Israel were preparing another operation, surveillance could help it locate commanders, monitor weapons movements and identify suspected military infrastructure. But Magnier stressed that these remained possible objectives rather than evidence of a decision to launch an attack.
"Nor does identifying a target establish that a political decision to strike has been taken," he said. Without comparative flight data or intelligence about operational orders, he added, it was difficult to distinguish routine surveillance from preparations for a particular attack.
Nasser Khdour, an analyst at the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED), also said Israeli drone activity over Beirut was not new.
"Israel has continued gathering intelligence and identifying possible targets in preparation for another round of fighting," he told The New Arab.
Khdour suggested the more conspicuous drone presence was likely intended to increase pressure on Hezbollah and the Lebanese government during negotiations between Lebanon and Israel, with the Iran-backed militant group’s disarmament remaining a central point of disagreement.
The latest round of US-mediated military talks between Lebanese and Israeli delegations began in Tampa, Florida, on 20 October. The talks came amid continued Israeli attacks and demolitions in southern Lebanon, as well as renewed threats by Israeli officials against Hezbollah.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has warned Hezbollah against joining Iran in an attack on Israel, threatening a "powerful response" against Beirut’s southern suburbs, which would include a forced evacuation of the whole area. He has also threatened to expand the invasion towards Nabatieh and the Litani River in the south.
Hezbollah has refused to disarm as long as Israeli forces remain in Lebanon.
Could tensions with Iran draw Hezbollah into a wider war?
The risk of escalation also extends beyond Lebanon. With Israel’s general election scheduled for 27 October, renewed threats involving Iran have added another layer of uncertainty to the regional picture.
Magnier said electoral considerations were relevant to the analysis, but cautioned against presenting speculation about a war being launched for political reasons as an established plan. He said there was no publicly established evidence that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu intended to initiate a war to disrupt an election he expected to lose.
A renewed confrontation between Israel and Iran could, however, create a separate decision point for Hezbollah. Magnier said the group’s involvement would become a more serious possibility in such a scenario, but would remain a choice rather than an automatic consequence.
He also cautioned against assuming that Hezbollah’s weakened deterrence meant it had no remaining military capabilities. The group could seek to preserve its personnel and organisational structure while continuing to impose costs on Israel over time, rather than responding to every attack with a major escalation.
That calculation could change, he added, if civilian casualties mounted, senior leaders were targeted or Israel expanded its ground operations.
The conflict between Hezbollah and Israel began in October 2023 and was dramatically escalated by Israel into a full-scale war in September 2024. Fighting resumed on 2 March this year, alongside the US-Israeli war on Iran. Much of Hezbollah’s senior command structure has been eliminated over the past three years, and thousands of its fighters are believed to have been killed.
The drone flights therefore need to be viewed alongside the wider military and political context, rather than in isolation. Israel’s continued strikes, its threats against Beirut’s southern suburbs and the unresolved dispute over Hezbollah’s weapons all contribute to an already volatile situation.
For Magnier, the distinction remains between sustained pressure and a decision to launch a broader campaign. The visible presence of drones demonstrates Israel’s ability to monitor and threaten Hezbollah and its stronghold in Beirut's southern suburbs, but it does not reveal what Israeli leaders intend to do next.
"The drone flights show exposure and pressure. They do not yet tell us whether the next step will be surveillance, a targeted strike or a wider campaign," he said.

articles.title: How the upcoming U.S. and Israeli elections could lead to the third round of the Iran war
articles.body:
There is little doubt that the United States and Israel are about to renew the war on Iran that they started without provocation, or any real planning, back in February. The question is only about the timing.
In fact, by the time you read this, the war may have resumed in full force. More likely, though, it will be delayed until after the U.S. midterm elections. That will put it after Israel’s elections as well.
Israel may find itself with an entirely new leadership after its upcoming elections on October 27, which, while still seeing Iran as a hated enemy, might have different ideas about how to attack that enemy.
The United States is even more uncertain following the midterm elections on November 3. Donald Trump will remain president and free of electoral concerns, as he will not be allowed to run in the next election. But a Congress hostile to this war can make it harder for him to continue his current course. Conversely, an indecisive Congress unwilling to confront Trump on the war could unleash his worst tendencies.
Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu both have personal interests that the war might serve. Both could seek to undermine their country’s election results, and a war that escalates into a global economic crisis could give them the cover they need.
Iran and the Israeli election
Netanyahu has been pushing hard for a renewed war. In a public phone call with Trump, Netanyahu told him, “We have a job to finish.”
Beyond the bombast, there have been concrete actions. The United States and Israel have been busy drawing up plans for another attack on Iran even if it seems that Netanyahu is not content to wait as long as Trump wants him to.
Trump has repeatedly said that the U.S. would not attack Iran before the midterm elections. Given his history, there is no reason to take Trump at his word. To the contrary, Trump has repeatedly broken such promises, sometimes due to impulsiveness, sometimes because he lied intentionally to try to get Iran to drop its guard. Moreover, Trump has not said that he would continue to block Israel from attacking before the midterms.
But in this case, there is good reason to believe that Trump is telling the truth. Nothing is certain, but the United States is moving a considerable number of troops and a third aircraft carrier to the Gulf. By most accounts, they are slated to arrive in late November.
That works for Trump, but less well for Netanyahu.
For Trump, an escalation against Iran will be useful for months, from the election until the beginning of January, when the new Congress would be seated.
Netanyahu has less time.
The Israeli election will take place next week. Many analyses in the United States have misunderstood how a renewal of war affects Netanyahu’s position.
Had it happened a few weeks before the election, Netanyahu might have been able to postpone the election (which would require approval from 80 of 120 members of the Knesset), or sway some voters toward his camp. Now, with only a few days left, those prospects are very dim.
But an Israeli election is not like an American one where votes are cast, someone wins, and that’s supposed to settle the matter. Israel’s unstable coalition politics mean the real intrigue happens after the votes are counted, as the leaders of the top parties jockey for the right to form a coalition government.
Netanyahu is not going to win this election, according to almost every poll that has been conducted recently and since the beginning of the year. The parties that would join with his Likud coalition simply won’t have enough seats to form a majority unless a real miracle happens.
But the opposition, although in a better position, also doesn’t have a good chance of forming a majority coalition. Their only hope, which is not available to Netanyahu, is support from the parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up around 20% of the population.
But that is complicated. The opposition leader, Gadi Eisenkot, has vowed not to form a government with Arab parties. But he could form a government with less than a majority of seats by getting support from Arab parties outside the governing coalition.
That’s a fraught path in as racist a society as Israel’s. Even the non-nationalist, conservative United Arab List (called Ra’am) would trouble some of Eisenkot’s other coalition partners. And it is hard to imagine parties led by right-wing figures like Avigdor Lieberman or Naftali Bennett agreeing to a coalition that gets any support from the Joint List, which is much more representative of Palestinian national sentiment than Ra’am.
And even with Ra’am’s support outside the coalition, the opposition could still fall short of the 61 votes needed to form a government.
Netanyahu is counting on the opposition’s inability to form a coalition. If that should happen, Netanyahu can try to poach parties or even individual Knesset members from the opposition to reach a majority. That would be difficult, but possible.
Or he could simply ride the impasse to another round of elections, leaving him in charge of a caretaker government, the most likely scenario at present.
In either case, a hot war with Iran is a significant boon to Netanyahu.
Under the threat of Iranian missile attack, Netanyahu can make the case that Israel needs continuity to win the war, to stop Iran’s nuclear program, and all the other accusations Netanyahu will make. If polls don’t show he is gaining ground, he can also propose a national unity government, and a hot war will absolutely bolster that case.
Netanyahu needs the stalemate that comes with the opposition failing to form a government. Yet, if he gets it, and there are no Iranian or Hezbollah missiles raining down on Israel, his failings will only come under even more scrutiny, and he will stand even less chance in the next round of elections. So he needs a war even more than usual.
Netanyahu’s push for an early resumption of the war, against Trump’s preferences, was motivated by several factors.
First, given Trump’s indecisiveness and strong tendency to flip-flop, he wanted to lock in American support for renewing the war. Second, he wanted to refocus the war’s guiding principle on regime change, an idea he has been banging on in recent days but that has largely fallen out of favor in Washington, even among the most hawkish voices.
Finally, Netanyahu knows that the U.S. is planning a quick, impactful strike. He also knows this is almost certainly not going to happen, and he wouldn’t want it to. He wants prolonged engagement to maximize both his own political gains and the chances of stressing Iran to the point of threatening the Islamic Republic’s continued existence. Time is not on his side, as he knows that this may be his last chance to defeat Iran.
So, Netanyahu pushed to rekindle the war earlier this month, knowing that it would almost certainly last until well after Israel’s election.
Iran and the U.S. midterms
Trump is probably sincere about his desire to hold off the attack on Iran until after the midterms, but this is just another indication of how little he grasps the depths of his own failure.
The damage to the Republican chances in the midterms is done, and resuming the war on Iran won’t make things much worse. But, even more than with Netanyahu in Israel, the Republicans are about to take a beating at the ballot box. The only question is how bad it will be.
It is overwhelmingly likely that the Democrats will take back the House of Representatives, and they stand a good chance of taking the Senate as well. For Trump, even though he is not on the ballot, this will be a humiliating loss, and we have already seen how he reacts to such things.
This is where a renewed war on Iran comes in for him. Trump is sure to do all he can to throw the results of the election into doubt, and to stir up suspicions as he did in 2020. With a smaller base of support now than before, and no pandemic, he will need to sow even more chaos than he did then.
A war with Iran will do that for several reasons.
First, the war itself will be intense and will immediately send shock waves through the global economy.
But that will only be the start. Iran has been clear that it is going to respond more forcefully than before and that it will calibrate that response to the intensity of the American and Israeli attack.
Iran has warned that they will target data centers, which they know are important to Trump, as well as underwater fiber networks that are key to the internet. That will cause disruption across many different industries.
And that will be added to Iran’s targeting of Gulf energy infrastructure if the U.S. and Israel target theirs. They could also target civilian infrastructure, including desalination plants, which would devastate the entire region.
None of this will matter to Israel, which will see it as pressure on the Gulf Arab states to join in the war effort. Israel wants to see as much chaos as possible, because that is the road to the regime change in Iran they crave.
But Trump should be concerned about the potential crash of Gulf economies and the massive impact this will have on the entire world.
Crippling Gulf infrastructure will send oil prices soaring much higher than they already are. It will greatly expand the fertilizer-export crisis from the region and could further devastate the liquefied natural gas market. Global inflation could surge, and the measures used to date to keep prices from that kind of massive inflation are unlikely to be sufficient.
Yet the chaos it will cause in the United States might offer Trump an advantage in forestalling the seating of a new Congress, or increasing his opportunities to once again cast doubt on the election results.
These efforts are unlikely to get Trump what he wants. His base is too small, the country is more aware of this potential, and many of the foot soldiers Trump had six years ago now recognize that he betrayed and used them.
But an attack on Iran will succeed in causing global devastation, beginning in Iran itself, and quickly expanding outward.
Israel, too, is much more vulnerable than it was last time around. The protective ring of American installations and support from places like Saudi Arabia and Jordan in intercepting Iranian missiles and drones is severely diminished. Many American bases are gone, and the Americans stationed in the region have few interceptors left.
Israel has managed to save many interceptors of its own, having relied on American missiles against Iran. But even they had to use quite a few to defend against attacks from Lebanon. More to the point, because Iranian missiles will have a much clearer path to Israel than they did before, more missiles will be shot down above Israeli space, meaning more debris will fall on Israel, while more Iranian missiles are likely to get through Israel’s defenses since so many more will get into range.
Perhaps Trump is not thinking about how to use a war to undermine elections in the U.S. Maybe he is tired of losing the war and is desperately grasping at the idea that this time the bloodshed and destruction that have repeatedly failed will work.
That sad fact is the very definition of murderous insanity.

articles.title: Speed limits for Starlink, Starshield remain in effect – Zelenskyy
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that speed limits on SpaceX's Starlink satellite communication terminals and their military version, Starshield, remain in effect, creating problems for the Ukrainian military.
"The speed restrictions on Starlink and Starshield are still in place; speeds have not been restored, and the delivery of interceptors to defend against Russian ballistic missiles is still delayed. We are waiting for the interceptors that have already been agreed upon, but they still haven't arrived. We hope they're already on their way. And this is a real problem for us, since Russian attacks are happening almost daily – Russia is launching massive strikes. That's how the situation looks today," Zelenskyy said during an online meeting at the Hudson Institute on Friday.
According to him, this is happening while Ukraine continues its "fairly successful operations on the front lines" and continues to defend its positions. "The situation has become more complicated, partly due to the policies regarding Starlink and Starshield and the speed restrictions. But our front line is still holding, and we are doing everything possible to ensure our logistics continue to function, and we continue to defend ourselves," the president added.
At the same time, the head of state stated that he "truly wants our relations with America and all our other partners to be as strong as possible, genuinely friendly, and, of course, free of misunderstandings."
"After all, without America – without a strong America that cares about what's happening in the world – the world today would undoubtedly be a worse place. People ask why Ukraine is increasingly opening up and speaking directly to the world. The answer is simple: we want people to understand us-and by that I mean people, societies, nations, as many people as possible. And when people understand what is really happening, political leaders can choose a more decisive course – one that will truly bring us closer to peace. And peace is what we want more than anything else. And I hope that our conversation today will help people in America better understand our position and see what we can achieve through diplomacy," Zelenskyy said.
As previously reported, on the night of October 14, the Ukrainian military noted disruptions in the operation of Starshield terminals – the military version of the Starlink satellite communication system. According to Interfax-Ukraine sources in the Ministry of Defense, the terminals lost connection while moving at speeds exceeding a set threshold, which ranged from approximately 72 to 161 kilometers per hour depending on the equipment. This complicated the operations of interceptor drones and strike UAVs, as well as logistics, reconnaissance, and communications relay. The Ministry of Defense held consultations with the United States, SpaceX, and NATO partners and tested backup communication channels.

articles.title: US taxpayer money laundered back through Ukraine – Musk
articles.body:
US taxpayer money laundered back through Ukraine – Musk
Billionaire Elon Musk has accused US politicians of putting Kiev’s interests ahead of their own country’s, alleging that American taxpayer money sent to Ukraine is being laundered back into political campaigns.
Writing on X on Friday, the SpaceX founder suggested that financial interests could explain why some American lawmakers remain staunch supporters of Kiev in its conflict with Russia.
“Some of that US taxpayer money comes back through multiple laundry machines to fund political campaigns in America, which is why you see some politicians caring more about Ukraine than America!” Musk wrote, without identifying the beneficiaries.
And some of that US taxpayer money comes back through multiple laundry machines to fund political campaigns in America, which is why you see some politicians caring more about Ukraine than America!
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 23, 2026
In March, US outlet Just the News cited a declassified intelligence summary describing a plan to divert hundreds of millions of dollars in American aid earmarked for clean-energy projects in Ukraine into then-President Joe Biden’s 2024 reelection campaign.
Trump shared the report on Truth Social, while then-US intelligence chief Tulsi Gabbard reportedly asked officials at the US Agency for International Development (USAID) to investigate whether the alleged scheme had been carried out.
Musk also accused Ukrainian elites of profiting from Western assistance while ordinary Ukrainians bear the human cost.
“The former have grown very rich off the hundreds of billions flowing to Ukraine, while the latter’s children are conscripted to die in trenches,” he wrote.
Kiev’s increasingly coercive mobilization campaign has been marked by numerous documented cases of forced detentions and violent confrontations involving recruitment officers. Corruption investigations have also exposed schemes allowing wealthier Ukrainians to evade military service.
Ukraine has been rocked by major corruption scandals involving figures close to Vladimir Zelensky. One centered on his longtime associate Timur Mindich and an alleged $100 million bribery and money-laundering operation at state nuclear energy company Energoatom. The scandal forced senior officials from office, including former presidential chief of staff Andrey Yermak, while Mindich fled Ukraine.
Ukrainian investigators have also uncovered what they say is fraud to the tune of $5.6 million involving military drones purchased at prices up to 90% above market rates.
Even Kiev’s staunchest European backers have criticized its failure to deliver promised anti-corruption reforms, warning that billions of euros in assistance could be withheld.
Zelensky is seeking at least €70 billion ($81 billion) in additional foreign assistance for 2027, estimating Ukraine’s total conflict-related spending needs for next year at €155 billion.
European Council President Antonio Costa said on Friday that the EU expects to cover roughly two-thirds of the additional funding, or around €46.7 billion, with a decision potentially coming in November. That sum would come on top of the €45 billion already earmarked for Kiev next year.

articles.title: Kyiv's power ring under attack: why the capital faces a winter of blackouts
articles.body:
Kyiv's power ring under attack: why the capital faces a winter of blackouts
Hopes for a mild winter or inaccuracies in Russian strikes will not help Kyiv get through this winter without problems with its electricity supply. The only question is how long the power cuts will last and whether air defence forces and power engineers will manage to prevent the worst-case scenario.
The Russians are continuing their systematic attacks on Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast, seeking to completely destroy the city's combined heat and power plants and break the so-called power ring in order to plunge the capital entirely into darkness and cold.
The city has already lost a significant proportion of its own power generation capacity, while strikes are destroying substations through which electricity is supplied from other regions. In the event of severe frosts and further hits, a scenario involving 20 hours without electricity no longer seems far-fetched.
What is Kyiv's power ring, what risks does damage to it pose, and what should the capital's residents prepare for?
What is Kyiv's power ring?
This article does not disclose any sensitive information. The configuration of the power system is no secret to Russia, as Ukrenergo, Ukraine's state-owned electricity transmission operator, has warned. What does remain secret are the protection systems, equipment redundancy arrangements and power restoration procedures following attacks.
In the narrow technical sense, Kyiv's power ring is a system of high-voltage power lines and 330-kilovolt (kV) substations that connects the capital to Ukraine's integrated power grid and enables electricity to be transmitted to the city from different directions.
A key element of the capital's power supply is the 750 kV Kyivska substation, through which electricity from the Rivne and Khmelnytskyi nuclear power plants can be delivered to the capital.
Given their strategic importance, these facilities are under constant attack by Russian forces. The aim is to cut Kyiv off from Ukraine's integrated power grid and cause a blackout.
Put simply, the ring is a kind of road network for electricity. Transmission lines carry electricity to the capital, while substations step down its voltage and feed it into distribution networks for consumers.
If one section of this "road" is damaged by attacks, electricity flows can be rerouted through other lines. This helps maintain the power supply after damage occurs.
The ring is a critically important element of Kyiv's energy supply because the city consumes far more electricity than its own sources generate.
How much electricity does Kyiv consume, and why have power cuts begun?
Kyiv is the largest consumer of electricity in Ukraine. According to estimates by energy experts, the city consumes 1-1.2 GW, or 12-15% of the national total. In winter, depending on the temperature, demand can rise to 1.8-2 GW.
In 2025, before the large-scale winter attacks, local generation played a key role in supplying electricity to the city. According to sources at one of the energy companies who spoke to Ekonomichna Pravda, it may have accounted for as much as 1.3 GW. This came primarily from Kyiv CHP-5, CHP-6 and Darnytsia CHP (CHP-4) – combined heat and power plants (CHP plants) that produce both electricity and heat for the city's district heating network.
These plants are now no longer able to generate electricity. Nevertheless, all three CHPs were hit again by the Russians during the large-scale attack on the night of 13-14 October.
The capital is now forced to rely more heavily on electricity supplied from other regions via the power ring. The problem is, however, that its key components have been under constant attack for more than a month. Some of these attacks result in damage to equipment.
To cause significant problems, the Russians do not necessarily have to destroy the entire power ring. It is enough to damage a few critical nodes through which a large share of the electricity flows.
As a result, a situation may arise where there is electricity in the system, but the grids cannot transmit it to the capital in the required volume. If the city lacks its own power generation, the situation becomes even more complicated.
Under such conditions, dispatchers are forced to restrict consumption, including by introducing emergency or scheduled power cuts. This makes it possible to maintain a balance between available capacity and consumption and to prevent a large-scale failure in the power system.
The time needed for repairs depends on the extent of the damage. Some equipment can be repaired quickly. Replacing a large power transformer or other complex equipment may take longer, especially if the necessary equipment is not held in reserve.
Further complications are caused by repeat attacks, air-raid warnings being in effect for long periods, risks to repair crews and government attempts to reduce the proportion of energy company employees eligible for deferral from mobilisation. Following emergency repairs, the situation can deteriorate again, as strikes have been relentless lately and power workers face the risk of further attacks.
What to expect this winter
The main risk for Kyiv is a combination of three factors: low air temperatures, high consumption and Russian strikes that restrict the ability to transmit electricity to the capital. Given this combination, even fully functioning power generation in other regions does not guarantee that Kyiv will receive enough electricity, making various scenarios possible.
In a relatively favourable scenario, energy workers will repair damaged equipment and new strikes will not cause critical losses. In that case, restrictions may be moderate, although avoiding power cuts altogether will be difficult. For consumers, this would mean 8-10 hours without electricity per day.
If the attacks continue and some equipment remains damaged, Kyiv could face longer power cuts during moderately cold spells. Under this scenario, outages could last 12-16 hours per day.
The worst-case scenario involves regular large-scale strikes on key substations and other elements of the power system amid severe frosts. In that case, restrictions could last up to 20 hours per day. However, sources in the energy sector interviewed by Ekonomichna Pravda do not believe in a scenario in which the Russians would manage to destroy everything and "plunge Kyiv into darkness".
The consequences will depend on which facilities are damaged, how quickly they can be repaired and how much electricity can be transmitted to the capital.
A separate challenge is keeping critical infrastructure running, including water supply pumps, heating systems, transport, hospitals and communications.
Read also: No electricity means no water: an interview with the deputy CEO of water utility Kyivvodokanal
The capital needs approximately 200 MW of generating capacity for these purposes, primarily from combined heat and power units and high-capacity generators. According to Ekonomichna Pravda's sources, 150 MW of distributed generation has been brought into operation in Kyiv. By the end of 2026, this is expected to increase to 180-185 MW. Private facilities accounting for another 55-60 MW could become operational before winter, around half of which are already ready.
* * *
It is clear that protecting energy facilities critical to Kyiv from ballistic missiles depends primarily on the effectiveness of air defence. The engineering protection built at most substations can reduce the impact of individual strikes, but it cannot guarantee the survival of critical equipment after a direct hit.
Amid a shortage of missiles for Patriot systems, it is important to have the necessary amount of backup equipment, trained repair crews and clear action protocols for crisis situations.
Experience from previous winters shows that energy workers have learned to work under conditions of large-scale destruction. However, this does not cancel out the physical limitations of the grid and does not guarantee an uninterrupted electricity supply under every attack scenario.
Three things will be decisive for Kyiv this winter: how much electricity can be delivered to the city, how quickly energy workers can repair damaged equipment and whether backup generation can sustain critical facilities.
How long the power cuts last will depend on this. Kyiv can get through the winter without a collapse of its power supply, but it would be naive to expect the capital to avoid prolonged power outages if constant attacks continue.
By Mykola Topalov
Translated by Anna Kybukevych and Solomiia Shvak
Edited by Susan McDonald

articles.title: Beijing’s priority is peaceful coexistence between Iran and neighbors
articles.body:
Beijing’s priority is peaceful coexistence between Iran and neighbors
Majid Sharifi, an international affairs analyst, told the Iran newspaper that China’s approach toward Iran is not based on identity ties or ideological alignment. As a result, Beijing does not necessarily view stronger relations with Tehran as entering into confrontation with the United States.
 
China defines its ties with Iran within the broader network of its regional relationships and seeks to maintain balance among them. Therefore, the expansion of Tehran-Beijing relations cannot be explained solely by the intentions of the two sides or by existing opportunities for bilateral cooperation. From this perspective, one of the key prerequisites for deeper economic cooperation and stronger political relations is Iran’s achievement of peaceful coexistence and stable ties with neighboring countries. Such a situation could reduce the complexity of China’s strategic calculations and create more favorable conditions for expanding cooperation.
Kayhan: US not seeking negotiations
Kayhan addressed Trump’s unsuccessful effort to force Iran into submission through negotiations. The newspaper wrote that the confrontation between Iran and the United States spans four dimensions: military, economic resilience, diplomacy, and cognitive-psychological warfare. According to the article, the last of these has become the backbone of Washington’s strategy. It argued that the Trump administration, having failed to achieve its goals in reality, has relied heavily on psychological and influence operations. Recent US military movements, while appearing to signal war preparations, were portrayed as part of a broader strategy aimed at creating the illusion of diplomacy and inducing miscalculations among officials and the public. Referring to the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding and Washington’s repeated violations of its commitments, the paper argued that these experiences demonstrate that the United States is not genuinely interested in real negotiations or meaningful concessions.
Ettelaat: Short but intense
Ettelaat explored the possibility of another military confrontation in the Persian Gulf region. The newspaper argued that the previous round of conflict involving Iran, the United States, and Israel increased energy prices, accelerated global inflation, weakened Middle Eastern security, and placed significant pressure on Pentagon air defense stockpiles. Citing reports from The New York Times, it said that the United States and Israel have prepared plans to resume military operations against Iran after the US midterm elections in early November. According to the article, planning is underway for a short but highly intense operation. Some officials reportedly believe that another large-scale wave of attacks could push Iran’s economy toward crisis and force Tehran to make political concessions. Iranian officials, however, have stated that they are aware of such plans and are developing new targets and tactics in response. Tehran has also warned that any future conflict would not be brief and could extend to infrastructure in the region, including submarine internet cables and major Saudi oil facilities such as Aramco.
Hamshahri: Iran knows how to play the game
Hamshahri argued that the Islamic Republic, through its firm adherence to its principles, has sent a clear message to the White House that it does not trust the United States. According to the article, Trump and Netanyahu openly speak of weakening or destroying Iran, while soaring energy prices have become the main source of pressure on Trump. Rising oil prices have increased diplomatic activity by mediators seeking engagement with Tehran. The paper suggested that Munir’s recent visit was intended to help stabilize oil markets and provide political relief for Trump ahead of elections. Nevertheless, it argued that the united stance of Iran’s political leaders and senior military officials demonstrated that Tehran fully understands regional power politics. As a result, Munir reportedly left without achieving his objectives.
Sazandegi: America’s strategy through psychological warfare
Sazandegi examined remarks attributed to Trump regarding the possibility of Iranian attacks on cities such as Los Angeles and San Diego. The newspaper argued that, if the statements were accurately reported, they could serve several purposes. First, they may be designed to amplify perceptions of an Iranian threat among the American public and justify confrontational policies or potential military action. Second, they could help rally international allies, increase pressure on Iran, and strengthen support for containment policies. Third, the rhetoric may carry domestic electoral benefits, ranging from reducing voter dissatisfaction to boosting Republican candidates. The article also suggested that such statements could indirectly strengthen the political position of Netanyahu and his allies in Israel. According to Sazandegi, the success of this strategy depends on the credibility of the claims, developments on the ground, and public reaction. It concluded that Iran’s most effective response would be fact-based communication, active diplomacy, and efforts to prevent the country from being portrayed internationally as a threat.

articles.title: Pakistan can mediate between Washington and Tehran, but it cannot manufacture trust
articles.body:
When Field Marshal Asim Munir, Pakistan’s army chief, met Iranian leaders in Tehran last Tuesday, he heard a familiar message in a harder form. President Masoud Pezeshkian said Washington must lift sanctions and pressure before talks resume. Security chief Mohsen Rezaei said no enriched material would leave Iran. After Munir left, a Qatari delegation arrived, a reminder that Islamabad no longer carries this file alone.
The real test is not whether Pakistan can soften Tehran’s opening position. It is whether it can help two adversaries negotiate commitments neither believes the other will honour.
The Islamabad Memorandum, signed on 17 June, extended the ceasefire for 60 days and promised to reopen Hormuz and lift the US blockade. It also pledged oil-export waivers. By 8 July it had collapsed after Iranian strikes on commercial vessels and a US response, and Washington reinstated the blockade six days later. The lesson is not merely that signatures are cheap. The text allowed each side to claim a different meaning. Iran read a “best efforts” clause on passage as giving it some authority over the strait, while the two sides disagreed over the strait provisions from the start. No neutral body existed to say who was right.
Pakistan deserves credit for building a channel between enemies. Few governments can speak to Iran, keep close ties with Washington and engage the Gulf capitals. But access is not leverage.
Islamabad cannot lift American sanctions, settle the enrichment dispute or guarantee that armed actors across the region will respect a ceasefire.
Nor is Pakistan an uninvolved broker. It shares a border with Iran, depends on Gulf energy and is a party to the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, under which it has pledged to defend Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks hit Saudi infrastructure. A mediator that has promised to defend one side’s partner cannot claim neutrality. It can claim something narrower and more useful: both sides have reason to keep its channel open.
That is why Pakistan should narrow its ambitions. It should not chase a grand reconciliation. It should help build a process in which limited cooperation does not require either capital to trust the other’s intentions.
The core problem is credible commitment. Tehran sees sanctions, blockades and strikes as proof that American assurances are unreliable. Washington sees enrichment and regional military activity as proof that Iranian promises are. Each wants the other to move first. Reuters has reported Iranian officials saying Tehran is deliberately slowing talks to weaken President Trump before the November midterms. If so, deadlock is a strategy for some, not just a failure.
The strongest objection to mediation is therefore serious: Islamabad cannot change either side’s strategic calculation, and its ties to Washington and Riyadh complicate any claim to impartiality. Iran’s decision-making is also fragmented. Munir’s August visit followed a change in Iran’s military hierarchy, so an understanding with civilian officials could fail elsewhere.
Even so, neutrality is not the only measure of a useful intermediary. What matters is whether messages are conveyed faithfully, whether the channel is trusted and whether steps can be independently checked.
A modest agenda would start at sea. Agreed procedures for reporting attacks on shipping, exchanging operational notices and investigating alleged violations would not need a nuclear settlement. But Iran’s claim to administer the strait is a sovereignty question, not an incident-management one. The June memorandum left the strait’s future administration to Iran in consultation with Oman and other Gulf states. That question must be put on the table, with partners such as Oman, which has facilitated US-Iran channels before, rather than papered over with vague wording.
The second track should pair reciprocal, time-limited steps. The June memorandum already linked the strait to sanctions waivers, so the difference this time must be design: smaller steps, explicit sequencing, reversibility and no side surrendering its main leverage on a promise.
The nuclear file needs different machinery. Iran’s refusal to export its stockpile and Washington’s demand for limits are substantive disagreements, not misunderstandings. The IAEA can verify agreed limits, but it cannot invent the bargain or inspect without a legal basis and access. Reports of a Qatari–Pakistani proposal linking inspections to interest on frozen funds rest on anonymous sources, and an Iranian parliamentary spokesman described Munir’s trip as bilateral only. Still, they point in the right direction: link access to relief.
READ: After Mecca, why Badr? Because this pact builds, not binds
Any new arrangement should specify who verifies compliance, how disputed incidents are judged and what happens after a breach. A joint implementation group with independent technical expertise could set deadlines, document performance and resolve accusations before they trigger retaliation.
Pakistan should also resist competing for credit. Qatar is already a co-mediator, and Oman has long experience with Gulf security channels. The goal is an effective process, not Pakistani ownership of it.
None of this guarantees peace. If either government believes time or escalation favours it, the best verification system will sit unused. Regional actors can also wreck understandings reached in negotiating rooms.
For the world, the stakes are tangible. Threats to Gulf shipping unsettle energy markets and raise costs for households and importers everywhere. For Pakistan, the danger is closer still.
Islamabad has shown it can bring adversaries toward an agreement. The harder, less theatrical task is helping them build one that survives the next crisis. Pakistan can open the door to diplomacy. It cannot supply the trust Washington and Tehran lack. What it can help supply is a system that makes cooperation possible without it.
The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Monitor.

articles.title: Iran slams IAEA for silence towards attacks on its sites
articles.body:
The statement criticized the IAEA for applying double standards and discriminatory approaches, emphasizing that the Statute is a binding legal document and must not be used as a political instrument to serve the interests of certain powerful states.
Iran also condemned the unacceptable silence of the Agency’s governing bodies regarding the military attacks by the US and the Zionist regime on its peaceful nuclear facilities in 2025 and 2026. Furthermore, it highlighted the IAEA's failure to address the lack of comprehensive safeguards on the Zionist regime’s nuclear activities.
The Islamic Republic also called for the full, balanced, and non-discriminatory implementation of the IAEA Statute for all member states, particularly regarding technical cooperation and access to peaceful nuclear energy.
The full text of statement by the Iranian permanent mission in Vienna is as follows:
Permanent Mission of the Islamic Republic of Iran  
  
to the United Nations and other International Organizations in Vienna 
 
PRESS RELEASE  
   
On the Anniversary of the Approval of the IAEA Statute   
   
23 October 2026  
   
Seventy years after the adoption of the Statute of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) 
 
on 23 October 1956, a fundamental assessment is required as to the level and extent of the 
 
adherence to the principles and objectives of the Agency’s founding document. 
This anniversary must therefore be more than an occasion for commemoration; it must serve as 
 
a moment of critical reflection, institutional accountability and a renewed commitment to the full, 
 
impartial and non-discriminatory implementation of the Statute. 
The Statute: A Binding Mandate, Not a Political Instrument
The continued relevance of the IAEA Statute lies in the objective it establishes and the principles 
 
it enshrines. It implementation over the past seven decades has produced achievements in 
 
important areas. However, the failure to implement it fully, consistently, effectively and without 
 
discrimination, under all circumstances and with respect to all Member States, has caused the 
 
Agency to drift away from its core objective and priorities, undermine the principles governing its 
 
conduct, compromise its professionalism, and tarnish its authority and credibility. 
The undeniable fact is that the Statute is the Agency’s constitution, not a document to be invoked 
 
selectively or interpreted according to the interests of powerful States or a group of States. 
Beyond Safeguards: Upholding the IAEA’s Full Statutory Mandate
Article II establishes the Agency’s fundamental objective: to accelerate and enlarge the 
 
contribution of atomic energy to peace, health and prosperity throughout the world. Article III.A.1 
 
requires the Agency to encourage and assist research, development and the practical application 
 
of atomic energy for peaceful purposes. Article III.B.3 further requires the Agency to allocate its 
 
resources efficiently to achieve the greatest possible general benefit, with due regard to the special 
 
needs of developing countries. 
While safeguards are part of the IAEA’s mandate, the Agency is not merely a “watchdog” 
 
organization, as some Member States, in contravention of the Statute, seek to portray it. Such a 
 
narrow and politically motivated characterization distorts the Agency’s mandate and shifts its 
 
priorities away from its broader statutory objective that is the promotion of peaceful nuclear 
 
applications and international scientific and technical cooperation. Verification must not eclipse 
 
peaceful nuclear cooperation, development and the legitimate rights of Member States. An Agency 
 
that concentrates on scrutiny while failing to advance its key statutory responsibilities cannot claim to be fulfilling its mandate in a balanced manner.
Sovereign Equality Cannot Coexist with Double Standards
Article IV.C expressly establishes that the Agency is based on the sovereign equality of all its 
 
members and requires them to fulfil their statutory obligations in good faith. Article III.C prohibits 
 
the Agency from making assistance subject to any political, economic, military or other conditions 
 
incompatible with the Statute. Article III.B.1 requires the Agency to conduct its activities in 
 
accordance with the purposes and principles of the United Nations, while Article III.D requires 
 
due observance of the sovereign rights of States. 
These provisions are neither optional nor subordinate to geopolitical calculations. Sovereign 
 
equality requires that every State be treated fairly and without discrimination under the legal 
 
instruments applicable to it, free from double standards, selective interpretation and politically 
 
motivated action. 
A clear example is the continuing disparity between the scrutiny applied to Iran and the absence 
 
of comprehensive safeguards covering all nuclear activities of the Israeli regime, which remains 
 
outside the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. This disparity raises 
 
fundamental questions about the credibility and consistency of the international nuclear non-
 
proliferation norms. A credible, comprehensive and non-discriminatory approach to nuclear 
 
verification throughout the Middle East is a legitimate demand and a longstanding objective of 
 
regional countries that are parties to the NPT. Regional security cannot be built on selective 
 
scrutiny and unequal expectations. 
Peaceful Nuclear Cooperation: A Right, Not a Political Privilege
Peaceful nuclear cooperation must not be subject to political pressure. Article III.C of the Statute 
 
is clear: assistance must not be subjected to conditions incompatible with the Agency’s legal 
 
mandate. Political pressure and geopolitical rivalries must not obstruct legitimate scientific 
 
cooperation or turn access to peaceful nuclear technology into a privilege reserved for selected 
 
countries. The Agency is expected to defend the integrity of its technical cooperation mandate 
 
and ensure that its programs serve the development needs of all Member States fairly and without 
 
discrimination. 
Attacks on Nuclear Facilities and Unacceptable Institutional Silence
Attacks on safeguarded nuclear facilities demand strong and unequivocal condemnation. The 
 
military attacks by the U.S. and the Israeli regime against Iranian nuclear facilities in 2025 and 2026 constituted serious and material breaches of peremptory norm of international law on the 
 
prohibition of aggression.  They presented a grave challenge to nuclear safety, nuclear security, 
 
peaceful uses of nuclear energy, the credibility of the IAEA and its safeguards system.  
The Agency’s General Conference and Board of governors has repeatedly adopted resolutions 
 
expressly stating that armed attacks on, or threats against, nuclear facilities devoted to peaceful 
 
purposes violate the principles of the UN Charter, international law and the Agency’s Statute. 
 
Nevertheless, the Agency’s governing bodies and Secretariat failed to issue even a simple statement to condemn clear acts of aggression against Iran’s nuclear facilities – unprecedented in the Agency’s history. This failure represents a serious institutional shortcoming and raises troubling questions about the consistent application of the principles the Agency is mandated to uphold. 
The Agency cannot credibly defend the integrity of safeguards while treating attacks against 
 
facilities subject to those safeguards as a secondary concern. The Agency must therefore 
 
unequivocally reaffirm that attacks against peaceful nuclear installations are unlawful and 
 
unacceptable and must not be tolerated under any pretext.
Safeguarding the IAEA’s Independence, Integrity and Confidentiality Principle
Independence, confidentiality and professional integrity must be protected. Article VII.F of the 
 
Statute prohibits the Director General and Agency staff from seeking or receiving instructions 
 
from external sources. It also requires the protection of confidential information acquired in the 
 
course of their official duties and obliges Member States to respect the international character of 
 
their responsibilities and refrain from seeking to influence them improperly. 
These are concrete institutional safeguards, not ceremonial principles. Reports, assessments and 
 
decisions must be based on verifiable evidence, sound technical analysis and applicable legal 
 
obligations—not political demands, unsupported allegations or selective approaches. Any breach 
 
of confidentiality or attempt to instrumentalise safeguards information undermines cooperation, 
 
erodes trust and may compromise the safety and security of nuclear activities. The Agency must 
 
address credible concerns, protect sensitive information and ensure accountability. 
Restoring the IAEA’s Credibility: From Selective Implementation to Full Compliance
Cooperation must be matched by institutional responsibility. Iran recognises the importance of 
 
credible safeguards and professional verification and remains committed to engagement within 
 
the framework of its applicable legal obligations and its inherent and sovereign rights and interests. 
However, cooperation requires good faith, mutual respect, professional integrity and the 
 
consistent implementation of agreed legal commitments.  
On this anniversary, Iran calls upon Agency, particularly the Board of Governors and the Director 
 
General to end double standards, resist politicisation, protect confidential information, condemn 
 
attacks against peaceful nuclear facilities, and restore the full and balanced implementation of the 
 
Agency’s statutory mandate. Iran also calls for an effective and non-discriminatory technical 
 
cooperation policy that enables all Member States, particularly developing countries, to benefit 
 
from nuclear science and technology. 
The Agency’s credibility cannot rest solely on its authority to inspect. It depends equally on its 
 
adherence to the law, its impartiality, its independence and its willingness to uphold the legitimate 
 
rights of all its members. 
The Statute must be implemented as a whole, equally and in good faith—not selectively, not 
 
conditionally and not according to political convenience. The Agency owes this obligation to every 
 
Member State. On the seventieth anniversary of the Statute’s adoption, the Agency is expected to 
 
honour letter, spirit, object and purpose of the Statute through concrete action, not merely words, 
 
and to uphold its principles without political selectivity, discrimination or exception. 
MNA
Seventy years after the adoption of its Statute, the IAEA’s credibility rests on upholding its Statute 
 
in full, serving all Member States equally, and demonstrating that international law and statutory 
 
principles cannot be sacrificed to political convenience.

articles.title: Iran calls for end to double standards in IAEA’s implementation of its statute
articles.body:
Iran urges end to double standards in IAEA’s implementation of its statute
TEHRAN — Iran has called on the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to end the selective and politically motivated implementation of its founding statute, urging the organization to uphold its legal obligations impartially and ensure equal treatment of all member states.
In a statement issued on Friday, October 23, to mark the 70th anniversary of the adoption of the IAEA Statute, Iran’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations and other international organizations in Vienna stressed that the agency’s founding document must be implemented fully and consistently, without discrimination or political interference.
The mission said the anniversary should serve not merely as an occasion for commemoration but as an opportunity to assess the agency’s adherence to its founding principles, restore institutional accountability and renew its commitment to impartiality.
“The Statute is the Agency’s constitution,” the statement said, emphasizing that it must not be invoked selectively or interpreted according to the interests of powerful states.
The IAEA’s full mandate
Iran stressed that the agency’s responsibilities extend beyond nuclear safeguards and verification to include promoting the peaceful use of nuclear energy and advancing international scientific and technical cooperation.
Citing Articles II and III of the Statute, the mission said the IAEA is mandated to expand the contribution of atomic energy to global peace, health and prosperity, support peaceful nuclear research and applications, and ensure that its resources benefit all member states, with particular attention to the needs of developing countries.
The statement warned that an approach focused disproportionately on inspections, at the expense of technical cooperation and peaceful nuclear development, would undermine the agency’s ability to fulfil its mandate in a balanced manner.
Sovereign equality and NPT
The Iranian mission said the principles of sovereign equality and non-discrimination must guide the agency’s dealings with all members, regardless of geopolitical considerations.
It cited Article IV.C, which establishes the sovereign equality of the agency’s members, and Article III.C, which prohibits making assistance conditional on political, economic or military considerations incompatible with the Statute.
As an example of a discriminatory approach, Iran pointed to the scrutiny of its nuclear activities alongside the absence of comprehensive IAEA safeguards covering all nuclear activities of Israel, which is not a party to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT).
The mission said this disparity raised questions about the consistency and credibility of international nuclear non-proliferation efforts, calling for a comprehensive and non-discriminatory verification framework across the Middle East.
It added that regional security could not be built on selective scrutiny and unequal expectations, stressing that all relevant legal obligations must be applied fairly.
Iran also called for the agency to protect the right of all member states to benefit from peaceful nuclear technology and scientific cooperation.
Independence and institutional credibility
Iran further emphasized the importance of safeguarding the IAEA’s independence, professional integrity and confidentiality.
Referring to Article VII.F of the Statute, the mission said the agency’s director general and staff must remain free from external instructions, while sensitive information obtained in the course of their duties must be protected.
It maintained that the agency’s reports, assessments and decisions should be based on verifiable evidence, sound technical analysis and applicable legal obligations rather than political pressure or selective interpretations. Any misuse of confidential information, it added, could undermine trust and compromise nuclear safety and security.
Reaffirming the importance of credible safeguards and professional verification, Iran said it remained committed to engagement within the framework of its applicable legal obligations and its sovereign rights and interests.
However, the mission stressed that meaningful cooperation required good faith, mutual respect, professional integrity and the consistent implementation of legal commitments.
It called on the IAEA, particularly its Board of Governors and director general, to end double standards, resist politicization, protect confidential information, condemn attacks against peaceful nuclear facilities and restore the full implementation of its statutory mandate.
The mission also urged the agency to pursue an effective, balanced and non-discriminatory technical cooperation policy, enabling all member states, especially developing countries, to benefit from nuclear science and technology.
Concluding its statement, Iran said the IAEA’s credibility depended not only on its authority to conduct inspections but also on its impartiality, independence, respect for international law and commitment to the legitimate rights of all members.

articles.title: Zelenskyy imposes sanctions on Russian missile manufacturers and military industry suppliers
articles.body:
Zelenskyy imposes sanctions on Russian missile manufacturers and military industry suppliers
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has enacted two decisions by the National Security and Defence Council imposing sanctions on Russian companies and individuals involved in the production of ballistic and cruise missiles, drones, military aircraft and other weapons.
Source: President's Office
Details: The first sanctions list includes 51 individuals and 44 legal entities involved in the production and supply of components for Iskander, Kalibr, Kh-101 and Kinzhal missiles.
They include the G.S. Petrov Institute of Plastics, the Kometa Corporation for Special-Purpose Space Systems, VitaReaktiv, Promenergo and other companies in Russia's military-industrial complex.
The second package covers 32 Russian nationals and 35 Russian companies that supply high-precision industrial equipment, electronics, raw materials and components used to manufacture missiles, drones, armoured vehicles and military aircraft.
Sanctions have also been imposed on companies belonging to the RUSAL group, whose products, according to the President's Office, are used in the production of Russian weapons.
The President's Office said it would work with international partners to synchronise these sanctions.
