articles.title: Interview: Stratonex wants to bring Ukraine’s innovation loop to Britain
articles.body:
- British company Stratonex Defence Technologies is developing the VARAN unmanned ground vehicle, which has completed initial mobility and remote-operation testing but is not yet operationally ready.
- Co-founder Ben Everitt told The Defence Blog that Ukrainian feedback pushed Stratonex to prioritize affordable unmanned logistics over autonomy.
British defense technology company Stratonex Defence Technologies is developing a range of unmanned ground vehicles, tactical drones, counter-drone systems and military mobility platforms, with a focus on reducing the exposure of personnel to battlefield threats.
The company’s VARAN unmanned ground vehicle is among its central projects. The platform has undergone initial mobility and remote-control testing, but further engineering and integration work is required before it can be considered ready for operational deployment.
In an interview with The Defence Blog, Stratonex co-founder Ben Everitt discussed the development of VARAN, the company’s relationship with technology partners, its approach to manufacturing and the challenges of moving military hardware from prototypes into serial production.
Everitt also outlined the company’s plans for 2027, including closer cooperation with British manufacturers, universities and military operators. He described lessons drawn from Ukrainian battlefield innovation and explained why Stratonex is placing increasing emphasis on connecting ground vehicles, aerial drones, sensors and other technologies into integrated mission systems.
The following interview is presented in full, with the interviewee’s answers reproduced without editorial changes.
Q: Stratonex Defence Technologies is entering a market where established defense contractors and smaller technology companies are competing to develop autonomous military systems. What specific technological or industrial gaps are you seeking to address, and how does your business model differ from that of traditional defense manufacturers?
A: I think you have to start with what’s actually happening on the battlefield, because it’s changing incredibly quickly.
The traditional idea of a frontline is becoming increasingly meaningless. What you’ve really got is a contested kill zone, potentially 20 kilometres or more either side of the line, where drones, sensors and precision weapons mean that if you can be seen, you can potentially be targeted.
So that’s the problem we’re building Stratonex around. How do you operate in that environment without unnecessarily putting people in it?
That’s where the product set starts to make sense. We’ve got unmanned systems that can move equipment, sensors and other capabilities into that space. Then we’ve got fast, stealthy, relatively inexpensive mobility platforms for those occasions when people do need to go into it and need to get back out again quickly.
The phrase we’ve started using is: keep the humans in the kill chain, but out of the kill zone. I really like it because it sums up what we’re trying to do.
The other thing that’s really struck me is the speed at which all of this is changing. I was recently out in eastern Ukraine, near the frontline, in a car with the manager of a UGV factory. His phone goes and it’s a battalion commander on the frontline who is using his vehicles. He’s basically saying, “This works, this doesn’t, and this is what I want the next batch to do.”
I remember thinking: this is extraordinary. You’re watching the innovation loop happening in real time. The customer is on the battlefield and the factory manager is taking the next requirement directly from him.
Obviously we’re operating in a very different environment in Britain, but that sense of pace and urgency is something we really want to capture at Stratonex. We’re not trying to recreate a traditional defence prime. We want to be agile, work with really good technology partners and get really, really cool technology integrated and into the hands of operators quickly.
Q: Stratonex has presented a portfolio spanning unmanned ground vehicles, tactical aerial systems and counter-UAS technologies. How much of this portfolio is being developed internally, and what role do technology partnerships, licensing arrangements and third-party integration play in bringing these products to market?
A: It’s deliberately a mixture. I don’t think there’s any great virtue in saying that every nut, bolt, sensor and line of code has to have been invented inside the same building.
There are technologies and IP that sit within Stratonex, and then there are areas where we work with partners, licence technology or integrate specialist systems developed by other people.
And that’s exciting, because there is some really, really cool technology being developed by smaller companies in Britain and elsewhere. The problem is often not the technology. It’s getting it integrated, tested, manufactured and ultimately bought.
That’s where I think Stratonex can add a lot of value. We can start with the operational problem and ask: what’s the best combination of platform, sensor, communications, autonomy and payload to solve it?
We’re quite deliberately technology-agnostic about that. If somebody has already invented a brilliant sensor, I don’t want to spend three years and a fortune inventing another one just so we can put our badge on it. I’d rather work with them, integrate it and get the capability out there.
Q: VARAN is presented as a modular unmanned ground vehicle capable of operating in GNSS-denied environments using passive 3D sensing and onboard autonomous navigation. How mature is this technology today, what capabilities have been demonstrated during physical testing, and what engineering challenges remain before the platform can be considered operationally ready?
A: VARAN is a real vehicle. We’ve built it, driven it, tested it and spent quite a lot of time getting it muddy, which is the fun bit.
But we’re also careful not to pretend that having a really good prototype is the same thing as having a fully operationally proven military system. There is still engineering, integration and testing to do.
We’ve demonstrated the fundamental mobility of the platform, remote operation and elements of the sensing and navigation architecture. The next phase is about making all of that increasingly robust across different terrain, payloads, communications environments and operational conditions.
What’s been particularly interesting is the feedback we’ve had from Ukraine. We started out, naturally enough, being really enthusiastic about the autonomy. It’s technically fascinating and there are some really cool things you can do with it.
But the Ukrainians keep bringing us back to something much simpler: the really important thing is that it’s unmanned.
If you can remotely drive ammunition, water, batteries or other equipment those last few kilometres instead of putting people in a vehicle and sending them into the kill zone, you’ve already achieved something incredibly valuable.
So we’re still developing the autonomy, absolutely. But we’re not developing autonomy because autonomy happens to be fashionable. We’re developing the capabilities operators actually want.
Q: Published information describes VARAN as a multi-mission platform capable of carrying reconnaissance, electronic warfare and counter-UAS payloads. How does the vehicle’s modular architecture accommodate different power, communications and payload requirements, and which mission configurations have progressed beyond the design stage?
A: This is one of my favourite things about VARAN because you can get terribly technical about modularity, power, data and payload integration, and I have a tendency to do exactly that.
We took VARAN away for a weekend of testing and filming with a group of former Special Forces guys who our Chairman, Major General John Holmes, knows.
I’m there waving my arms around getting incredibly enthusiastic about all the clever things we can do with it. We can forward-deploy surveillance drones on it. We can remotely recharge them. We can put different sensors and payloads on it. We can use it as part of a much wider unmanned system. All really, really cool stuff.
And the former SAS guys basically looked at it and said: “Yeah, but we can chuck all our kit on that and it’ll carry it for us.”
And they’re absolutely right.
Sometimes the simplest use case is the best one. Logistics is the backbone of successful warfighting. If VARAN can carry the heavy stuff while the operator concentrates on doing his job, that’s incredibly useful.
It also goes back to what the Ukrainians have been telling us. Sometimes we get very excited about the word “autonomy” when the thing the soldier really values is the word “unmanned”.
That’s why modularity matters. VARAN isn’t supposed to be one exquisite vehicle designed around one exquisite mission. The base platform gives you mobility, power and communications and then we can configure it around what the operator actually needs, whether that’s logistics, surveillance, EW, counter-UAS or something we haven’t thought of yet.
Q: VisionWave announced a conditional $20 million purchase order for 200 STRATUM VARAN vehicles in September 2026. What role does Stratonex play in the development, integration and potential production of these vehicles, and what milestones must be achieved before the programme moves into manufacturing and customer deliveries?
A: VisionWave is an important partner of ours and we have a distribution agreement with them, but they are a completely separate company, so I don’t really want to speak for them or get into the detail of their commercial announcements.
What I can talk about is what we’re doing with VARAN.
Our focus is on continuing to develop the platform, testing it, integrating different capabilities and getting it ready for manufacture at scale. And that’s a really exciting challenge in itself.
As I said earlier, the defence technology world is actually pretty good at producing prototypes. The difficult bit is getting from prototype to procurement and then into repeatable, affordable production.
That’s what we’re concentrating on. Making VARAN faster, tougher and more useful, testing it properly, listening to operators and making sure that when demand comes we can actually build the thing at meaningful volume.
Ultimately, I’d much rather be judged on the vehicles we build and deliver than the numbers in a press release.
Q: Moving from prototypes and technology demonstrations to serial production remains a major challenge for emerging defense companies. How is Stratonex addressing manufacturing scalability, supply-chain resilience, unit costs and long-term maintenance, and what production capacity do you realistically expect to achieve?
A: Price really matters to us, particularly with VARAN.
Its three big advantages are its price point, speed and durability. It’s more cost-effective than the heavier platforms in this space, it’s fast and agile, and it’s designed to take punishment.
And you have to be realistic about why the price point matters. These things are going into war zones. At some point some of them are going to get blown up.
One Ukrainian battalion commander put it brilliantly when we were talking about equipment: “If you can make it out of wood, make it out of wood.”
That’s obviously an exaggeration, but there’s a really important philosophy behind it. Don’t add cost and complexity unless they actually give the operator something useful.
There’s a tendency in defence to make everything exquisite. But if making something twice as expensive only makes it ten per cent more capable, and you’re operating in an environment where you’re going to lose platforms anyway, that’s not necessarily a good trade.
So we’re designing around manufacturability, modular components, repairability and supply-chain resilience from the start. We don’t want to build a vast Stratonex factory and manufacture every component ourselves. We’d much rather work with established manufacturing partners and scale production as demand develops.
That’s also why durability and field repair matter. Make it tough. Make it repairable. Make it affordable enough that commanders are actually prepared to use it.
Q: Beyond VARAN, your portfolio includes the D-FLY counter-UAS interceptor and TALON tactical unmanned aircraft. What technical or operational capabilities are you prioritising in these programmes, and can you share any previously undisclosed details concerning prototypes, testing results, new configurations or upcoming product introductions?
A: Again, I think it makes more sense if you look at the portfolio through the kill-zone problem rather than looking at each product individually.
You’ve got this 20-kilometre-plus contested space. So how do I see into it? How do I move equipment through it? How do I operate inside it without unnecessarily exposing people? How do I counter the drones that are creating part of the threat?
VARAN answers part of that. TALON answers another part through tactical aerial capability. D-FLY tackles the counter-UAS problem, including the really important question of cost exchange.
And then you’ve got the mobility platforms, which I think are fascinating. E-bikes and e-scooters might look slightly odd sitting next to drones and UGVs until you think about the operational problem. If somebody does have to enter that kill zone, you want them moving quickly and quietly with as little signature as possible.
That’s the common thread.
What gets me really excited now is joining those things together. A UGV shouldn’t just be a UGV and a drone shouldn’t just be a drone. How do the platforms, sensors, communications and effectors start working together as one mission system?
That’s where I think some of the really, really cool stuff is going to happen.
Q: Looking ahead to 2027, which developments do you expect to define Stratonex’s next phase of growth? Are there any new programmes, industrial partnerships, customer agreements or technological milestones that you are prepared to announce or discuss in greater detail with The Defence Blog readers?
A: There’s loads going on and I’m genuinely really excited about 2027.
Obviously there’s the product side. VARAN will continue developing, we’ve got other products coming through, and we’re increasingly interested in what happens when you connect all these different capabilities together rather than thinking about a UGV, a drone or a sensor in isolation.
But the bigger idea we’re working on is what I’d describe as on-shoring the innovation loop.
That comes directly from what I’ve seen in Ukraine. I keep going back to that phone call in the car between the battalion commander and the factory manager. Operator feedback, engineering, testing and production are happening incredibly close together. That’s one of the reasons they are innovating at such extraordinary speed.
We’re obviously not going to recreate the circumstances that have driven that in Ukraine, but we absolutely can learn from it.
So how do we build our own version of that loop here in Britain? How do we bring operators, engineers, SMEs, manufacturers and academia much closer together, so that an operational problem can become an engineering problem, become a prototype, get tested, generate feedback and go around the loop again quickly?
That’s why we’re looking at academic partnerships as well as product-development partnerships. Universities bring extraordinary engineering expertise, research capability, testing facilities and, importantly, really bright people. Industry brings products, manufacturing and commercial pace. Then you need the operator constantly feeding reality back into the process.
For me, that’s potentially much bigger than any individual product.
Britain doesn’t have an innovation problem. There is some really, really cool technology being developed here. The challenge is connecting it, testing it against real requirements, iterating quickly and then actually manufacturing it.
If we can help build that ecosystem around Stratonex, shorten the distance between the operator saying “I need this” and somebody putting a working solution in their hands, then I think we’ve got something genuinely exciting.
That’s a big part of where I want us to go in 2027: on-shore the innovation loop, build sovereign capability and keep turning really good British technology into things that operators can actually use.
And all of it still comes back to the same mission: keep the humans in the kill chain, but out of the kill zone.

articles.title: Xi Jinping May Have His Own Reasons to Avert a China-Russia-US Summit
articles.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin have put Xi Jinping in an unusual position by expressing interest in a trilateral summit with the Chinese leader at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen mid-November. Xi’s cautious response so far – Moscow and Washington have confirmed discussion, while Beijing has yet to commit publicly – could help Europe and Ukraine avoid the worst: major powers making decisions about the region in their absence.
The idea for a meeting came from Russia and it’s not hard to see why. Moscow’s ideal outcome would reportedly be a “Yalta-style” agreement on Ukraine, echoing the 1945 conference at which the United States, the United Kingdom, and the Soviet Union discussed the post-war order in Europe. But even much more modest results would count as a success. Simply taking part in such a summit would elevate Russia’s status alongside the U.S. and China, help break its diplomatic isolation, potentially drive a further wedge between the U.S. and Europe, and provide an important platform for its narrative of Western threats to Russia.
A three-way meeting would play to Trump’s self-regard as a dealmaker and peacemaker – and quite possibly his appetite for economic gain. The United States recently eased sanctions on Russian diesel fuel exports, with an initial shipment of 40,000 tonnes reportedly on its way to the U.S. Moscow has also offered to increase fertilizer exports amid shortages caused by the Middle East crisis. But Trump may also have a larger strategic motivation. He has said that nuclear disarmament, not Ukraine, should be at the top of the agenda.
With the APEC summit in China being discussed as the venue, Xi would surely welcome the huge symbolic win of being seen as the world leader capable of hosting such an important gathering – while possibly helping to widen the divide between the U.S. and Europe. But Xi also has very good reasons to avoid such a meeting. China has benefited from dealing with Washington and Moscow separately, and it has in the past insisted that both Russia and Ukraine must be involved in any peace process. A China-Russia-U.S. summit to discuss Ukraine’s future without Kyiv would undermine both those positions.
A high-profile trilateral could overshadow the APEC summit, which Beijing wants to use to showcase its economic leadership and promote openness, innovation, and cooperation. A highly publicized gathering of three major powers also would sit uneasily with Beijing’s repeated calls for inclusive multilateralism, particularly at a forum intended to promote regional economic cooperation.
A successful trilateral might make the risk worthwhile. But such an outcome is uncertain – not least because of the unpredictability of Trump and Putin. The meeting could end up dominating APEC at the expense of Beijing’s economic agenda, without producing any significant outcomes.
Lastly, while Putin and Trump have major strategic incentives to meet, Xi has a strategic reason to avoid doing so. Trump’s insistence on putting nuclear arms reduction at the top of the agenda is problematic for China. Beijing has long emphasized that its nuclear arsenal is far smaller than those of the United States and Russia – and that Washington and Moscow must make substantial reductions before China joins any talks. Abandoning this position would risk China being bound by the same rules as Russia and the U.S., despite the gap in nuclear capabilities.
But Xi may recognize that he cannot dismiss the idea of a meeting altogether. Chinese diplomats have reportedly indicated that they would not rule out a trilateral. If Xi cannot prevent such a meeting, he could at least use his position as host to shape it – a less prominent, more informal encounter with a loose agenda focused on major power relations or the global economy, rather than a formal summit focused on Ukraine or nuclear arms control that would raise public expectations. Xi could even cast himself as the host of a Trump-Putin meeting rather than a participant in three-way talks.
Such stage-management would not protect Europe and Ukraine from the United States, Russia, and China talking about them behind their backs. But it would allow European governments to frame such a meeting as nothing more than an exchange of views. A formal summit explicitly devoted to Ukraine, by contrast, would risk signaling to the world that the three leaders are entitled – by right or by force – to make strategic decisions about Europe in Europe’s absence. That alone would send a terrible precedent for the continent.
Much can still happen until the APEC summit next month. Another round of U.S.-mediated talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi are reportedly under discussion, while Trump’s views on Ukraine and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy continue to shift. But whatever summitry emerges in Shenzhen, European governments must continue to insist on Ukrainian participation in any talks about the country’s future. Apart from pressing Washington to take them into account, Kyiv and European capitals should also appeal to Xi’s own reservations about a trilateral summit that also carries many risks for Beijing.

articles.title: Iran has plans to hit Gulf undersea cables if war resumes
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran has detailed plans to hit Gulf undersea cables if war resumes, officials say
Tehran has drawn up detailed plans to target undersea communications cables in the Gulf if the United States and Israel attack Iran again, two senior Iranian security officials told Reuters.
Their comments followed warnings by Iranian officials that undersea cables in the region could become targets in any renewed conflict if diplomacy with Washington collapses.
The two Iranian security officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, gave few details and did not say how or where exactly Tehran would carry out such attacks. But one of them said Iran would aim to prevent repairs after any attacks to prolong disruptions to communications, including internet connections.
"If Iran is attacked, there will be no more red lines ... from undersea cables to military bases, including covert ones," one of the officials said.
The official warned Washington not to "play with fire", and said Iran had full access to the undersea cables and could easily destroy them.
Yadollah Javani, the deputy head of political affairs for Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC), said on Wednesday that Iran could target seven major internet cables beneath the Strait of Hormuz if Iranian infrastructure came under attack.
Undersea cables carry around 99% of global internet traffic, according to the International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency. But the global impact of such attacks by Iran could be limited as less than 1% of international bandwidth passes through the Strait of Hormuz, said Alan Mauldin, research director at telecommunications research firm TeleGeography.
The strait separates Iran and Oman, linking the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea.
The US Department of State and Iran's Foreign Ministry did not respond to Reuters' requests for comment on the Iranian security officials' remarks. There was no immediate comment from Gulf states.
'Stronger response'
The plans for possible attacks on undersea cables reflect a conviction in Iran's leadership that a renewed US military campaign would have to be met with a stronger response than before.
Top security official Mohsen Rezaei warned this month that US-linked digital infrastructure across the Gulf, including data centres and AI facilities, could be targeted in a renewed conflict.
Washington's Gulf allies have invested heavily in such infrastructure and they "should hold Washington, not Tehran, responsible for any damage to undersea cables," the second Iranian security official said.
Alex Vatanka, director of the Iran program at the Middle East Institute in Washington, said such threats were intended to deter renewed conflict and put pressure on Washington by making Gulf governments and US companies fear for their investments in the region.
"Tehran wants Gulf states and corporate executives to press (US President Donald) Trump over the risks his policies pose to their investment plans," said Vatanka.
Multiple cable cuts could slow internet services and disrupt financial transactions, e-commerce and cloud computing, analysts said. The impact would depend on how operators rerouted traffic and the capacity available on alternative connections, Mauldin said.
Restoring connections during wartime could be difficult, experts said, and higher insurance costs and delays in obtaining permits to enter territorial waters could further complicate repairs.
The Red Sea could offer a more significant target than the Strait of Hormuz, particularly if Iran had support from its Houthi allies in Yemen, though Tehran has made no public statement indicating it plans to target cables there.
The Red Sea carries data between Europe, East Africa and Asia, with capacity routed through it accounting for about 3% of global international demand and around 10% of traffic travelling between regions, Mauldin said.
Gulf governments have been investing heavily in technology to diversify beyond oil and become global artificial intelligence hubs, deepening ties with US technology firms.
Iranian strikes directly hit two Amazon Web Services facilities in the UAE in March and damaged infrastructure near one of its facilities in Bahrain. The IRGC named US tech companies including Microsoft, Google, Apple and Nvidia as legitimate targets at the height of the war in March.
Land-based connections can provide alternative routes for internet traffic, and Gulf states and US technology companies are investing in additional infrastructure to improve resilience.
Microsoft plans to invest more than $400 million in subsea and terrestrial connectivity across the Middle East by 2030.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Only thing we really need from USA is shipment of interceptor missiles
articles.body:
Ukraine's biggest challenge for the winter, amid intensifying attacks from Russia, is its air defense capabilities, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
"Air and missile defense remains a real challenge, especially the availability of interceptors for the Patriot systems. We are facing a shortage in this area. We are negotiating with various countries – in Asia, the Middle East, and with our European partners. And, of course, we are counting on an aid package from the United States. This primarily involves energy support and interceptor missiles – which are the most important – as well as funding," Zelenskyy said during an online meeting at the Hudson Institute on Friday.
According to him, effective communication has been established with the United States and the EU. "The necessary decisions are being made every week in Brussels. The Europeans support us; they understand who we are and what challenges we face. I think we'll be ready. The only thing we really need from the United States is a shipment of interceptor missiles. We urgently need interceptors for the Patriot systems, and we hope that the U.S. administration will help us. We expect the Pentagon to ensure the delivery and to provide other necessary support," the President of Ukraine said.
He also noted that Ukraine has agreements with partners regarding gas supplies. "In addition, we have our own natural gas reserves – in this regard, we've prepared quite well," Zelenskyy said.

articles.title: Russia launches 126 UAVs at Ukraine; 101 neutralized
articles.body:
Overnight into Saturday, Russian occupation forces launched 126 drones of various types at Ukraine, including 61 jet-powered UAVs, as well as Banderol loitering munitions and decoy drones. Ukraine’s air defense forces shot down or neutralized 101 of these, including 50 jet-powered drones, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
"Hits by enemy aerial weapons were recorded at 14 locations, while debris from intercepted drones fell at five other locations," the Air Force stated on its Telegram channel.
The aerial attack was countered by Ukrainian aviation, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
As of the time of the announcement, the attack was still ongoing, with Russian strike drones remaining in Ukrainian airspace.
Consequently, the effectiveness of Ukraine’s air defense overnight exceeded 80%; specifically, the interception rate for jet-powered drones reached 82%.

articles.title: How Ukrainians in US advocate for Ukraine’s interests
articles.body:
How Ukrainians in US advocate for Ukraine’s interests
For decades, the Ukrainian community in the U.S. has been working to ensure that relations between Ukraine and the U.S. remain strong and that Ukraine has reliable partners in Washington.
The Ukrainian Congress Committee of America (UCCA), a nonpartisan organization of Ukrainian Americans, has represented the community's interests since 1940. Our position does not depend on which party is in power; our mission is to defend Ukraine's interests. In our work and communications, we consistently explain to the American public that supporting Ukrainian sovereignty is important for America itself.
One focus of our advocacy is increasing economic pressure on Russia. As part of this effort, we have supported legislative initiatives by Senators Lindsey Graham and Richard Blumenthal to strengthen sanctions against the Kremlin.
The latest decisions by U.S. President Donald Trump's administration – in particular, regarding the return of Russian diesel fuel to the global market and the easing of sanctions against Russia – contradict our position on the need to increase economic pressure on the Kremlin, as they provide Russia with additional resources to continue the war.
While the U.S. Administration might couch the rationale for the diesel deal to 'lower fuel prices' for American consumers, the easing of sanctions should be evaluated in light of their consequences. A decision that claims to offer only minor benefits for U.S. citizens but simultaneously increases Russia's revenues – which it uses to finance the war – runs counter to the long-term security interests of the U.S., and most importantly to worldwide democratic values and principles.
Similarly, we disagree with the U.S. government's criticism of Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure as an argument in favor of making concessions to the Kremlin. Ukraine is defending itself against a state that launched a full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, and still shows no willingness to end its aggression. Unilateral concessions by partners do not, in and of themselves, guarantee peace.
Moreover, the experience of recent years shows that Vladimir Putin is not seeking a compromise for the sake of a just peace, but rather the opportunity to continue the war on terms favorable to himself. Therefore, in its communications with the American audience, the UCCA strives to clearly explain Russia's true intentions and outline the real mechanisms for deterring the aggressor.
At the same time, we see that concerns about such decisions are shared not only by Democrats but also by Republicans in Congress. This is important because support for Ukraine must not become a pawn in intra-party struggles.
Not just protests
When talking about the influence of the Ukrainian community in the U.S., it is important to understand the unique characteristics of the American political system. American democracy has its own mechanisms for influencing the government, and mass street protests are just one of them. They can draw attention to an issue, but they do not guarantee a change in political course.
Large-scale demonstrations on various domestic and foreign policy issues take place regularly in the U.S.. However, our experience shows that if we want to achieve concrete results for Ukraine, we must work simultaneously on many levels – in Congress, in the media, with civil society organizations, business representatives, and various ethnic communities.
The UCCA's activities are not limited to public events; we also maintain regular contact with members of the House of Representatives and the Senate, convey our position to political circles in both parties, collaborate with journalists, and strive to ensure that Ukrainian issues remain on the American public agenda.
We have developed partnerships with other communities, including Polish, Baltic, Georgian, Jewish, and Cuban. For example, in 1994, the UCCA was instrumental in founding the Central and East European Coalition (CEEC), which unites the concerns of over 20 million Americans citizens of Central and East European descent. Many of them have their own historical reasons to take a close interest in Russian aggression, authoritarianism, and international security issues. Working together helps us better explain to the American public why supporting Ukraine is in the interests not only of Ukrainians, but also of the U.S. and its allies.
We also work with business leaders. When influential businesspeople publicly support decisions that could weaken Ukraine's ability to defend itself, it is important for Americans to understand the consequences of such decisions, especially in bringing attention to the American businesses that have been targeted by Russian attacks in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022. We view public communication and peaceful protests near commercial facilities as one way to draw attention to the responsibility businesses have for their influence on societal processes.
Our task is not simply to express disagreement, but to convey our arguments to as broad an audience as possible and to translate public support for Ukraine into concrete policy decisions.
We see a basis for this work. According to the sociological studies on which we rely, the majority of Americans supports aid to Ukraine and views Russia as an existential threat to American interests. At the same time, this support cannot be taken for granted – it must be constantly reinforced by explaining to Americans what is at stake.
Strength lies in unity
The Ukrainian community in the U.S. is not homogeneous; among Ukrainian Americans, there are supporters of both Democrats and Republicans, representatives of different generations of immigrants, and people with diverse experiences and views on US domestic policy.
From the very beginning, the UCCA has been an organization that unites the community around shared national interests, rather than party affiliation. We have contacts with people who have worked in both Republican and Democratic administrations, and we collaborate with representatives of both parties. This allows us to convey the Ukrainian position to various political circles, regardless of who is in the White House or leading Congress.
The diversity of our community is not a weakness but a strength. It enables us to speak to different audiences in the language of their values and interests. For some, the main argument is the defense of democracy; for others, it is national security; and for still others, it is the need to prevent aggressive authoritarian regimes from changing international borders by force.
Ukrainians who arrived in the U.S. after the start of the full-scale invasion deserve special attention. The issue of their future and immigration status remains critical, and we are working with our partners in Congress and other government officials to advocate for their interests.
At the same time, their contribution to supporting Ukraine is already extremely significant. The Ukrainian community in America is raising funds, organizing humanitarian aid shipments, and assisting hospitals and the civilian population. Since the start of the full-scale war, tens and hundreds of millions of dollars in aid have been sent to Ukraine through various community initiatives and charitable projects.
Not everyone can attend a demonstration or speak out publicly against a particular political decision. But helping Ukraine takes many forms, and each one is important. Our goal is to create opportunities for everyone who wants to get involved, regardless of their background, political beliefs, or life circumstances.
One area of our work is direct humanitarian support for Ukraine. I recently joined the Ukraine Focus mission to deliver ambulances that were collected in Europe and transported to Ukraine. This time, there were about fifty vehicles intended for the needs of Ukraine's territorial defense forces and other units requiring medical transport.
Another important area is political advocacy. As early as 2000, the UCCA launched Ukrainian Days in Washington so that representatives of Ukrainian communities from across the country could meet with their congressmen and senators, representatives of research centers, diplomats, and other influential figures. Following Russia's aggression in 2014, we stepped up this work.
We also collaborate with other initiatives to strengthen U.S. support for Ukraine. Overall, our guiding principle is that the voice of the Ukrainian community must be heard consistently, not just when another crisis arises.
Ukraine's security is America's security
For decades, American leadership and cooperation with European allies have been key factors in the stability of the democratic world. If the U.S. distances itself from its partners in Europe or gives the impression that aggression can be rewarded with concessions, the consequences will be felt not only by Ukrainians. This will affect allies' confidence in American commitments, the ability to deter future conflicts, and the international system, in which the sovereignty of states should not depend on the strength of their neighbors.
We work earnestly to ensure that cooperation between the White House and Congress will pave the way for a more consistent policy toward Ukraine. It is important that our security issues not be turned into a tool for domestic political struggles, and that support for Ukraine remain a shared strategic interest of the U.S.
I often recall the words of American pastor Mark Burns, who, after visiting Ukraine and seeing things with his own eyes, said: "Ukraine is America First". These words are particularly telling in the context of the "America First" slogan frequently used by President Trump. Their meaning is that defending Ukraine does not conflict with American interests. On the contrary, Ukraine is part of the democratic world, and the outcome of this war will affect security, stability, and the future far beyond its borders.
That is why we will continue to explain to Americans that aid to Ukraine is not just a matter of solidarity, but an investment in international security and the protection of the principles of American democracy.
To the people in Ukraine, I want to say that we are constantly working for victory for Ukraine. Ukraine remains in our thoughts, in our humanitarian work, in our meetings with politicians, and in every effort to convince the American public that our struggle matters to the entire democratic world.
Having been to Ukraine several times since Russia's full-scale invasion, I, and my organisation, understand how difficult it is to live under constant rocket and drone attacks and how much depends on the support of our partners, so we will continue to work – in the humanitarian sphere, in political advocacy, and in building partnerships that help Ukraine endure.
I would like to thank Ukrainian Americans for their tireless work. Regardless of when they or their families arrived in the U.S., what political views they hold, or how they choose to help, their contribution is of great importance.
We must remain united around a common goal. We don't have to agree on every issue of the American domestic policy to understand that a free, democratic, and sovereign Ukraine is in the interests of both Ukraine and the U.S.
Our task is to continue our work, expand our circle of partners, find new ways to convey our position, and turn support into concrete actions. I am convinced that a strong, democratic, and sovereign Ukraine will remain an important strategic partner of the United States for infinity. And that is precisely what we are working toward.
Michael Sawkiw, President of the Ukrainian Congress Committee of America (UCCA) and Director of its Washington, DC bureau – the Ukrainian National Information Service (UNIS), Chair of the Ukrainian World Congress (UWC) Foreign Policy Council, and recipient of the Order of Merit II degree.
