articles.title: Poland intends to deploy French and US nuclear weapons on its territory — Defense Ministry
articles.body:
WARSAW, October 24. /TASS/. Poland is seeking to participate in the US nuclear deterrence program and is conducting similar negotiations with France, said Defense Minister Wladysіaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said.
In an interview with the WNP.pl portal, he noted that the initiative to jointly use nuclear weapons by some NATO countries could be implemented as part of cooperation with the United States to establish an American base on the republic’s territory. Kosiniak-Kamysz did not specify the timeframe for making decisions due to the need for preliminary consultations with the European allies.
He noted that Poland is also actively developing nuclear cooperation with France. "Participation in the American nuclear cooperation program does not preclude the establishment of relations with France," he said. He added that Paris is offering its European partners a larger share in the nuclear deterrence system.
On June 3, Kosiniak-Kamysz suggested to Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth that the United States establish a permanent base in Poland. In early September, an American delegation visited Poland to inspect potential locations. On September 17, US President Donald Trump announced "significant progress" in the negotiations on this matter.

articles.title: No single nation can unilaterally rewrite NPT: Iran UN envoy
articles.body:
Addressing the UN General Assembly, Ambassador Gholamhossein Darzi pushed back against Western pressure, asserting that Article IV of the NPT (Non-Proliferation Treaty) guarantees all state parties the right to develop peaceful nuclear energy, including the full nuclear fuel cycle.
The following is the full text of the statement which is read:
Mr. President,
The Agency’s reporting must remain professional, objective, factual, and free from political influence. Its credibility depends on impartiality and technical integrity.
Nuclear energy is indispensable to development and energy security. Article IV of the NPT affirms the inalienable right of all States Parties to develop research, production, and use of nuclear energy for peaceful purposes, without discrimination and in conformity with Articles I and II. Yet certain States systematically demonize this right and weaponize proliferation concerns to pressure States into abandoning their national nuclear fuel cycles.
The United States, an NPT depositary, openly questions the very existence of States Parties’ right to pursue the full nuclear fuel cycle, including uranium enrichment. Denying States access to this essential technology while claiming to uphold their right to peaceful nuclear energy violates Article IV. No State can unilaterally rewrite the Treaty or impose its own political veto on the legitimate rights of other States Parties.
In response to Iran’s resolute defense of its inalienable rights under the NPT, the United States and the nuclear-armed Israeli regime launched two wars of aggression against Iran in 2025 and 2026, massively targeting its peaceful nuclear facilities under IAEA safeguards.
These aggressions caused immense destruction and killed thousands, including our martyred Leader, whose well-known fatwa rejects nuclear weapons and other weapons of mass destruction. They also violated international law, the UN Charter, the IAEA Statute, relevant IAEA General Conference resolutions, and Security Council resolution 487 (1981).
Neither the IAEA General Conference, the IAEA Board of Governors, nor the Director General has condemned these attacks. The Security Council has likewise failed to do so. The Director General has once again failed to condemn these attacks in his statements delivered today under this agenda item. Instead, pressure is directed against the victim while the aggressors escape accountability.
Certain Western delegations continue to invoke so-called proliferation concerns while refusing to condemn attacks against safeguarded peaceful nuclear facilities. This is not a consistent commitment to non-proliferation; it is the weaponization of non-proliferation for political purposes.
The hypocrisy of this approach is blatant. Iran, an NPT State Party since 1970, has consistently affirmed its commitment to its international obligations and diplomacy. Yet its peaceful nuclear program and safeguarded facilities have been subjected to political pressure and military attacks, while the Secretariat’s withholding of technical cooperation deprives Iran of the benefits of peaceful nuclear development that the Agency is mandated to promote. Meanwhile, the Israeli regime—the region’s sole possessor of nuclear weapons, with unsafeguarded nuclear facilities—continues to enjoy impunity. This selective application of non-proliferation standards exposes the political motives behind the pressure on Iran and undermines the credibility of the international non-proliferation regime.
These same delegations demand access for inspectors while military threats persist, disregarding the extraordinary circumstances created by aggression. Let us be clear: Iran has neither abandoned nor formally suspended its safeguards obligations. However, aggression has fundamentally altered the physical and security conditions for their implementation. The Agency’s own reports acknowledge that verification activities ceased and inspectors were withdrawn for safety reasons. Those same safety concerns cannot be ignored when their return is demanded.
The continued existence of safeguards obligations does not eliminate the need to assess whether verification can be performed safely and effectively. No country can reasonably be expected to provide access amid military operations and persistent threats without adequate safety guarantees. Responsibility for creating these circumstances lies with the aggressors, not their victim.
Iran will continue to cooperate with the Agency to the extent circumstances permit. However, such cooperation cannot come at the expense of the safety of its people, facilities, or IAEA inspectors.
Thank you.
MNA

articles.title: Arabian coalition shoots down Houthi ballistic missile over Riyadh
articles.body:
DOHA, October 24. /TASS/. The Arabian coalition led by Saudi Arabia has destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis from the Yemeni rebel movement Ansar Allah in the direction of Riyadh, said the alliance’s official spokesman Turki al·Maliki.
"The air defense forces have intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by Houthi terrorists in the direction of Riyadh," he wrote on X.
Saudi Arabia’s General Directorate of Civil Defense activated the National Early Warning Platform for Emergencies, notifying the Riyadh residents about a possible threat. Later it said on X that the alert had been lifted. "The danger to the city of Riyadh passed," the statement said.
AFP news agency reported two explosions in Riyadh amid the activation of air·threat warning systems.
An armed conflict in Yemen between government forces supported by the Arabian coalition and Houthi rebels has been ongoing since August 2014.
On October 19, military representative of the movement Yahya Saree said that Saudi Arabia had carried out a series of strikes, including on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, as well as on Saudi Aramco and military bases.

articles.title: China’s Liaoning carrier: 10 years from training ship to warship
articles.body:
- China’s Liaoning carrier group completed its second Western Pacific training deployment of 2026, ten years after the carrier’s first such voyage.
- Japan’s Joint Staff observed fighter takeoffs and landings about 250 km south of Ishigaki-jima on Oct. 13, and Japanese fighters scrambled in response.
China’s Liaoning carrier group has carried out its second far-seas training deployment to the Western Pacific this year, a decade after the carrier’s first such voyage in 2016, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported on Oct. 24, describing the ship’s path over those 10 years as a three-step climb from training ship to combat ship to the command core of a carrier group.
Japanese forces first spotted the carrier on Oct. 13 with Renhai-class destroyers 103 and 104 and Luyang III-class destroyer 123. The group sailed southeast between Okinawa and Miyako-jima into the Pacific on Oct. 14, and the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force observed carrier-based fighters taking off and landing in waters about 250 km (155 miles) south of Ishigaki-jima, Japan’s Joint Staff said. Japan Air Self-Defense Force fighters scrambled in response. On Oct. 15, the four ships were confirmed sailing toward the South China Sea.
China’s Ministry of National Defense confirmed that a naval task group led by the Liaoning was training in the Western Pacific, Stars and Stripes reported. The carrier’s flight operations came days before Keen Sword, a U.S.-Japan exercise running from Oct. 19 to 29.
CCTV said the Liaoning’s Western Pacific deployments are routine training organized under the navy’s annual plan and are not aimed at any specific country or target. Military commentator Du Wenlong told the broadcaster that the training complies with international law.
“If we do not train, our level cannot improve and our readiness cannot be maintained,” said Du Wenlong.
Du traced the change in how Chinese state media describe the navy’s carrier drills. In October 2024, the Liaoning and the Shandong held China’s first dual-carrier exercise in the South China Sea, which was described as a joint drill. When the two carriers operated together again in June 2025, the wording shifted to “real combat confrontation,” with each side looking for the other’s weaknesses and building strike plans without a script.
“In future naval battles, no one will tell you what they will do next,” said Du Wenlong.
The Liaoning began life as the Soviet Kuznetsov-class carrier Varyag, laid down in 1984 at a shipyard in what is now Ukraine. China rebuilt the unfinished hull, and Du said the work taught Chinese engineers the basic principles of carrier design. After further upgrades, he said, the ship moved from simply being able to go to sea to being able to fight, with improved command and weapons systems and a major step up in its carrier aviation. With new information and command systems installed, the Liaoning now serves as the flagship at the center of its carrier group.
“Over ten years, the Liaoning has completed its ‘three steps,’ and in just ten years our overall capability has made a huge leap,” said Du Wenlong.
The October voyage follows a 40-day deployment from May to June, when the Liaoning group, including cruiser Wuxi (104), destroyer Kaifeng (124), frigate Luohe (545) and supply ship Hulunhu (901), trained in the South China Sea and the Western Pacific. Japan’s Joint Staff counted about 170 aircraft takeoffs and landings over three days in late May, and the group held joint drills with an amphibious assault ship group before returning to Qingdao on June 22.
China now operates three aircraft carriers: the Liaoning, the Shandong and the Fujian, which was commissioned in November 2025.

articles.title: Trump’s Iran pause is for November
articles.body:
President Trump’s pre-midterm pause on strikes against Iran landed as a claim of diplomatic momentum, not a concession of failure. The pause was framed as proof that negotiations are working. Look closer, and a different mechanism appears. The war meant to project strength has become an electoral liability, and the president’s response is to bury its most visible costs until voters have finished deciding. Then the option can reopen.
The White House insists Washington is negotiating from strength. Military options remain on the table. The blockade stays in force. The administration has not ended the war, only hidden its sharpest edges from the campaign season. That sequence matters. It allows Republican candidates to campaign without the immediate risk of new strikes or another energy-price spike, while preserving the argument that renewed action may be warranted later. Nothing has been settled. Everything has been postponed.
Trump’s political identity rested on rejecting costly, open-ended foreign interventions. His appeal to swaths of the MAGA movement included the claim that American leaders had squandered resources and neglected domestic problems chasing overseas conflicts. “America First” was a promise about priorities as much as power.
The Iran war has strained that promise to its breaking point.
Back in February 2026, it looked like a pressure campaign: force Tehran to accept Washington’s terms. Months later, it’s a drawn-out confrontation with no clear settlement. Rising fuel prices, stubborn inflation, and the uncertainty over how long the war will last have turned it into a domestic political problem.
Consumer sentiment has fallen close to a record low, dragged down by rising living costs linked to the conflict.
This creates a tension the Republican coalition cannot easily absorb. Some supporters prioritize nationalist strength and a confrontational stance toward Iran. Others were drawn by pledges to avoid costly wars and focus on economic grievances at home. An extended conflict makes satisfying both impossible. Pausing attacks before the midterms offers a way to postpone the reckoning.
The question is whether this pause is a genuine step toward peace or simply an attempt to protect Republicans from the political costs of an unpopular war. The attacks may have stopped, but the naval blockade remains in place, economic pressure on Iran continues, and neither side appears any closer to a lasting agreement. Trump has ruled out further strikes before 3rd November. What he has not ruled out is a return to military action once the election is over. This sequence allows the administration to present the pause as controlled progress, lets Republican candidates campaign without the immediate risk of new strikes or energy-price spikes, and preserves the option of arguing later that renewed action may be warranted.
The reports tell a different story than the public messaging. The Pentagon has been instructed to prepare for a potential resumption of large-scale operations. Discussions involving Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have touched on a major new operation before elections in both countries. The White House calls such reports false. But the military remains on alert, and preparations are being finalised.
For many MAGA voters who supported Trump in part because he promised to reject endless wars, a purely electoral pause represents a significant contradiction.
An unpopular foreign war won’t turn MAGA loyalists into Democrats. The real hazard for the GOP is exhaustion: an endless conflict paired with painful pump prices gives frustrated voters every reason to leave their ballots on the kitchen table.
By removing the immediate threat of renewed attacks, Trump can try to prevent the war from becoming the dominant symbol of Republican failure and shift attention toward negotiations. If the conflict remains relatively quiet until November 3, Republican prospects improve. If Democrats gain control of one or both chambers, congressional scrutiny of military spending and presidential war powers would intensify.
This is where the powerless ballot enters the picture. Elections are meant to give citizens influence over decisions made in their name. That relationship weakens when a president can temporarily reduce the visibility of a policy’s costs until after ballots are cast, then resume the same course. Trump’s approach could turn the midterms into a debate over whether he appears willing to pull back from the war, rather than whether his Iran policy has actually changed. Americans are already feeling the strain of higher living costs, and consumer confidence has fallen sharply. A brief pause in the fighting will do little to ease that burden, much less resolve the underlying conflict. What is needed is a lasting diplomatic settlement, not a temporary break that leaves the same problems unresolved.
Neither a Republican nor a Democratic outcome automatically resolves the strategic problem. Iran has its own calculations.
Iranian officials continue to demand sanctions relief and an end to the blockade while Washington insists on further concessions. A pause that leaves these disagreements unresolved may simply delay the next confrontation.
The bigger question is not whether Trump keeps his promise before the election, but what he plans to do once the votes are counted and the political pressure has eased. If the coming weeks bring a verifiable agreement backed by credible safeguards, the pause could be a genuine first step toward ending the war. If instead November 3 is treated as the moment political restraints disappear, then the restraint will have functioned primarily as an electoral maneuver.
In that case the danger is clear. Voters are being asked to endorse the appearance of an ending while the means to continue the conflict remain intact. The ballot becomes a ratification of a decision already made elsewhere.
If the fighting resumes after the votes are counted, the question will no longer be whether Trump delivered peace, but whether his supporters were ever given a genuine choice between peace and a war that had only been postponed.
The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Monitor.

articles.title: Chinese navy flotilla returns after record 378 days at sea
articles.body:
- China’s 48th naval escort task force returned to Qingdao on Oct. 23 after a record 378-day mission in the Gulf of Aden.
- The destroyer Tangshan, frigate Daqing and supply ship Taihu sailed more than 150,000 nautical miles and escorted 423 vessels.
China’s 48th naval escort task force returned to a military port in Qingdao on Oct. 23 after 378 days away, the longest deployment in the history of the Chinese navy’s anti-piracy missions in the Gulf of Aden and the waters off Somalia, China’s Ministry of National Defense said.
The task force, made up of the guided-missile destroyer Tangshan (Hull 122), the guided-missile frigate Daqing (Hull 576) and the supply ship Taihu (Hull 889), sailed more than 150,000 nautical miles (about 278,000 km) during the mission and escorted 423 Chinese and foreign vessels, according to the ministry.
The three ships left Qingdao on Oct. 11, 2025, to take over from the 47th task force, carrying two helicopters and dozens of special operations personnel, Xinhua reported at the time. Before departure, the crews trained on weapons use, convoy escort procedures and replenishment at sea.
The deployment extends a run of successively longer missions. The 46th escort task force spent 339 days on deployment and the 47th spent 368, China Defense Blog noted, putting the 48th task force’s 378 days at the top of a steady climb in time on station across three consecutive rotations.
“Incremental progress, repeated often enough that one day it no longer looks incremental at all,” China Defense Blog wrote.
Beyond escort duty, the task force took part in the “Will for Peace 2026” joint maritime exercise in South Africa and the China-Pakistan “Sea Guardian IV” naval exercise in Pakistan. It joined a parade marking the 50th anniversary of Seychelles’ independence, paid visits to Bangladesh, Myanmar and Malaysia, and made technical stops in Oman, Kenya, Singapore and other countries, the ministry said.
China began sending warships to the Gulf of Aden and the waters off Somalia in December 2008, after a surge in piracy attacks on commercial shipping in one of the world’s busiest sea lanes, which links the Indian Ocean with the Red Sea and the Suez Canal. Each task force typically pairs combat ships with a supply vessel and an embarked special operations team, and hands over the mission to the next rotation on station.

articles.title: Labs that design U.S. Navy reactors get $2.4B more
articles.body:
- The U.S. Navy awarded Fluor Marine Propulsion a $2.4 billion modification for naval nuclear propulsion work at the Naval Nuclear Laboratory.
- The laboratory designs and supports reactors for U.S. Navy submarines and aircraft carriers, with work in Pennsylvania, New York and Idaho.
The U.S. Navy has added $2.4 billion to Fluor Marine Propulsion’s contract to run naval nuclear propulsion work at the Naval Nuclear Laboratory, the network of government labs that designs and supports the reactors powering every U.S. Navy submarine and aircraft carrier.
Naval Sea Systems Command awarded the $2,409,077,590 cost-plus-fixed-fee modification on Sept. 24, 2026, according to a Department of War contract announcement. Work will be split among the laboratory’s main sites near Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania (47%), Schenectady, New York (45%), and Idaho Falls, Idaho (8%). The announcement lists $582,062 in fiscal 2026 Navy operations and maintenance funds and $15,838 in fiscal 2026 shipbuilding funds obligated at the time of award, with the shipbuilding portion expiring at the end of the fiscal year.
The Naval Nuclear Laboratory is owned by the Department of Energy and overseen by Naval Reactors, a joint Energy Department and Navy program. It includes the Bettis Atomic Power Laboratory in West Mifflin, Pennsylvania, outside Pittsburgh, the Knolls Atomic Power Laboratory in Niskayuna, New York, near Schenectady, the Kenneth A. Kesselring Site in West Milton, New York, where sailors train to operate naval reactors, and the Naval Reactors Facility at the Idaho National Laboratory.
The labs develop new nuclear propulsion systems, provide technical support to keep the fleet’s reactors safe and reliable, and train the sailors who run them at sea. Knolls is the lead design laboratory for the Virginia-class attack submarines and is leading reactor design work for the Columbia-class ballistic missile submarines, while Bettis supports the Nimitz-class aircraft carriers and Seawolf-class submarines. The laboratory employs more than 7,500 engineers, scientists, technicians and support staff.
Fluor Marine Propulsion, a wholly owned subsidiary of Fluor Corporation, took over management of the laboratory from Bechtel Marine Propulsion Corporation on Oct. 1, 2018. The Navy-funded portion of its contract started with a cost-plus-fixed-fee base of about $1.2 billion and options that could bring its total to about $13 billion, alongside a separate Energy Department contract for the same laboratory. Earlier modifications have included a $1.78 billion award in March 2020 and a $1 billion option in 2021.
The new modification covers continued naval nuclear propulsion work across all three regions, and the Department of War contract announcement did not list a completion date for the effort.

articles.title: Russia running sabotage campaign across Europe
articles.body:
Russia is conducting a campaign of hybrid attacks and sabotage across Europe, and Britain is working with the United States to deter and contest activity that threatens Euro-Atlantic security, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Jim Shannon, the Democratic Unionist Party member for Strangford, had asked what steps are being taken to work with the United States to reduce the Russian threat to both home territories.
Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “As our closest defence and security partner, we engage and collaborate with the US regularly on a range of issues. We know Russia is conducting a campaign of hybrid attacks and sabotage across Europe. The UK does not seek confrontation with Russia, but we will continue to deter and contest activity that threatens Euro-Atlantic security.”
Answering a separate question from Shannon on support for Poland and Lithuania, Sandher-Jones said: “The UK stands ready to defend every inch of Allied territory, with NATO remaining the cornerstone of the UK’s defence and security. This is reflected in our commitment to reach NATO’s defence spending target of 3.5% of GDP by 2035. Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty makes clear that an armed attack against one NATO Ally is considered an attack against the entire NATO Alliance.
“As the third-largest cash spender on defence in NATO, the UK contributes significantly towards the security of NATO’s eastern flank, which includes Poland and Lithuania. This is demonstrated through rotational air policing, troop deployments, and joint exercises, including maritime surveillance in the Baltic region. NATO is a defensive alliance and does not seek confrontation with Russia, but Russia should understand that any attack on a NATO ally would be a grave miscalculation.”
Wes Streeting told the Defence Committee this month that hybrid activity of this kind amounts to state backed terrorism. European governments have attributed arson, parcel bombs, rail sabotage, cable damage and drone incursions over airports and military sites to Russian intelligence services or to proxies recruited through messaging apps.

articles.title: Zelenskyy says restrictions on Starlink remain in force
articles.body:
Zelenskyy says restrictions on Starlink remain in force
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has confirmed that speed restrictions for Starlink satellite communications terminals in Ukraine remain in force.
Source: Zelenskyy during an online meeting at the Hudson Institute on 23 October, as reported by Interfax-Ukraine
Quote: "The speed limits on Starlink and Starshield are still there. The speed has not been restored. And the delivery of interceptors to protect us against Russian ballistic missiles is still delayed.
We are waiting for interceptors that were already agreed on but they are still not coming. Hope that everything is on the way. And this is a real problem for us because the Russians attack almost every day, Russia attacks us massively. So that's where things stand today."
Details: The president said that this is happening while Ukraine continues successful operations on the front line.
Zelenskyy added that he wants relations with America and all other partners to be as strong as possible.
Quote: "Without America, without a strong America and an America that cares about what happens in the world, the world would definitely be a worse place. These days people ask why Ukraine is speaking more openly directly to the world.
The answer is simple. We want people to understand us, and I mean people, societies, nations, as many people as possible. And when people understand what is really going on, political leaders can take a stronger path. The one that can really bring peace closer."
Background:
- The WSJ, citing US and Ukrainian officials familiar with the matter, reported that Trump had called Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on the military version of Starlink in Ukraine.

articles.title: Ethiopia's Tigray rebels urged to disarm
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Ethiopia's Tigray rebels urged to disarm as commander vows to fight on
An official in Tigray’s new federal-backed administration urged rebel fighters to lay down their weapons Friday, hours after a rebel commander called for continued resistance despite losing the northern Ethiopian region’s capital.
The calls to surrender and fight on came nearly three weeks after rebels lost control of Mekelle. At a hospital in the city, two wounded men said a drone strike killed four civilians as they loaded goats onto a truck earlier this week.
Redae Halefom Woldeselassie, the caretaker administration’s chief executive for political and public mobilisation, said rebel forces were collapsing and urged fighters to enter a disarmament and reintegration program.
“This is not the time for settling scores, I call upon you to return to your homes and continue your civilian lives,” he said in Mekelle.
He dismissed the prospect of the rebels retaking the city and portrayed the conflict as serving a small group of leaders rather than the people of Tigray.
Hours earlier, Lt. Gen. Fisseha Kidanu, identified in a television broadcast as commander of the Tigray army, pledged to reverse recent military setbacks.
“Local militias across the region — alongside all volunteers joining the resistance — are expected to engage the enemy,” he said Thursday night on Tigray Broadcast Media, a new rebel television station. His location was not disclosed.
Fisseha urged attacks on government-held positions despite his opponents’ advantages in drones and heavy weapons. The Tigray People’s Liberation Front, or TPLF, has also claimed to have inflicted heavy losses on government forces. The Associated Press could not independently verify those claims.
Government-allied fighters entered Mekelle on Oct. 4 after the TPLF withdrew. Ethiopia’s government subsequently established a six-month caretaker administration promising to restore services, help displaced people return and prepare for elections.
The government’s allies include the Tigray Peace Force, comprising former members of the TPLF’s armed wing — a division within Tigrayan forces that has complicated the renewed conflict.
Redae said Ethiopian troops and allied forces were conducting joint security operations, including measures to prevent looting. He promised preparations for displaced residents to return but gave no timetable.
Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, speaking Monday to the Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation, accused the TPLF of acquiring weapons and forcibly recruiting young people instead of disarming under the November 2022 Pretoria peace agreement. He said his government had done everything within its capacity to implement the accord.
Wounded men describe drone strike 
At Ayder Hospital in Mekelle, Luel Berhanu, 22, and Samuel Belay, 20, said they were loading goats onto a truck in Finariwa, about 80 kilometers (49 miles) south of the city, when a strike hit around 9:30 p.m. Tuesday.
They said four civilians were killed and about six people wounded. The AP could not independently verify the casualties or establish who carried out the attack.
Luel said the truck’s headlights were on and a drone was hovering overhead shortly before the explosion. He said the blast severely injured his right eye and right arm, leaving him unable to see through that eye.
Samuel said they were working as day laborers loading the animals.
Hospital footage showed Luel with a bloodstained bandage covering his right eye and dressings around his shoulder and arm. Samuel lay on his side with an intravenous line attached to his arm.
A witness interviewed by the AP reported movements earlier that day by fighters identified as Agew Shengo, a militia that has previously fought alongside Tigrayan forces in neighboring Amhara region. Luel said rebel forces had been in the area several hours before the strike but none were present when it occurred.
Losing Mekelle may not end the war 
The renewed fighting has effectively shattered the Pretoria agreement, which ended the devastating 2020-2022 war.
Magnus Taylor, deputy Horn of Africa director at the International Crisis Group, told the AP last week that controlling towns and roads would not necessarily secure rural areas where Tigrayan fighters regrouped during the previous war.
“We shouldn’t imagine that this conflict is completely over just because the TPLF has lost Mekelle,” he said.

articles.title: Turkish foreign minister warns new attack on Iran would escalate regional conflict
articles.body:
The Turkish foreign minister warned on Friday that a new attack on Iran would further spread war and conflict across the region, Anadolu reports.
“Military intervention in Iran is by no means a solution. No one supports this at the moment,” Hakan Fidan told reporters after an R4+E3 meeting in Istanbul, the first-ever meeting in this format.
The US and Israel are said to have developed plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the American midterm elections.
The war that began in late February has yet to be settled despite a ceasefire and a memorandum of understanding to finalize a peace deal.
Speaking on the Russia-Ukraine war, Fidan said: “Either the war must stop, or, if it does not, parties must agree to exemptions for energy and grain issues.”
The R4 mechanism was established by Türkiye, Egypt, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia on the basis of regional ownership, with the aim of supporting lasting stability and strengthening dialogue on regional issues.
The E3 mechanism, made up of Germany, the UK and France, emerged from trilateral diplomatic cooperation on Iran’s nuclear program launched in 2003.

articles.title: Iran vows to block US warships from Gulf amid Trump threats
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran vows to block US warships from Gulf as Trump threatens fresh attacks
Iran said on Saturday that US military ships would never be allowed to enter the Gulf "under any circumstances" and that President Donald Trump would "take that dream to his grave".
The remarks came amid mounting US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran, as US ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack warned that Washington could "absolutely" strike Iran as soon as this weakened.
"We will not allow US military ships in the Persian Gulf under any circumstances and at any time," said Iran's armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi, according to Iranian state television.
"The US president must dream of seeing the armed forces enter the Persian Gulf. He will take that dream to his grave."
Iranian forces have restricted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital energy conduit and gateway to the Gulf, since the war with the United States broke out on 28 February.
In retaliation, the United States has imposed a counterblockade on Iranian ports and ships.
Tehran has required vessels to seek permission to transit, and repeatedly targeted ships attempting to pass through Hormuz via a southern route close to the Omani coast.
According to the Guards, several tankers attempting to transit Hormuz through the route Tehran considers "illegal" were hit by mines in recent days.
On Friday, the Guards said two supertankers carrying more than 4.5 million barrels of crude oil have been abandoned at sea after hitting mines in the strategic waterway.
"Their engine rooms were disabled by an explosion and a fierce fire," the Guards said in a statement carried by their Sepah News website.
In peacetime, around a fifth of the world's oil and gas passed through Hormuz.
US spy chief warns Iran has ramped up efforts to target Americans
Iran has "substantially increased" its efforts to target Americans in the Middle East and beyond, US national intelligence chief Jay Clayton warned on Friday.
The warning comes after Washington ordered non-essential US embassy staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia this week, following increasing attacks from Yemen's Houthis.
The kingdom has come under near-daily attacks this month from the Iran-backed group, including a strike on Riyadh's international airport that was the kingdom's deadliest in years.
"We have received intelligence that Iran has substantially increased efforts to target US personnel," Clayton said in a memo sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, according to a US official.
"The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against US citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," said the memo, which was first reported by Axios.
Washington previously ordered non-essential staff to leave the Gulf ahead of the start of its war against Iran and again in July before Trump called off a new wave of strikes.
The US official said: "When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment."
"The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting US officials are informing our decisions," the official added.
Trump suggested on Friday that the US might launch renewed military operations against Iran.
"We may do another little Epic Fury", Trump said, referring to the US name for its attacks on Iran. He gave no indication of timing.

articles.title: King Fahd Airport, Defense Ministry attacked as US tells diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia
articles.body:
King Fahd Airport, Defense Ministry attacked as US tells diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia
TEHRAN - At least two people were killed in a strike on a major airport in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday evening, as Washington ordered some U.S. diplomatic staff to leave the kingdom following weeks of deadly attacks by the Nasrallah military forces.
The Saudi authorities said in a statement on Thursday morning that a Saudi national and an Indian resident died in the strike on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, a city in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province that is home to the state oil giant Saudi Aramco, according to the New York Times. Eight other people were wounded, the statement said, adding that airport was operating normally on Thursday.
In a separate incident, two people were killed and two others were wounded on Wednesday when a drone was intercepted over Aramco’s Shaybah oil field, also in the Eastern Province. Falling drone fragments sparked a fire in a contractor’s vehicle, killing a Filipino and a Nepali, the Saudi Energy Ministry said.
The Ansarallah’s military spokesman, Yahya Saree, said they had also targeted the Saudi Defense Ministry's headquarters building in the capital, Riyadh, an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, and Abha International Airport in the south of the country.
The Ansarallah also reiterated on Thursday that they had attacked Saudi Arabia in retaliation for deadly Saudi air strikes on the territory they control in western Yemen.
The Ansarallah have been pummeling Saudi Arabia’s aviation and energy infrastructure for weeks, killing at least 22 civilians and roiling energy markets.
The price of oil jumped about 3 percent on Thursday, with the global benchmark topping $112 a barrel, the highest level since mid-May.
Saudi Arabia announced a bombing campaign against the Ansarallah in support of its puppet government in Yemen, which has been at war with the Ansarallah since 2014. That was when the Ansarallah seized the Yemeni capital, Sanaa — which they still hold.
A fragile truce in Yemen unraveled earlier this year. The war resurfaced after Saudi Arabia bombarded Sanaa airport and refused to lift the blockade of their territory.
As the fighting has spilled onto Saudi soil, the United States ordered all “non-emergency government employees and their family members” to leave Saudi Arabia, a State Department spokesman, Tommy Pigott, said in social media post on Wednesday night.
Washington had pulled many diplomatic staff out of the Middle East earlier this year after the start of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. But it started sending some back in late August.
Then in September, the Ansarallah seized areas of strategic territory on Yemen’s Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive, gaining greater control over a crucial choke point for global trade.
The Red Sea has become an increasingly important route for Saudi oil exports since Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway in the Persian Gulf, after the United States and Israel attacked Iran in late February. The Ansarallah’s attacks on Saudi oil facilities and tankers traversing the Red Sea have heaped further pressure on energy markets.
Saudi Arabia, under Mohammed bin Salman, seems adept at getting his country into trouble. In March 2015, when he was serving as defense minister, he ordered an attack on Yemen, expecting to restore the Saudi-backed Yemeni government within weeks and defeat Ansarallah. Instead, he opened Pandora’s box. More than a decade later, the consequences of that decision continue to haunt Riyadh, and it is difficult to imagine the Saudi capital remaining immune to the repercussions of the conflict.
He reopened old wounds when Saudi Arabia bombed Sanaa airport on July 13 in an attempt to prevent a plane carrying a Yemeni delegation from Tehran from landing. The delegation had participated in the funeral procession of Iranian Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was assassinated in a U.S.-Israeli air raid on his office and residence on February 28.

articles.title: UAE reports oil spill from tanker as ships attacked during war
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UAE reports oil spill from tanker as ships attacked during war
The United Arab Emirates reported an oil spill from a tanker off its coast on Friday, as vessels in Gulf waters come under attack during the Middle East war.
Frequent attacks on ships have been reported in recent weeks near the Strait of Hormuz, at the heart of the conflict between Iran and the United States.
The authorities "detected a tanker oil spill affecting Umm Al Quwain's beaches," the Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said in a statement, referring to an emirate north of Dubai.
It said "teams immediately began containment, cordoning, clean-up and remediation... to limit environmental impacts," adding that the emirate's beaches had been closed.
Access to the area in Umm Al Quwain was restricted by police, AFP journalists who went there said.
The neighbouring emirate of Sharjah also closed one beach, Al Hamriyah, "as a proactive precautionary measure", the local government said.
Satellite images analysed by AFP showed a hydrocarbon slick on October 19 surrounding a vessel, likely the tanker GEM NO.2, located about 20 kilometres (12 miles) off the coast of Umm Al Quwain.
Images from October 21, analysed by Wim Zwijnenburg from Dutch NGO PAX, revealed a slick about 40 kilometres long and covering an area of 190 square kilometres, stretching to just six kilometres from shore.
The British maritime security agency UKMTO reported on October 9 that a vessel had been hit by a projectile off the UAE coast, causing a fire that was later brought under control.
Maritime security company Vanguard also identified the vessel as the oil tanker GEM NO.2, sailing under a Panamanian flag.
Owned by Taiwan's Global Energy Maritime, the ship loaded 2 million barrels of oil in early March from a Saudi port.
Since then, it has been regularly transferring cargo with other ships along the Emirati and Omani coasts near the Strait of Hormuz, according to tracking data from maritime company Kpler.
The images do not make it possible to determine whether it is thick crude oil or "a thin light oil sheen," Zwijnenburg said.
"If it is crude oil, then it is a serious pollution risk as this will end up on the beaches, affect marine ecosystems, including birds and turtles that can get stuck," he said.
"If it is a light oil sheen and mostly diluted oil, the hope is that it evaporates fast, and (you) only have short-term risks," Zwijnenburg added.
Foul odours
Many residents in the north of the country have reported chemical smells on social media in recent days, including residents in northern districts of Dubai, the largest city in the UAE.
"For the past two days it smelled like 10 gas stations spilled their gas everywhere," a Sharjah resident told AFP, asking to remain anonymous.
"I was on my balcony and panicked thinking gas was leaking in my house and I will blow up everyone."
The UAE says the odours "pose no health risks to residents".
Beyond efforts to contain the oil spill, "monitoring and assessing its environmental impact will also be essential to protecting marine ecosystems and the communities that depend on them," Inesaf Benzaki, campaigns lead at Greenpeace MENA, told AFP.
Since the start of the Middle East war in February with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, Tehran has claimed control over the Strait of Hormuz and regularly targets ships that transit there without its authorisation.
Washington, in response, has imposed a blockade on Iranian ports and escorts tankers through the passageway.

articles.title: Iran has "increased efforts to target U.S. personnel," intel chief warns
articles.body:
Iran has "increased efforts to target U.S. personnel," intel chief warns
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Friday that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries.
The warning, contained in an unclassified memo that was sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and obtained by CBS News, comes as the State Department adjusts staffing at diplomatic posts across the Middle East, and the U.S. military pares back its footprint in the region, amid concerns about direct threats from Iran and threats from the Iranian-backed Houthi movement in Yemen.
"The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," Clayton wrote.
The memo, which was issued as the Trump administration weighs resuming military strikes against Iran, does not identify specific targets or countries where the alleged plots are underway, or indicate whether attacks may be imminent.
Clayton said the U.S. intelligence community is working to downgrade sensitive intelligence — received through various channels — so it can be shared more broadly with State Department personnel. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was copied on the memo.
Axios was first to report on the memo.
The warning follows a series of precautions at U.S. diplomatic facilities across the region. Earlier this week, the State Department ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel and their families to depart Saudi Arabia. Several other American embassies in the region adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status, which allows them to reduce the number of personnel without formally going on ordered departure, CBS News previously reported.
"When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment," a U.S. official told CBS News on Friday. "The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting U.S. officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO [Restricted Operations] Status in the region."
A U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official also told CBS News this week that the military has been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing threats.
Houthi militants have stepped up drone and missile attacks against Saudi Arabia, targeting oil infrastructure and airports. One strike on Riyadh's King Khalid Airport earlier this month killed at least a dozen people, including a U.S. citizen, and injured hundreds more.
Last weekend, U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and other countries warned Americans to exercise caution due to Houthi attacks.
Although the U.S. and Iran have refrained from striking each other in recent weeks, President Trump has not ruled out restarting hostilities after next month's midterm elections. Iran has also continued to take responsibility for attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.
At a campaign rally in Florida on Friday, Mr. Trump suggested the U.S. could launch another operation against Iran if Tehran failed to reach an agreement.
"We may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," the president said, invoking the name of the U.S. military campaign launched in February.

articles.title: Saved wounded soldiers since 2015: Journalist and veteran Olena Sharhovska dies
articles.body:
Saved wounded soldiers since 2015: Journalist and veteran Olena Sharhovska dies
Olena "Jane" Sharhovska, a veteran of the Hospitallers medical battalion who worked as a translator and journalist in civilian life, has died. Olena had been saving wounded soldiers since 2015.
Source: Yana Zinkevych, commander of the Hospitallers medical battalion; Sharhovska's former colleagues at Novynarnia
Details: Olena had extensive experience in the media, working as a journalist, translator, editor and social media specialist. Over the course of her career, she worked in television and print media, as well as on projects for Ukraїner and Osvitoria.
From 2015 onwards, she dedicated herself to saving others. Jane volunteered on the front line with the First Volunteer Mobile Hospital named after Mykola Pyrohov. She later joined the Hospitallers.
"Having mastered tactical medicine, Jane went to evacuate the wounded from the hottest sections of the front line, snatching the lives of our soldiers from the jaws of death on the way to stabilisation points," Zinkevych said.
In addition to helping the wounded, the paramedic and her fellow servicewomen campaigned for women's right to serve in the Armed Forces of Ukraine on an equal footing with men.
In particular, she became a co-organiser of the Invisible Battalion March, an event held in Kyiv in 2016. Participants called on the authorities to allow women to hold military positions that had previously been open only to men.
Jane was in Portugal when Russia launched its full-scale invasion. An injury prevented her from returning to Ukraine immediately, but she supported the country as a volunteer.
On 10 September 2022, her birthday, Olena joined the military. Serving with the International Legion of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, she was deployed in Bakhmut, Toretsk and Kharkiv Oblast.
In addition to carrying out medical evacuations, Jane provided tactical medicine training to other service members and, as a member of the Women's Veteran Movement, campaigned for female defenders to receive proper equipment.
She was discharged from military service in August 2024 due to health reasons.
"Olena was a person of words and travel, with a deep interest in the world and in people [...] Despite all the difficulties and trials, she retained her love of words and people, continued helping her brothers- and sisters-in-arms with fundraising, and bought vehicles for the front.
"Her motto in life was: 'Do what you believe needs to be done, and then come what may,'" Novynarnia said.
Bohdan Lohvynenko, a serviceman, journalist, writer and founder of Ukraїner, also shared his memories of Olena.
"We lived in neighbouring buildings in Vynohradar and often sat in one of our kitchens discussing editorial matters. You were an enormous source of support and a driving force behind many processes, while at the same time remaining quite harsh towards the unknown. I would always remind you of what you had once said about those whose ranks you later joined. And we often laughed about it," her former colleague wrote.
Background: Earlier, Yaryna Nishtuk, a defender from Lviv who served as a platoon commander of strike unmanned aerial systems, was killed in action.

articles.title: Polish PM says Zelenskyy will not support Lviv Oblast's move to declare 2027 Year of UPA
articles.body:
Polish PM says Zelenskyy will not support Lviv Oblast's move to declare 2027 Year of UPA
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said during a press conference as part of his visit to India that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had made it clear he would not support any further steps by Lviv Oblast Council concerning the designation of 2027 as the Year of the UPA The UPA, or Ukrainian Insurgent Army, was a nationalist paramilitary organisation that fought for Ukrainian independence during and after World War II, primarily against Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union and Roman Shukhevych, one of its commanders-in-chief.
Source: European Pravda, citing Ukrinform;
Details: Tusk said Zelenskyy had signalled that, if the subsequent procedure depended on him, he would not support the initiative in any way. Tusk added that Zelenskyy had been very unhappy about what had happened.
Tusk also said he had made considerable efforts to resolve the "orders crisis" and to explain why decisions of this kind harmed Ukraine's interests and needed to be considered in the context of the two nations' difficult shared history.
He acknowledged the complexity and ambiguity of the history of both countries, while stressing that Ukrainians could not seek any justification regarding the Volyn tragedy The Volyn (Volhynia) tragedy was a series of events that led to the ethnic cleansing of the Polish and Ukrainian populations in 1943 during World War II. It was part of a long-standing rivalry between Ukrainians and Poles in what is now Ukraine's west. Poland considers the Volyn tragedy a genocide of Poles and Shukhevych.
Tusk said he understood all the complexities and wanted Poles to understand that there was considerable ambiguity in both Polish and Ukrainian history. However, he stressed that genocide could not be justified in any way. He warned that Ukraine would face serious difficulties with its integration into the EU if it failed to respect Poland's sensitivities on the issue, adding that Poland was not demanding anything extraordinary in the first place.
Tusk added that he had spent many hours explaining the Polish perspective on the issue to Zelenskyy and had come away with the impression that the Ukrainian president understood it.
Meanwhile, Tusk said he could hardly be held responsible for decisions taken by individual members of Lviv's district or oblast councils. He described the move as resembling a planned provocation by a local nationalist and called it very unwise and unnecessary.
Background:
- On 20 October, Lviv Oblast Council voted to designate 2027 as the Year of Roman Shukhevych, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) and Oleh Olzhych. The decision immediately drew criticism from Polish officials. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, in particular, said the move was helping Ukraine's adversaries.
- European Pravda previously reported that Poland had suspended the delivery of a military aid package to Ukraine over Lviv Oblast Council's decision to designate 2027 as the Year of the UPA and Roman Shukhevych. The information was provided by a source in the Ukrainian government.
- Poland's Ministry of National Defence later denied reports that the delivery of a major aid package had been suspended because Lviv Oblast Council had designated 2027 as the Year of the UPA and Roman Shukhevych.

articles.title: Ukraine-Russia war sees more strikes in occupied territories as Starlink speeds return to normal
articles.body:
A Ukrainian strike in part of the northeastern Kharkiv region held by Russia killed at least three people and gravely wounded another on Saturday, according to the Moscow-backed authorities.
"Three civilians were killed and a woman was seriously wounded as a result of a strike by a Ukrainian drone on a car in the village of Pisky in the Kharkiv region," Vitaliy Ganchev, a local Russia-installed governor, wrote on Telegram.
Russia's defence ministry reported having shot down a total of 616 Ukrainian drones during the night across more than 20 regions of the country.
Several people were wounded as a result of falling drone debris, which also started fires, according to local Russian authorities.
Another drone barrage damaged industrial infrastructure in Togliatti, on the Volga river in southeastern Russia, said the city's mayor, Ilya Sukhikh.
Three bodies were pulled from the rubble after a Friday night attack on a factory in Oryol, about 370 kilometres (230 miles) southwest of Moscow, the Russian authorities said.
Five people were also seriously wounded and are in intensive care, according to the emergency services.
On the Ukrainian side, the air force said that Russia had launched at least 126 drones at Ukraine overnight, of which 101 were shot down.
Two people were wounded in the capital, Kiev, according to the emergency services.
Ukrainian attack cuts water, power in occupied Crimea
Meanwhile, a separate Ukrainian attack led to water and power cuts in occupied Crimea on Saturday, when a drone barrage hit southeastern Russia, according to the Russian authorities.
"As a result of an incident that occurred on the main power grids outside our region, caused by an enemy attack using a drone, restrictions on the supply of electricity and water have been put in place," Sergei Aksyonov, the Moscow-installed head of the Crimean peninsula, wrote on Telegram.
He did not specify the number of households affected in Crimea, which is home to more than 2.5 million people.
The peninsula, which was seized from Ukraine by Russia in 2014, is a regular target for Ukrainian attacks.
Ukraine says Starlink and Starshield operating at 400 kph after week of throttling
The Starlink satellite communications system and its military version Starshield are operating again at speeds over 400 km per hour, Kiev's defence minister said on Saturday, after over a week of service restrictions that slowed connections and disrupted military operations.
"The Ministry of Defence's monitoring systems are recording a return to normal speed for Starlink/Starshield. We are recording a speed of over 400 kph. The connection is stable," Evhenii Khmara told reporters.
The Ukrainian military does not disclose the systems' maximum operating speeds, and the defence ministry did not say whether service had been fully restored.
"Monitoring systems had previously recorded disruptions to the Starlink/Starshield service. The speed metrics have now returned to normal," the ministry said.
The restrictions, first reported on October 14, undermined Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian attack drones and disrupted frontline communications, Ukrainian officials said.
Sources said connection speeds had been reduced to about 160 kph or less.
Ukraine's problems with SpaceX-owned Starlink came after US President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel and waived new sanctions on Moscow while pressing Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil refineries.
Neither SpaceX boss Elon Musk nor the US government has acknowledged responsibility for restricting Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine. Both have said publicly that any such decision could only have been taken by the other.

articles.title: The US naval blockade of Iran: an illegal act of coercion
articles.body:
The US naval blockade of Iran: an illegal act of coercion
TEHRAN - An examination of the legal grounds for the US blockade of Iranian ports, what the UN Charter says, and how international law experts assess the action.
Imagine a country deciding to stop another country’s commercial ships, prevent goods from reaching its ports, and effectively impose its own rules on vessels travelling through international waters. Does military power, combined with claims of national security, give that country the right to do so? If the answer is yes, what would stop any major power from turning the seas into tools of pressure and blockade whenever it has a dispute with another country?
These questions lie at the heart of the US naval blockade of Iran. A naval blockade is not simply a matter of stopping ships. It can disrupt a country’s trade, drive up economic costs, and affect people’s daily lives. For that reason, international law does not give countries unlimited authority to restrict maritime traffic simply because they have military superiority or claim to be acting for security reasons.
Under international law, the US naval blockade of Iran cannot be justified simply by Washington’s announcement or its claims of national security. Given the absence of UN Security Council authorisation and the lack of a valid legal basis for self-defence, the blockade, as part of the use of force against Iran, is illegal. One important distinction must be made, however: even during wartime, rules govern how a naval blockade may be carried out. Possible compliance with some of those rules does not, by itself, make the original use of force lawful.
What does the UN Charter say?
The main legal document relevant to the US action is the United Nations Charter. Article 2(4) prohibits states from threatening or using force against other states. The purpose of this rule is to prevent governments from using their military strength to impose their will on other countries.
The Charter recognises two principal legal grounds for the use of force: authorisation by the UN Security Council and self-defence under the conditions set out in Article 51. A country seeking to justify a military blockade of another country must therefore demonstrate that its actions fall within one of these legal frameworks.
In the case of the blockade of Iran, the United States cannot create its own legal authority simply by declaring a security emergency or seeking to put economic pressure on Iran. If the military action lacks a valid basis under the UN Charter, it cannot become lawful merely because Washington gives it an official name or announces a justification.
What do international law experts say?
One important contribution to the legal debate is an article by Michael Schmitt, a professor and specialist in international law, published by Just Security. In his article, “Iran’s Conditions for Reopening Hormuz: What International Law Requires, Permits, and Forbids,” Schmitt examines the legal basis for the US use of force against Iran.
Schmitt explains that, under the UN Charter, the use of force must generally be based on Security Council authorisation or the right of self-defence in response to an armed attack. According to his analysis, most international law experts believe that the initial US attack was not authorised by the Security Council and did not meet the necessary conditions to qualify as self-defence. He therefore considers the start of US military operations to be inconsistent with the country’s obligations under the UN Charter.
His analysis is directly relevant to the blockade. If the legality of the original use of force is in question, the blockade cannot be treated as an entirely separate action and declared lawful simply by referring to the rules of naval warfare.
Steve Prest, a retired naval officer and analyst at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), raises similar concerns in his article, “The ‘US Blockade’ of Iran: How It Might Function (Or Not!).” He argues that the legality of the US action depends on whether the necessary conditions for using force have been met. Without Security Council authorisation, self-defence is the principal legal justification available to Washington, but Prest points to serious questions about whether that argument can justify the operation.
These analyses highlight the central issue: the question is not merely how the United States stops ships, but on what legal grounds it claims the right to use military force to blockade Iranian ports.
Do the laws of war make the US blockade legal?
The United States may argue that naval blockades are a recognised method of warfare. That claim reflects part of the legal picture, but it does not tell the whole story.
The San Remo Manual on International Law Applicable to Armed Conflicts at Sea, adopted in 1994, sets out restrictions on naval blockades. Under its rules, a blockade must be declared, its limits must be specified, and it must be effectively enforced. It must also respect the rights of neutral states. Rules protecting civilians and ensuring access to essential supplies must be observed as well.
The San Remo Manual is not, in itself, a binding treaty. However, it is a recognised reference for assessing the law governing naval warfare.
The key point is simple: the fact that certain methods of warfare may be lawful does not mean that starting a war or using force is lawful.
A legal analysis published by German broadcaster Tagesschau on 18 July 2026 makes the same distinction. Citing Pierre Thielbörger, a professor of international law at the University of Bochum, the report explains that the legality of resorting to force must be distinguished from the legality of how military operations are conducted. In other words, a particular action may be assessed separately under the rules of naval warfare, but that does not erase the possibility that the war itself was unlawful.
For this reason, citing the rules governing naval blockades does not, on its own, answer the fundamental question: did the United States have the legal right to use force to blockade Iranian ports in the first place?
US sanctions do not give Washington the right to shut down Iran’s trade
Another issue is the attempt to link the naval blockade to US sanctions. Washington may place companies or ships on its sanctions lists, but a decision made by one government does not automatically become international law.
Keri Batsov, a former US Treasury Department official, said: “Iran will not surrender under sanctions; the naval blockade has worn down the US military, and Iran’s low-cost drones have challenged Washington’s expensive weapons.”
Article 92 of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea recognises the principle that ships on the high seas are generally subject to the jurisdiction of their flag state. Article 110 sets out specific circumstances in which foreign ships may be boarded on the high seas.
These provisions make clear that the seizure of ships in international waters requires a legal basis. A vessel’s commercial links to Iran, or its inclusion on a US sanctions list, does not by itself give the United States unlimited authority to seize it.
Mark Nevitt, a legal scholar specialising in military and maritime law, raised concerns about this issue in an article published by Just Security on 1 May 2026. He warns that the United States is grouping several types of maritime operations, each with a different legal basis, under the single label of a “blockade.” He distinguishes a blockade of Iranian ports from the seizure of US-sanctioned ships in different parts of the world, stressing that each operation must have its own clear legal justification.
This distinction is crucial. Even if a limited blockade under certain conditions of armed conflict can be defended on legal grounds, that does not give the United States the authority to stop every ship linked to Iran anywhere in the world.
The human cost of a naval blockade
A naval blockade is not just a military measure directed at ports. Its effects can reach deep into the economy and people’s everyday lives. Restrictions on ships entering and leaving ports can disrupt trade, raise shipping costs, and make essential goods more difficult to obtain.
International humanitarian law contains rules intended to prevent unjustifiable harm to civilians. Using starvation of civilians as a method of warfare is prohibited, and a blockade must not be used as an excuse to disregard people’s essential needs.
Ismail Kowsari, an Iranian parliament member and member of the National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, has called for legal action over US measures against Iran. He said international legal mechanisms lack sufficient power and enforcement guarantees to address violations and hold those responsible to account. This, he said, has allowed some powers to pursue their interests without sufficient regard for the rights of other countries and peoples.
Kowsari said it was necessary to stand firmly against this approach and to drive the United States out of the region so that international law could be implemented in practice. Criticising international judicial institutions for failing to address US violations earlier, he said this should not bring legal efforts to a halt. Iran’s judiciary, he argued, should carefully document US actions and violations against Iran, including the naval blockade, and pursue them through legal channels.
Kowsari also stressed the need to document the humanitarian consequences of sanctions, particularly in the medical and pharmaceutical sectors. He said patients and vulnerable groups depend on essential medicines and medical equipment, and that any disruption to access could have serious consequences. Despite these needs, he added, sanctions can obstruct access to essential supplies while those imposing them continue without sufficient regard for the human impact.
He said the effects of these measures should be recorded accurately through credible documents, evidence, and other supporting material so that they can be pursued before the competent international bodies.
Assessing a blockade therefore requires more than counting the number of ships stopped or measuring the economic pressure it creates. Its impact on civilians must also be examined, including whether essential supplies remain available in practice.
A naval blockade can thus become more than an instrument of military pressure. It can develop into a humanitarian and legal crisis, and governments cannot escape responsibility simply by declaring that their actions serve security objectives.
The UN Charter and the analyses of international law experts show that the blockade of Iran cannot be assessed solely through the technical rules of naval warfare. The fundamental question remains: on what legal basis is the United States using force to blockade Iranian ports?
Michael Schmitt, writing for Just Security, questions the legal basis for the initial US attack. Steve Prest, writing for RUSI, raises serious doubts about whether self-defence can justify the operation. Mark Nevitt, also writing for Just Security, explains why a limited blockade cannot be turned into a blanket licence to seize sanctioned ships around the world. The UN Charter sets out the underlying principle: the use of force must be justified under international law.
The US naval blockade of Iran is therefore illegal in the absence of Security Council authorisation and a valid legal basis for the use of force. The rules of naval warfare cannot, on their own, resolve this fundamental problem. Nor do unilateral US sanctions give Washington unlimited authority to control Iran’s maritime trade.
This is not just about Iran. It is about whether major powers will abide by the rules they accepted as part of the international order established after the Second World War. If military power is allowed to replace the law, naval blockades will no longer be exceptional measures. They could become tools that powerful countries use whenever they want to force another state to submit to their demands.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Ukraine received only 24 Patriot missiles from US over 3 months
articles.body:
Zelenskyy: Ukraine received only 24 Patriot missiles from US over 3 months
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that Ukraine has received only 24 interceptor missiles for Patriot air defence systems from the United States over the past three months.
Source: Zelenskyy in an interview with ABC News, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Zelenskyy said he did not feel betrayed by the US but expressed regret over the lack of American assistance.
"I feel what I feel. It's not supportive," Zelenskyy said.
Zelenskyy also noted that Ukraine has received only 24 Patriot interceptor missiles from the US over the past three months, while it needs far more.
He said that 30 ballistic missiles had struck the Ukrainian capital Kyiv on the night of 21-22 October alone. According to Zelenskyy, Ukraine needs an average of 350 Patriot interceptor missiles per month.
Background:
- A few days ago, Zelenskyy said that the US Department of Defense was delaying the delivery of resources needed by Ukraine.
- Earlier, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused the United States of trying to pressure Kyiv into capitulating to Russia.

articles.title: Land phase of Russian-Indian Indra 2026 exercise over in Chelyabinsk Region
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. The land phase of the joint Russian-Indian military exercise Indra 2026 has concluded at a training ground in the Chelyabinsk Region, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"The land phase of the Indra 2026 maneuvers concluded with a combat rehearsal at a training ground of the Central Military District in the Chelyabinsk Region. According to the exercise scenario, a simulated enemy had occupied a settlement and established strongpoints there," the statement said.
During the combat rehearsal, unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) and ground robotic systems crews conducted aerial reconnaissance of enemy positions. Artillery units, in coordination with attack UAVs, struck detected concentrations of enemy personnel, weapons, command and observation posts, and supply depots, creating favorable conditions for offensive operations by Russian and Indian assault groups.
Assault troops, supported by FPV interceptors, mobile armed units, air defense systems, and tank crews, inflicted heavy casualties on the enemy, captured its positions, and liberated the settlement.
During the pursuit of the enemy, Russian and Indian troops destroyed the remaining personnel and equipment of the simulated enemy, thereby concluding the combat rehearsal of the Indra 2026 drills’ land phase.
Afterward, a formal closing ceremony for the land phase of the joint exercise was held on the field camp’s parade ground.

articles.title: U.S. air base in Japan to block Chinese BYD cars over data fears
articles.body:
- Kadena Air Base will bar all BYD vehicles from Oct. 26, including private cars, taxis and delivery vans, Yonhap reported.
- The U.S. Air Force’s 18th Security Forces Squadron will turn back BYD vehicles at every gate with no exceptions.
Kadena Air Base in Okinawa will bar all vehicles made by Chinese electric carmaker BYD from entering the installation starting Oct. 26 over concerns that the cars could expose sensitive military information, Kangnam Times reported.
The ban covers privately owned cars as well as contractor vehicles, taxis, delivery vans and other commercial vehicles. The 18th Security Forces Squadron, which guards the base’s key facilities, will stop BYD vehicles at every gate and direct them to turn around, and the base does not plan to grant exceptions, according to the report.
Kadena is one of the U.S. Air Force’s largest bases in the Indo-Pacific and home to the 18th Wing, part of Fifth Air Force, which operates fighters, aerial refueling and surveillance aircraft from the island.
The concern centers on how modern electric vehicles work. Many use cameras and sensors to map their surroundings and rely on software and network connections that can send data to outside servers or allow remote access. Information gathered by a car driving through a base could reveal the layout of facilities and patterns of military activity.
A similar problem surfaced last month in Norway, where rental cars used by the Norwegian Armed Forces during Exercise Hovedstad near Oslo Airport from Sept. 14 to 18 recorded soldiers, their movements and the access codes they typed at military gates. At least two of the vehicles were Deepal models built by Chinese state-owned automaker Changan and supplied by Hertz Norge, which is indirectly owned by China’s Geely group, Norwegian business daily Dagens Næringsliv reported.
Other militaries have already restricted Chinese-made cars. Poland has barred Chinese-made vehicles from certain military facilities, citing the risk that onboard sensors and cameras could collect sensitive data, and the Israel Defense Forces has banned Chinese vehicles from its bases.
The U.S. military has tightened rules on Chinese technology at its installations for years. In 2018, the Pentagon ordered base exchanges worldwide to stop selling smartphones made by Huawei and ZTE over security concerns. In June 2026, the U.S. Department of War reportedly added BYD to its list of Chinese military companies operating in the United States, a list that does not by itself ban the use of a company’s products.
BYD has been expanding in Japan, launching models tailored to the Japanese market and opening more dealerships, particularly in regional areas where public transportation is limited.
