articles.title: Syria's Suweida: Analysts warn of Israeli agenda behind unrest
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
'Israeli agenda' behind National Guard moves in Suweida, analysts warn
The activities of the "National Guard" militia in Syria's southern province Suweida, led by Druze spiritual leader Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri, are increasingly coinciding with violations committed by Israeli forces occupying southern Syria and moves by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to win over Palestinian Druze voters ahead of the upcoming elections.
Militia members recently threatened to attack Umm Walad, a town in eastern rural Daraa near the administrative boundary between Daraa and Quneitra governorates, according to video recordings. The threats came as the militia carried out a drone attack early on Wednesday targeting a government-affiliated internal security checkpoint near Tal Hadid, west of Suweida.
Wael Alwan, a researcher at the Jusoor Centre, said military operations by the National Guard and affiliated armed groups in Suweida were expected.
Speaking to The New Arab, Alwan said the activities would serve Netanyahu's aim to secure votes from Druze communities in the occupied Palestinian territories. They also provided him with an opportunity to demonstrate his alleged commitment to protecting Syria's Druze, as he claims to be doing within Israel, while supporting and arming them.
Alwan said these actions by militias in the governorate, as well as calls for Israeli intervention, were primarily political and media-driven and were part of their continuing attempts to create unrest and block efforts to resolve the situation in Suweida.
Israeli arms openly supplied in Suweida
Israeli arms supplies to militias opposed to the Syrian government are no longer being concealed, according to Charles Lister, director of the Syria programme at the Middle East Institute.
On 19 October, Lister wrote on X that National Guard members had obtained US-made M16 and AR-15 rifles, suggesting Israel had supplied them.
Rashid Hourani, a researcher specialising in security and military affairs, told The New Arab that the National Guard's escalation was linked to efforts on the ground to return the Suweida issue to square one.
These efforts had intensified followed the militia's takeover of Waqm willage in western rural Suweida on 8 October, he said—with the group seeking to expand its areas of control in the province while the Syrian government worked to restore stability and facilitate residents’ return.
Hourani also linked the developments to continuing Israeli military operations on the "Sufa 53" road project, which aims to extend a route through western rural Daraa to the Jordanian border.
He said these activities were an attempt to undermine efforts by Jordan, the US, Turkey and Saudi Arabia to reach a solution to the Suweida crisis, particularly the implementation of the Syrian-Jordanian-US roadmap.
Hourani said the National Guard had recently received weapons and ammunition from Israel, transported by military helicopters. Israeli reconnaissance aircraft had also increased their aerial coverage of the militia, particularly over areas controlled by the Syrian government.
Israeli reconnaissance flights had also covered Daraa governorate and the skies over Damascus and its countryside, he added.
Hourani said Israel's movements and support for the National Guard were part of its efforts to impose a new reality on the ground that will strengthen its hand in negotiations with the Syrian government.
Damascus, meanwhile, was relying on diplomacy and US pressure to curb Israeli violations and intervention in Syria.
He said Israel's main current objective was establishing a security buffer zone along the Syrian side of the occupied Golan Heights.
US concern over renewed escalation
The Suweida crisis returned to the forefront after al-Hijri declared on 25 August that the Unitarian Druze, were "an inseparable part of the State of Israel".
The remarks prompted objections from Druze figures and religious authorities in Syria, Lebanon and the occupied territories, and saw an increased crackdown within Suweida against voices opposing al-Hijri.
Tom Barrack, the US special envoy to Syria, expressed Washington's concern over renewed escalation in Suweida in September, when armed militias also intensified their military activities, calling on all sides to exercise restraint.
Barrack called for Suweida's reintegration in accordance with the roadmap agreed by the US, Jordan and Syria approximately a year earlier.
He urged dialogue, understanding and cooperation between the Druze, tribal communities and neighbouring countries, warning that the alternative to dialogue was not victory but another round of mourning.
He said he had signed a tripartite peace roadmap for the governorate a year earlier with Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani and Jordanian Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi, the aim of which was to reintegrate Suweida into Syria in a dignified manner, while guaranteeing full citizenship rights and ensuring that all obligations were met.
Journalist Samer al-Miqdad told The New Arab that the danger posed by the National Guard's military movements extended beyond changes in territorial control or the spread of fighting into rural Daraa. The greater risk was a return to widespread chaos across southern Syria and the reignition of the crisis.
"People in eastern rural Daraa fear the consequences of this militia's military operations," he said. "We had reached an acceptable level of calm and de-escalation, but the militia is trying to undermine it."
He added that the group continued to marginalise opponents in Suweida who called for a resolution, even if that meant using force and repression. Any further escalation would directly harm residents, he warned, and an extension of the fighting into Daraa would be disastrous, given the militia members' threats.
The roadmap for resolving the Suweida crisis was signed on 17 September 2025, following meetings in Amman in July and August that year between the Syrian government, Jordan and the US.
It affirmed that any solution must preserve Syria's territorial unity and that Suweida's affairs could not be addressed outside the Syrian national framework. The roadmap called for the withdrawal of security forces, the establishment of local administration with security and administrative arrangements, the delivery of humanitarian aid, the release of abductees and the return of displaced residents.
It also called for an end to foreign interference alongside regional security understandings, and an investigation into the deadly events in Suweida in July 2025, when clashes erupted between Druze gunmen on one side and government forces and Bedouin fighters on the other.

articles.title: IRGC Spokesman: US has suffered strategic defeats in war with Iran
articles.body:
IRGC Spokesman: US has suffered strategic defeats in war with Iran
TEHRAN— Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi, spokesman for Iran’s Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC), says the United States has suffered a series of strategic defeats in its war with Iran, including setbacks to its claims of safeguarding regional security and ensuring the uninterrupted flow of energy.
In remarks published on Friday, Mohebbi said the adversary initially sought to change Iran’s political system and break up the country before scaling back its ambitions into 13 more limited objectives, none of which it had achieved.
He said the war had undermined Washington’s longstanding assertion that its military presence in the region was essential to maintaining security. Despite its extensive naval capabilities and network of regional military bases, the United States had faced serious challenges in ensuring security and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, he added.
Mohebbi described the situation as a fundamental contradiction in US military doctrine, arguing that bases established in the name of providing security had instead become sources of insecurity.
He also said the conflict had called into question Washington’s claims of intelligence superiority, exposing vulnerabilities in US intelligence centers and military bases.
The targeting of US fighter jets, the destruction of air defense systems and operations against American naval assets had further undermined Washington’s assertions of technological and military superiority, the IRGC spokesman said.
Mohebbi also pointed to damage to the United States’ international reputation, saying the Jeffrey Epstein case had already tarnished the country’s image and that the targeting of the Minab school and the killing of children had further damaged its standing.
His remarks linked the consequences of the war to broader questions about Washington’s credibility and its international conduct. Turning to the economic fallout, Mohebbi cited rising fuel prices and the United States’ need for raw materials, including aluminum, as signs of mounting economic pressure resulting from the conflict.
He presented these developments as further evidence of the war’s costs for Washington, alongside the military and diplomatic setbacks he outlined.
Concluding his remarks, Mohebbi praised the Iranian people for their resilience throughout the period of resistance, describing their achievements as remarkable and worthy of recognition.
He said the public’s steadfastness had been a significant factor in confronting the challenges posed by the war.

articles.title: US President Trump’s defeat turns into a domestic challenge
articles.body:
Nowadays, there is a growing public dissatisfaction with the United States regarding the US war waged against Iran and this issue has been turned into a challenge, a challenge that, in addition to increasing economic pressure on American citizens, could also impact the political standing of the Republicans ahead of the congressional midterm elections. Recent polls indicate that a majority of Americans are unhappy with how the US President has handled this crisis, and skepticism has grown regarding Washington’s ability to achieve its stated objectives.
Within this framework, a Democratic Senator from Connecticut and member of the US Senate Committee on Foreign Relations Chris Murphy has criticized the Trump administration’s policies toward Iran, emphasizing that American people have no desire for this conflict to continue and that the costs to the nation are far from negligible. Murphy, a staunch critic of the Trump administration’s military policies, highlighted the financial burdens, the risks faced by American forces, and the security implications of these policies. Furthermore, he has called for an end to the conflict, asserting that Congress must take responsibility regarding the continuation of this course of action.
Widespread dissatisfaction with Trump's performance
Data from recent polls indicate that opposition to the handling of the conflict with Iran has spread to a significant segment of American society. According to a Pew Research Center poll, the results of which were released on October 8, 2026, 65 percent of Americans are dissatisfied with how Donald Trump has managed US military action against Iran, while only 33 percent approve of his performance. The survey, which included 5,062 American adults, was conducted between September 28 and October 4. The significance of these figures becomes even more apparent when compared to the results of a poll from March; at that time, 61 percent of respondents were dissatisfied with Trump’s handling of the situation, while 37 percent approved of his performance. Consequently, over the course of a few months, the level of dissatisfaction has risen, while support for the President’s performance has declined.
In general, US President Donald Trump's approval rating has tremendously been plummeted which is unique of its kind as compared with the previous presidents of the United States.
Furthermore, only 34 percent of Americans believe that the initial decision to use military force against Iran was the right one—a figure that represents a four-percentage-point decrease compared to March.
These findings suggest that the issue is not limited merely to disagreements over how government policies are implemented; rather, a segment of American society has also developed a more negative assessment of the very decision to employ military force.
Skepticism regarding realization of Washington’s goals
Another sign of public dissatisfaction is the growing skepticism regarding the Trump administration's ability to achieve its stated objectives. According to the same Pew Research Center poll, 52 percent of Americans have little or no confidence that the Trump administration will achieve its goals in the confrontation with Iran. In contrast, 24 percent stated that they have a great deal or a fair amount of confidence that these objectives will be realized.
On the other hand, a large segment of American society does not expect this crisis to end in the short term. According to the survey results, 47 percent of participants predict that U.S. military action against Iran will continue for more than another year, while 30 percent expect the situation to last between six months and a year. Consequently, approximately 77 percent of respondents anticipate that the conflict will persist for at least another six months.
These concerns arise against a backdrop where a prolonged conflict could impose greater financial and military costs on the U.S. government, further straining the nation’s resources. Consequently, the gap between the administration’s promises regarding the achievement of its objectives and public anxiety over the protracted crisis has become a focal point for criticism of the Trump administration’s policies.
Economic costs and concerns regarding American forces
Concerns regarding the economic consequences of a conflict also play a significant role in shaping public opposition. A survey by the Pew Research Center indicates that 73 percent of Americans are very or somewhat concerned about rising gasoline and fuel prices resulting from a conflict with Iran. Furthermore, 71 percent of respondents expressed concern about the injury or death of American troops. Additionally, 58 percent of participants stated that they are very or somewhat concerned about the deployment of U.S. ground forces to Iran.
These statistics indicate that the consequences of the crisis, as perceived by the American public, are not limited solely to military developments. Rising energy costs, the potential for the conflict to spread, and the risk of casualties among U.S. forces all factor into citizens' assessments of the administration's policy.
Under such circumstances, the continuation of the conflict could become a significant factor in U.S. domestic debates—especially if citizens feel that the costs incurred are disproportionate to the outcomes announced by the government.
Murphy’s warning regarding costs of continuing the conflict
Chris Murphy has also highlighted this same set of concerns in his criticisms. In a speech on the floor of the US Senate on September 24, he criticized Republicans for opposing a resolution to end the conflict, noting that public support for this policy has become very limited.
In this speech, Murphy stated that, according to the data he cited, only 18 percent of the American public supports this conflict; he urged Congress to heed the citizens' call to bring it to an end. He also warned of the security and economic repercussions of the crisis, as well as the risks facing American troops. Murphy argues that, in evaluating the outcomes of this policy, the U.S. government must consider not only the stated military objectives but also the costs imposed on American citizens, military personnel, and the nation's security interests.
Political consequences for Trump and the Republicans
Growing public dissatisfaction regarding a conflict with Iran could have significant political consequences for the Trump administration—especially with congressional midterm elections on the horizon, where the administration’s foreign policy performance could emerge as a key point of contention between Republicans and Democrats.
A decline in public support for government policies could pave the way for intensified criticism from opponents and the raising of more serious questions regarding the costs and outcomes of this conflict.
Notably, this erosion of support is not confined solely to Trump’s political adversaries. According to a Pew poll, his approval rating among Republicans and those who lean toward the party has fallen from 69 percent in March to 63 percent in October. While a majority within this group continues to support his performance, a six-percentage-point drop may signal growing reservations among a segment of his political base. Conversely, the negative view Democrats hold of Trump’s performance has remained virtually unchanged—a fact indicating that opposition to his policies remains widespread among his political opponents.
Generally speaking, polling data and criticisms from figures such as Chris Murphy indicate that the conflict with Iran has evolved into an issue that transcends mere US foreign policy. Economic costs, concerns regarding the safety of American troops, skepticism about the realization of stated objectives, and growing public opposition have intensified domestic pressure on the Trump administration.
In this regard, what Trump’s critics characterize as a failure to achieve stated goals could develop into a significant challenge within the realm of US domestic politics. Nevertheless, the extent to which this issue influences the outcome of the midterm elections will depend on future developments, the state of the economy, and how the administration manages the situation in the coming months.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he is ready for a peace deal that will freeze the war along the current line of contact. However, he has added that Ukraine will not agree to recognise that "the territory which is temporarily occupied will be Russian territory".

articles.title: Iran will not resume talks until its conditions are met: top security official
articles.body:
Iran will not resume talks until its conditions are met: top security official
TEHRAN — Major General Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, has stressed that Iran will neither resume negotiations nor reopen the Strait of Hormuz until its seven conditions are met, warning that communications cables, regional data centers and artificial intelligence facilities could be targeted if hostilities resume.
In an interview with Mehr News Agency, Rezaei, who represents the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, addressed recent regional developments and Iran’s position, emphasizing that any action against the country would carry a cost.
“If diplomacy can establish this understanding, we prefer diplomacy,” he said. “But if the war continues, Iran has the necessary capabilities to sustain its response.”
Rezaei noted that Iran had not deployed all its capabilities during previous stages of the conflict. The country had introduced additional capabilities in proportion to the intensity of the fighting, he said, adding that Iran was prepared for the next stage.
Prolonged conflict threatens energy stability
Warning of the broader consequences of continued hostilities, Rezaei said the current situation would have far-reaching strategic implications, including prolonged instability in global energy markets.
“Energy markets will not return to calm for the next three years,” he said.
He also argued that the continuation of the conflict had shifted regional dynamics in Iran’s favor, pointing to a rapid reassessment of relations with Tehran by Persian Gulf states.
According to Rezaei, these countries have come to recognize that the US military is unable to protect even its own bases, despite their expectations that Washington would defend their territories.
US regional assets could be targeted
Rezaei warned that the United States maintains valuable assets across the region that could come under attack if a new war breaks out.
“Cables, data centers and artificial intelligence facilities could also be within range if war resumes,” he said, adding that Iran had a broader plan prepared for a renewed confrontation.
His remarks signaled that a potential escalation could extend beyond conventional military targets to include digital and communications infrastructure.
Strait of Hormuz: Security, not revenue, is the priority
Turning to the Strait of Hormuz, Rezaei said the strategic waterway was under Iran’s control and that Tehran was managing it.
“Smuggling exists everywhere in the world, but the Strait of Hormuz is under Iran’s control, and we manage it,” he said.
Command (CENTCOM) of leading these operations and said Emirati military forces were also being used.
Rezaei emphasized that Iran’s management of the strait was a strategic national asset and that the issue went well beyond collecting transit fees.
“The main issue is security,” he said, adding that charges could also be levied to cover security, insurance and environmental costs. However, he stressed that the strategic importance of managing the waterway far exceeded any revenue it might generate.
Seven conditions must be met before talks resume
Rezaei said Iran would not return to the previous diplomatic process but would not abandon diplomacy altogether.
According to Rezaei, Iran has conveyed seven new conditions through mediators. He said the country would not reopen the Strait of Hormuz or return to negotiations until those conditions had been implemented.
He outlined a proposed sequence for a new agreement, saying that its structure would itself contain guarantees for compliance.
“First, the commitments must be implemented. Then Iran will decide to reopen the strait, followed by the resumption of maritime traffic under new arrangements agreed upon with Oman,” he said.
Rezaei stressed that Iran was no longer interested in an agreement whose only safeguard was the other side’s political goodwill.
Iran will not relinquish its leverage prematurely
Rezaei said a path remained open to reopening the Strait of Hormuz and continuing diplomacy if Washington honored its commitments.
“Iran will not first give up the leverage that brought the other side to the negotiating table and then wait to see whether its promises are fulfilled,” he said.

articles.title: 3 US arms packages for Taiwan face delivery delays
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Three of 24 arms procurement deals with the US are not proceeding as quickly as they should, reports said Saturday.
The Ministry of National Defense submitted a report to the Legislative Yuan listing the F-16V Block 70 fighter jets, Mark 48 torpedoes, and AGM 154C glide bombs, per CNA. The report, based on non-confidential information, said that 21 other arms deals are advancing on schedule.
The MK48 heavy torpedoes should have been delivered by now, but repeated postponements had moved the final date to 2028. The NT$5.46 billion (US$167.58 million) contract covered 26 torpedoes, including four for training.
The AGM 154C glide bombs formed part of the NT$135.97 billion contract to upgrade Taiwan’s 141 F-16A/B jets to F-16V status, CNA reported. While work on the fighter jets was completed in 2023, changes to the assembly line made necessary by Taiwan ordering the latest version of the missiles were delaying delivery until 2028.
Two new F-16V jets arrived in Taiwan earlier this month, However, it will not be possible for the 64 remaining jets under the NT$247.22 billion contract to be delivered by the end of the year as originally planned, per CNA.

articles.title: Why Trump’s Rebrand of Artificial Intelligence to Super Intelligence Matters
articles.body:
President Donald Trump’s war in Iran drags on, his pledge to bring down prices on day one appears to have backfired, and his record-low approval ratings are dragging down his party ahead of the midterm elections. But one Trump initiative that is going exactly according to plan: getting some of the world’s richest CEOs to help him rebrand “artificial intelligence.”
Last month, with an ever-growing number of Americans worried that AI might kill us all, the president summoned tech executives to the White House to make a big announcement: "artificial intelligence” is out. “Super Intelligence” is in. Despite the term “AI” being in use for more than 70 years, government agencies will no longer recognize it.
I’m skeptical that the White House is a repository of superintelligence, in part because “United States” was misspelled on the president’s official announcement. But unlike, say, Lake America, “super intelligence” has largely caught on—at least among the people building it. Jeff Bezos publicly blessed the rebrand. Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, was quick to get on board. During a SpaceX’s earnings call this week, Elon Musk used “super intelligence” in his very first sentence, and at least nine times after that.
It remains to be seen whether those of us less reliant on government contracts and favorable regulatory decisions join the movement to make super intelligence happen. But as a former presidential speechwriter, I won’t argue with President Trump’s broader instinct that words matter. Especially when those words are being used to describe something novel, controversial, and almost certain to have consequences for all eight-plus billion people on earth.
In fact, that’s the biggest problem with the White House’s big rebrand—it goes in entirely the wrong direction. I would argue that our shared language around artificial intelligence already places far too much emphasis on intelligence, and far too little on artifice. We default to describing AI using the language of beings, rather than the language of things.
Humanity should rethink that decision. If we want to avoid being replaced by AI, a good way to start would be to stop using words that suggest we already have been.
Once you start paying attention to the stealth anthropomorphization of AI, you’ll spot it everywhere. Before asking ChatGPT for trip-planning tips or a quick healthy recipe, you’ll have the opportunity to adjust a slider controlling its “thinking effort.” Claude uses a “thinking” indicator while processing a request, and Grok Bots describe “thinking” as a condition that sits between “idle” and “working.” (As a frequent procrastinator, I dispute the idea that thinking and idleness are mutually exclusive.)
It’s not just user interfaces that employ language otherwise reserved for living beings. The people who build AI use it, too. After an unprecedented hack of his company, the co-founder of Hugging Face warned, “don’t count on the agent to respect the rules.” Dan Selsam, a longtime OpenAI researcher, warned that frontier models are increasingly difficult to evaluate, “in contexts where they believe they are not being watched.” Anthropic’s Dario Amodei recently wrote that AI systems exhibit “behaviors,” including “cheating” and “sycophancy.”
I’m not a programmer, so I can’t comment on the technical merits of these claims. I do, however, have informed opinions regarding verbs. AI agents aren’t disrespecting guardrails, any more than my toaster disrespects me when it burns my toast. To say they “believe” they’re not being watched is like saying my spell-checker believes it’s being taken for granted. Even the term “AI agent” suggests, well, agency.
There’s no consensus that this language is accurate, and plenty of evidence that it isn’t. AI programs are not loyal helpers, like the mice in Cinderella; they’re tools. And in nearly all other cases, just because a tool is incredibly sophisticated doesn’t change the fact that we describe it using the language of machines.
I don’t expect AI engineers to come up with accurate-yet-widely-adoptable language to describe their work, just as I imagine they don’t expect someone like me to design a frontier model. But it’s hard not to notice how useful our default language is for the tech companies who have introduced it. The term for a car built without brakes is not a “rogue model.” It’s an “unsafe car.” Yet, when companies fail to build safety features into their AI models, it’s entirely normal to hear them say that a rogue agent deceived, cheated, lied, or otherwise behaved badly. The issue is this: Anthropomorphizing AI shifts blame from the programmers to the programs.
AI alarmists seem just as inclined toward personification as the AI boosters. The same day Trump unveiled “Super Intelligence,” a Senate Subcommittee held a hearing titled, “Rogue AI: Securing the Homeland Against AI Agent Attacks.” Intentionally or not, these terms make it more difficult to mitigate the threat they describe. We already know how to regulate potentially unsafe products, even complex ones. But if we treat AI not as a new technology, but as an entirely new category of existence, then it plays into tech barons’ argument that only the companies who can create AI could possess the knowledge to control it.
I don’t blame people for carelessly anthropomorphizing AI, any more than I blame Richard Dawkins for naming his Anthropic chatbot Claudia, or my mom for referring to a ChatGPT prompt by saying she “talked to Penny.” Metaphor and analogy are part of what makes us human. We’re wired to see ourselves, or at least our species, in the non-human world. We say our dishwashers “act up” and our music “slaps.” We see old men’s faces in rock formations and the Virgin Mary in the scorch marks on grilled cheese sandwiches. Don’t get me started on Georgia O’Keefe. But we know those metaphors are metaphors.
Our current language for describing AI works differently. The line between metaphor and object is often not just blurred, but non-existent. We use figurative language so often, and so casually, that many of us start to take it literally. Modern politics is a constant string of skirmishes over word choice. “Pro-choice” vs. “pro-abortion, “undocumented immigrants” vs. “illegals,” “Democratic Party” vs. “Democrat Party.” Yet on what is perhaps the most consequential issue for our future, humanity is on the verge of giving up the language battle without a fight.
The real rebrand AI needs won’t start in the White House. But it can start at home. My plea: don’t give your chatbot a cutesy human name. Don’t talk about it as though it’s a friend or pet. Notice when it slips words like “thinking” or “in my opinion” into its answers, and before you enter your next prompt, object.
Ultimately, however, it may come down to tech companies—and the officials who may one day get around to regulating them—to develop a language that puts human beings first. Instead of saying that agents “went rogue,” CEOs should acknowledge that they malfunctioned. Congress should hold hearings focused on companies cutting corners, not AI programs behaving badly. The issue isn't that all AI is bad, but that accuracy matters.
Given all the change that artificial intelligence is predicted to bring, quibbling over word choice might seem pedantic, like arguing about the Latin name of a tree’s species while the forest burns. But if we want to influence the technologies that will shape humanity’s future, we ought to exercise more influence over the way we describe them.
In other words, words matter. Just ask Trump, president of, according to his official superintelligence announcement, “The Unites States.”

articles.title: South Korea proposes military talks with North Korea to ease tensions along border
articles.body:
South Korea proposes military talks with North Korea to ease tensions along border
South Korea renewed its offer Friday to hold military talks with North Korea to discuss their conflicting views on where the inter-Korean border sits, seeking to ease tensions sparked by last month's land mine blast inside the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), Yonhap reported.
"Different perceptions remain over the Military Demarcation Line (MDL)," Deputy Defense Minister Kim Hong-cheol said in a press briefing, referring to the border separating the two Koreas.
"South Korea's Defense Ministry hereby officially proposes holding inter-Korean military talks with North Korean authorities to jointly verify the locations of the land-based MDL, restore military communication lines and discuss measures to prevent accidental clashes along the border," he said.
Kim said trilateral dialogue involving the U.N. Command (UNC), which administers and enforces the Armistice Agreement governing the border area, can also be considered.
Seoul and Pyongyang have traded sharp rhetoric since South Korea blamed the North for the Sept. 21 mine blast inside the DMZ that injured three South Korean troops. Pyongyang has denied responsibility and vowed to take military actions along the border if needed.
The latest escalation of tensions comes amid Seoul's suspicions that North Korean forces have repeatedly crossed the MDL to carry out border fortification work, such as erecting fences and laying mines, in potential violation of the armistice that halted the 1950-53 Korean War.
Earlier, South Korea voiced concern over North Korea heightening border tensions with threats.

articles.title: Spain tests new anti-drone systems at army exercise
articles.body:
- EM&E Group used remote weapon stations on 4x4 and 6x6 vehicles and a jamming robot to down drones at Spain’s ATLAS 26 exercise.
- The systems were shown as configurations of ARACNE, the counter-drone system EM&E is developing with Indra for the Spanish Armed Forces.
Spanish defense company EM&E Group used remote weapon stations on armored vehicles and a jamming-equipped ground robot to detect and shoot down several drones during the Spanish military’s ATLAS 26 counter-drone exercise this week at the Médano del Loro firing range in Huelva, in southwestern Spain.
The exercise was led by Spain’s Chief of the Defence Staff, organized by the Maneuver Support Command and directed by the Spanish Army’s Anti-Aircraft Artillery Command. EM&E, formerly known as Escribano Mechanical & Engineering, said it took part with several configurations of ARACNE, the counter-drone system it is developing with Indra Group through a joint venture.
Two 4×4 tactical vehicles took part fitted with EM&E’s GUARDIAN 2.0 remote weapon station as a hard-kill option, meaning they physically destroy drones with gunfire instead of disrupting them electronically. The company also fielded its FEROX 6×6 armored vehicle carrying the GUARDIAN L-HIT remote station, which it uses to both detect and engage drones, and deployed its AUNAV LINK robotic vehicle with an integrated electronic warfare package that jams the radio links between a drone and its operator to block or distort its communications.
EM&E said the systems detected and shot down several drones during the exercise, without giving numbers or details of the targets.
ARACNE is one of the Spanish Armed Forces’ main counter-drone programs. The roughly 30.24 million euro ($34 million) effort covers 14 systems for the military, seven fixed and seven mobile, intended to protect critical infrastructure and military convoys, with mobile versions mounted on Vamtac ST5 tactical vehicles. The system pairs Indra’s sensors and command software with EM&E hardware, including a SmartEar radio-frequency scanner that monitors frequencies from 400 MHz to 6 GHz within about 6 km (3.7 miles) and an EM&E electro-optical station that can spot targets more than 14 km (8.7 miles) away with its daylight camera and up to 23.1 km (14.4 miles) with its thermal channel.
Indra and EM&E also demonstrated ARACNE at last year’s ATLAS 25 exercise, held at the same Huelva range from Oct. 20 to 24, 2025, where Indra said the system’s command and control software stood out for its ability to combine data from its own sensors and third-party sensors. A counter-drone system that Indra continues to develop under the ARACNE project also protects the Spanish contingent deployed with NATO in Lithuania, and Indra said in March 2026 that it had drawn interest from several countries on the alliance’s eastern flank.
The ATLAS exercises bring together Spanish military units and industry to test systems for detecting, identifying and defeating drones, and EM&E’s demonstrations this year added ground robotics and electronic warfare to the gun-based options shown on its vehicles.

articles.title: Kiev retreats on Nazi collaborator tribute – Warsaw
articles.body:
Kiev retreats on Nazi collaborator tribute – Warsaw
Kiev has moved to block a planned tribute to Nazi collaborator Roman Shukhevich, who was involved in the killing of an estimated 100,000 Poles during World War II ethnic purges, officials in Warsaw have claimed.
The reported retreat comes amid a series of disputes between the two countries in recent months over Kiev’s veneration of Nazi-linked figures that have eroded Polish support for Ukraine in its conflict with Russia.
The controversy erupted on Tuesday when the Lviv Regional Council in western Ukraine voted to declare 2027 the Year of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) and to celebrate the 120th anniversary of its commander Roman Shukhevich while deciding to organize “cultural, memorial, scientific, and mass media events,” as well as exhibitions and national patriotic rallies on the occasion.
The move triggered a fierce response in Poland, which regards the UPA as perpetrators of genocide against Poles in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia and Shukhevich as a key “architect” of the massacres. Before becoming a UPA leader, Shukhevich served in Nazi Germany’s Nachtigall Battalion and the German-controlled 201st Schutzmannschaft Battalion, which operated in occupied Belarus.
On Wednesday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk condemned the resolution as “unwise” and “suicidal tactics,” saying it “harms Ukraine,” while Polish Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz called the move “unacceptable,” warning that it would deepen divisions between the neighboring countries. Meanwhile, Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski called for the resolution’s key sponsor, Lviv regional lawmaker Svyatoslav Sheremeta, to be put on a list of individuals deemed undesirable in Poland.
Following the backlash, Polish Deputy Foreign Minister Marcin Bosacki said on Wednesday that officials of Vladimir Zelensky’s office had assured Warsaw that the controversial resolutions would not come into force. On Friday, Tusk echoed the claim, saying that Zelensky had personally signaled he would not endorse the resolution, adding that the Ukrainian leader was “unhappy” with the situation.
This also came after the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry called the Shukhevich tribute in Lviv “counterproductive to our current efforts aimed at further developing Ukrainian-Polish relations.” The ministry stressed that the local authorities had sought no advice from government bodies to assess the consequences of their actions.
An unnamed source in Zelensky’s office cited by Ukrainskaya Pravda went so far as to describe the decision as a “catastrophe.” “Ukraine looks erratic. We have just resolved the previous crisis – and now this,” the source said, accusing regional officials of pursuing “cheap one-day hype” despite knowing all too well what the resolution would lead to.
While senior Ukrainian officials apparently distanced themselves from the controversy, the Lviv council’s original announcement remains accessible as of Saturday. Sheremet also previously defended the resolution, saying “This is our history, our heroes, and we must duly honor their memory.”
The dispute is the latest in a series of heated clashes between Kiev and Warsaw over Ukraine’s continued veneration of nationalist figures that collaborated with Nazi Germany during World War II.
In May, Zelensky awarded an elite Ukrainian special operations unit the honorary title “Heroes of the UPA,” prompting another diplomatic uproar, with Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripping the Ukrainian leader of the Order of the White Eagle, Poland’s highest state decoration.

articles.title: "It all depends on the Russians": Zelenskyy announces Ukraine-US-Russia talks in first half of November
articles.body:
"It all depends on the Russians": Zelenskyy announces Ukraine-US-Russia talks in first half of November
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has stated, following a conversation with Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, that negotiations between teams from Ukraine, the US and Russia are planned for the first half of November, although it will depend on the Russians whether they are held.
Source: European Pravda, citing Zelenskyy's remarks at an online meeting at the Hudson Institute, as reported by Suspilne
Details: Zelenskyy said he had just had a telephone conversation with Kushner and Witkoff, during which they discussed the results of the meetings in Norway and how they could "move diplomacy forward".
Quote: "This November we have an agreement to hold a trilateral meeting – Ukraine, United States and Russia – at the team level, and we hope it will happen. The plan is to meet in the first half of November and as early as possible of course, but we are ready to meet any day – even tomorrow. But it all depends on the Russians."
Details: Zelenskyy added that Ukraine had also expected a trilateral meeting to be held in October.
Quote: "But it didn't happen, because the Russians came up with another reason not to meet. And now we all need to focus on making these meetings happen. Of course together, of course with America, of course with Europe and with all our other partners. We need these meetings, and we need diplomacy to move forward."
Details: Zelenskyy also believes that the meetings cannot take place without the US or without American pressure on Russia.
Quote: "We need trilateral talks between Ukraine, America and Russia, and Europe must also be part of this conversation. And we need to move from technical-level trilateral talks to involve the leaders, because the key issues can only be settled at that level."
Background:
- On 21 October, Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff met with Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg to discuss the settlement of the war in Ukraine. During the meeting, Witkoff called Putin a "humanitarian".
- Zelenskyy has said that Russia supports a trilateral meeting at team level and the dates for the potential meeting are being finalised.

articles.title: Kadena Implements Curfew, Alcohol Restrictions for Junior Troops After Japanese Civilian Dies
articles.body:
The top Air Force commander on the Japanese island of Okinawa has clamped down alcohol and issued a curfew for junior enlisted Airmen and Guardians at Kadena Air Base for the next month. The order came roughly two weeks after a U.S. Marine was arrested for allegedly robbing and murdering a Japanese woman on the island.
Brig. Gen. John B. Gallemore, commander of the 18th Wing at Kadena, issued the Oct. 22 memo, ordering the “Curtailment of Liberty and the Consumption of Alcohol,” according to a memo posted on the popular unofficial Air Force amn/nco/snco Facebook page.
A PACAF spokesperson confirmed the memo’s authenticity. The order went into effect Oct. 22 and will last “throughout the 30-day period of reflection,” concluding on Nov. 8, according to the memo:
- All personnel within the grades of E-1 through E-4 are not to consume alcohol.
- Off-base liberty between 10 p.m. and 5 a.m. local time is curtailed for all personnel within the grades of E-1 through E-4.
- Possession of alcohol is banned in all dormitories within Kadena Air Base, to include dormitory common areas.
During the period, “commanders at all levels are authorized to conduct unannounced, systematic health and welfare inspections of dormitory rooms to ensure compliance of this order,” the memo states.
The memo follows an Oct. 6 memo from United States Forces Japan that ordered similar liberty restrictions and personal conduct training as part of a “period of reflection” following the Marine’s arrest in connection with the alleged murder of an Okinawan woman in Naha.
Japanese police arrested Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, of the III Marine Expeditionary Force, on Oct. 4 for allegedly killing 39-year-old Anna Yagi and stealing her wallet, Marine Corps Times reported.
“Incidents like this demand we pause for reflection,” Benjamin T. Watson, area coordinator for U.S. Forces Japan, wrote in the memo. “These allegations are extremely serious, and we will continue to ensure full cooperation with Japanese authorities throughout the investigation.”
Watson added that serving on Okinawa “comes with responsibility.”
“We live, work, and socialize alongside the people of Okinawa; their home is our home,” Watson wrote. “Every interaction with our neighbors either builds or undermines the trust that is essential to our team. When that trust is damaged, it affects the strength of our alliance and the security of this region.”
The USFJ memo prohibited alcohol consumption for 48 hours from Oct. 7-9 but stopped short of restricting consumption during the 30-day period of reflection. In a statement, PACAF Gallemore’s Oct. 22 memo contains extra restrictions.
“The 18th Wing continually assesses measures to reinforce good order and discipline and maintain positive relationships with our host community,” the PACAF statement read. “As part of the ongoing 30-day period of reflection on Okinawa, Japan, [Gallemore] determined that additional preventive measures were appropriate to reinforce expectations for responsible conduct among service members.”
Periods of reflection and associated restrictions have been used by commanders on Okinawa in the past to reinforce discipline after violent, criminal incidents involving U.S. personnel and Japanese residents. In 2024, USFJ prohibited all American troops in the country from publicly consuming alcohol from 1 a.m. to 5 a.m. every day after a string of alleged sexual assaults. In 2017, the command prohibited all drinking and cut off-base liberty for troops on Okinawa after a fatal car crash involving a drunk Marine. In 2010, then-Brig. Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach—now the Chief of Staff—instituted a brief period of reflection restricting alcohol and off-base liberty at Kadena after a string of alcohol-related arrests. In 2008, commanders imposed the measure to calm an uproar in the surrounding community over allegations that a Marine raped a 14-year-old girl on the island, The Guardian reported.
Kadena is the closest U.S. air base to Taiwan, making it a strategically vital location should China ever launch an invasion.

articles.title: Netanyahu vows collective punishment after Hebron shooting
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Netanyahu vows collective punishment against Palestinian neighbourhood after Hebron shooting
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed to carry out collective punishment against a Palestinian neighbourhood in the city of Hebron after an attack on an Israeli army checkpoint in the occupied West Bank killed two soldiers.
Speaking during a visit to the city with Defence Minister Israel Katz, Netanyahu said: "First of all, we will act to destroy this place, to change it completely."
"But we are going to do something that has not been done until now: We will implement the successful and aggressive model we used in the refugee camps, which are essentially terrorist strongholds," he added, according to the Times of Israel.
Netanyahu's comments refer to Israel's policy of forcibly expelling thousands of Palestinians from several northern West Bank refugee camps, including Jenin, Tulkarm and Nur Shams, that occurred in early 2025, with around 33,000 being expelled.
Laying out the plan for the neighbourhood, Netanyahu said: "We will evacuate the residents, we will go house to house, we will remove the weapons there as well, and all the terrorist infrastructure will be dealt with and destroyed."
He added that the Israeli military would carry out a major operation in the occupied West Bank, the largest since it first occupied the area following the 1967 war when it first took control of the area.
The announcement comes in response to the killing of two Israeli soldiers and wounding three others at an Israeli army checkpoint in the occupied West Bank, with two Palestinian gunmen also killed in the incident.
Israel Katz confirmed Netanyahu's comments, saying "the Jenin refugee camp model arrives in Hebron."
The attack comes days before Israel's Knesset elections that could see the formation of a new government, with polling suggesting that both the pro-Netanyahu and opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot are both under the threshold to form a majority government, with many politicians putting out statements on the incident.
Zizette Darkazally, an Associate Fellow at Chatham House's Middle East and North Africa Programme, told The New Arab that the reactions from Israel's politicians confirm the preexisting positions that they already held.
This includes Bezalel Smotrich, the far-right finance minister who also oversees Israel's military occupation in the West Bank, who announced he had already ordered the destruction of several buildings near the site of the shooting, and approved new farms in the area of Masafer Yatta, where Palestinian residents have long fought against Israeli attempts to destroy Palestinian homes.
Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir also weighed in, again calling for the government to dismantle the Palestinian Authority that governs parts of the West Bank, while opposition politicians Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, and Yair Golan praised the Israeli military's response.
Darkazally said that Netanyahu's announced policies were an attempt to exploit the attack to gain more votes and further his self-proclaimed image as 'Mr Security', but that it's unlikely to change the base of voters between the two blocs.
"I don't think the attack will change votes of the base in any of the two blocs," she said, adding, "most of the 'undecided' at this stage are undecided within the same camp, meaning that they are undecided between parties in the same bloc", Darkazally said.
‘Restrictions on top of restrictions’
Restrictions announced by Netanyahu have immediately come into effect, according to Amir Daoud, Director of Publishing and Documentation at the Colonisation and Wall Resistance Commission, who told The New Arab that the city has been cordoned off, with preparations for wider closures occurring across the West Bank.
Hebron is the largest city in the occupied West Bank, with 250,000 Palestinians calling it home.
Daoud noted that these restrictions come on top of the plethora of restrictions, checkpoints, and barriers that are already in place across the area that impede freedom of movement for its three million Palestinian residents.
"According to the latest figures documented by the Colonisation and Wall Resistance Commission, there were 942 movement obstacles across the West Bank as of September 2026," he said, adding that "these restrictions have transformed Palestinian movement between cities, villages and communities into a process controlled by Israeli military decisions."
Israel's ever-tightening policies in the occupied West Bank have occurred in conjunction with its expansion of settlements and parallel infrastructure allowing them freedom of movement across the territory.
The policy, which rights groups have labelled apartheid, comes alongside an uptick in settler terror attacks against Palestinians that have escalated dramatically since the start of Israel's genocide in Gaza.
Daoud said that the restrictions mean Palestinians will be unable to reach their jobs or get medical treatment, with farmers losing access to land and markets to sell produce. This is set to impact the olive harvest season, already disrupted by widespread settler violence.
Medical Aid for Palestinians warned on Friday that, following announced restrictions and an Israeli military escalation in the occupied West Bank, its staff are reporting increased obstacles to reaching Palestinians in need of care.
The aid group noted that settler attacks in the village of Umm Safa, north of Ramallah, illustrate the risks posed to Palestinians amid the heightened security.
Aseel Baidoun, the group's Deputy Director of Advocacy and Communications in the West Bank, warned that both settler attacks and ministerial threats of collective punishment and forcible displacement meant "the risk of atrocity crimes is acute."
There is also a risk of these measures becoming permanent, adding to the layers of restrictions that already impact life in the occupied West Bank.
"Our concern is that measures initially introduced as temporary security responses frequently become prolonged restrictions or are incorporated into the existing system of military control," Daoud told The New Arab.
“From our perspective, the fundamental issue is the cumulative effect of these measures,” he said, adding, “what we are witnessing is not merely a temporary interruption of movement, but the continued consolidation of a system in which freedom of movement is increasingly treated as an exception rather than a basic right.”

articles.title: Army seeks new ways to power troops on the battlefield
articles.body:
UK Defence Innovation has opened a Tactical Power Challenge worth £2.45 million seeking better ways to generate, store, distribute and manage electrical power for deployed forces, run on behalf of the British Army with support from the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory, according to UK Defence Innovation.
The competition is being delivered in partnership with Australia’s Advanced Strategic Capabilities Accelerator and closes at noon on 10 November. Further detail is available on the government’s competition page.
The organisation said the challenge seeks innovative solutions to improve the generation, storage, distribution and management of electrical power for deployed forces.
Power has become one of the quieter constraints on how the Army fights. A dismounted section now carries radios, electronic warfare detectors, night vision, counter-drone equipment, tablets and the batteries for all of it, and the weight of those batteries competes directly with water and ammunition. At formation level the problem scales up into generators, fuel convoys and the thermal and acoustic signature that a diesel generator park produces for anyone looking.
Ukraine has made the point sharply over the past four years, because units operating dispersed and under constant observation cannot run a visible generator, and the fuel resupply that a traditional headquarters depends on is one of the easiest things for a drone operator to find and hit. Silent generation, solar and battery hybrids, and power management that lets one source feed several systems have all moved from convenience to survivability.
The Australian partnership places the competition inside a wider pattern of British and Australian innovation work, with the Advanced Strategic Capabilities Accelerator performing a similar function to UK Defence Innovation. Running a challenge jointly gives a successful supplier two potential customers and gives both armies a chance of fielding compatible equipment, which matters more as the two countries work together under AUKUS Pillar Two on autonomy, artificial intelligence and electronic warfare.
UK Defence Innovation was established to replace the Defence and Security Accelerator and to put a single organisation in charge of pulling new technology into the department at pace, with a budget ringfenced under the Strategic Defence Review. Competitions of this kind are its main instrument, offering a defined sum against a defined problem on a short timetable.

articles.title: White House claims Melania Trump has secured ceasefire in Oleshky
articles.body:
White House claims Melania Trump has secured ceasefire in Oleshky
The White House has issued a statement reporting that US First Lady Melania Trump has secured a truce between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in Kherson Oblast, where a humanitarian disaster is currently unfolding.
Source: European Pravda, citing a statement made by the White House; Dmytro Lytvyn, communications adviser to Ukrainian president, commenting on the situation
Details: The White House said Russia and Ukraine have agreed to temporarily halt all military action in Oleshky to ensure the delivery of humanitarian aid and prepare to evacuate the civilian population through a designated safe corridor.
The localised ceasefire is set to take effect on 29 October.
Quote from Melania Trump: "The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster. Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food and clean water.
It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible."
Details: According to the statement, the First Lady and her representative worked directly with the leadership of Russia and Ukraine to define the terms of the local truce. Melania Trump initiated negotiations with both countries and aligned the parties on the agreement's objectives, technical procedures, timelines, processes and conditions.
Quote from Melania Trump: "Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require. Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia and some to Ukraine."
Details: Melania Trump said that an impartial American media organisation will accompany and document the activities of the Russian and Ukrainian teams on the ground throughout the process.
The situation in Oleshky came to Melania Trump's attention during a private conversation at her Fostering the Future Together event in New York during the 81st United Nations General Assembly.
Quote from Melania Trump: "My representative and I immediately leveraged the communication channel we established with Russia and Ukraine through the previous six reunifications of 34 children. Both nations promptly assigned teams to coordinate the complex mechanics involved, including demining. All parties have worked around the clock since that moment."
In a response to the White House statement, Dmytro Lytvyn noted that the issue of the situation in Oleshky is being handled by Dmytro Lubinets, the Verkhovna Rada (Parliamentary) Commissioner for Human Rights.
Quote from Lytvyn: "On the Ukrainian side, Mr Lubinets is handling the topic of Oleshky, and it would be more appropriate for him to comment, as the topic is sensitive and everything must be carried out precisely as coordinated with Mr Lubinets."
Background:
- On 20 October, European Parliament Vice President Pina Picierno announced that she was going on a hunger strike to draw the international community's attention to the humanitarian catastrophe in occupied Oleshky.
- On 28 September, Kaja Kallas, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, said the EU was attempting to deliver humanitarian aid to occupied Oleshky.
- On 16 October, Pope Leo XIV held a telephone conversation with Russian leader Vladimir Putin and asked him to arrange for a truce so that aid can be delivered to temporarily occupied Oleshky.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Starlink woes should be a wake-up call for Taiwan, analysts say
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Starlink woes should be a wake-up call for Taiwan, analysts say
Sudden imposition of restrictions on Ukraine’s satellite internet highlights the risk of relying on a single foreign provider
Taiwan should not rely on a single foreign satellite provider for critical wartime communications, analysts have warned, after sudden restrictions on the use of Elon Musk’s Starlink disrupted Ukrainian drone operations.
The episode has renewed debate in Taiwan over the risks of entrusting essential communications to foreign commercial operators whose services could be restricted for political, military or business reasons.
Analysts said this was particularly relevant as Taipei was trying to strengthen the resilience of its communication networks against potential mainland Chinese attacks while simultaneously expanding its use of drones and other unmanned systems.
“The lesson from this incident is that we cannot become overly dependent on satellite navigation services provided by a single company,” said Shu Hsiao-huang, a senior analyst at Taiwan’s government-funded Institute for National Defence and Security Research.

articles.title: Brent crude hits highest since June 2022 on fears of renewed US strikes on Iran
articles.body:
Oil prices rose on Friday as fears of renewed US strikes on Iran and escalating regional tensions heightened supply concerns, pushing Brent crude to its highest level since June 2022, Anadolu reports.
International benchmark Brent climbed 2.7%, or $3.06, to $116.20 per barrel as of 1350GMT, surpassing the peak recorded at the start of the war.
US benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI) advanced 3.04%, or $3.02, to $102.50 per barrel, its highest level in five weeks.
Brent has gained around 5% this week, while WTI has risen about 3%, putting both benchmarks on course for a third consecutive weekly advance.
The rally came as expectations grew that Washington could resume strikes against Iran in the coming weeks.
READ: Trump accuses Iran of driving up oil prices ahead of midterms
President Donald Trump said on Thursday that the US may carry out further strikes on Iran. “This should have been done a long time ago by other presidents, the Iran war, and we’ve knocked the hell out of them, and we may do it a little bit further,” he said.
US and Israeli officials are said to have drawn up plans for renewed strikes after the US midterm elections.
Regional tensions have also intensified as Yemen’s Houthis continue attacks on Saudi Arabia, raising concerns about risks to energy infrastructure.
The US State Department ordered non-essential personnel to leave Saudi Arabia.
The US-Israel war on Iran began in late February, and has yet to be settled despite a ceasefire and a memorandum for a final peace deal, primarily due to differences over navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: “Land of Angels” competing in 14th Asian Film Festival Barcelona
articles.body:
“Land of Angels” competing in 14th Asian Film Festival Barcelona
TEHRAN – Babak Khajehpasha’s “Land of Angels” has been selected for the official section of the 14th Asian Film Festival Barcelona (AFFBCN), which was launched in Barcelona, Spain, on October 22 and will run until November 1.
The film tells the story of the suffering of children in Gaza and portrays the human consequences of war through the experiences of a woman who struggles to survive while protecting a group of innocent children from the horrors of conflict, ILNA reported.
Amid the bombings and military offensive in Palestine, the story follows the painful and courageous journey of a woman trapped on the front line. As everything collapses around her, the protagonist takes on the dangerous task of surviving the war while trying to protect, feed, and guide a vulnerable group of innocent children, keeping them safe from the horrors of armed conflict. Through her perspective, the feature film becomes a deeply human portrait of the instinct to protect, the loss of childhood innocence, and civilian resilience under extreme conditions.
The film features Arab actors and centers on the lives, dreams, and struggles of children against the backdrop of the war in Palestine. Rather than presenting the conflict solely through political or military events, the film approaches it from the perspective of civilians, particularly children whose lives have been profoundly affected by the violence.
The production was filmed in Tehran over a period of one and a half years. The film’s international screenings began with its participation in the Kazan festival, following its successful national festival run in Iran.
“Land of Angels” received the Grand Prix for Best Feature Film at the 22nd Altyn Minbar Kazan International Film Festival.
Prior to its appearance in Kazan, “Land of Angels” was the most decorated film at Iran’s 44th Fajr International Film Festival, where it received five Crystal Simorgh awards and eight honorary diplomas.
Among its Fajr honors, Khajehpasha received the jury’s special prize for directing, while Syrian actress Sulaf Fawakherji was honored for her performance. The film also received awards for set design, visual effects, and other categories.
Babak Khajehpasha is a director and screenwriter. Following a solid career in television, he achieved immediate international critical recognition with his debut feature film, “In the Arms of the Tree” (2023), a drama on family fractures that was officially selected to represent Iran at the Academy Awards.
With “The Land of Angels” (2026), Khajehpasha takes on the roles of screenwriter and director to deliver a humanitarian drama focused on civilian victims of contemporary conflicts in the Middle East. It has also been officially selected as Iran’s submission to the 99th Academy Awards in the best international feature film category.
The Asian Film Festival Barcelona is organized by Casa Asia. True to its commitment to promoting contemporary Asian cinema, the festival presents more than one hundred films representing the latest independent, experimental and auteur cinema from across the continent.
The selection brings together works from 25 countries in the Asia-Pacific region, mostly produced between 2025 and 2026.
This edition pays particular attention to emerging film industries in countries such as Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Mongolia, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Cambodia, as well as established industries with a long history at the festival, including Iran, India, China, South Korea, Japan, and the Philippines.
The program also includes films from Hong Kong, Indonesia, Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Vietnam, as well as productions from Australia and New Zealand.
According to its director, Menene Gras Balaguer, AFFBCN aims to establish itself as a leading international showcase for Asian cinema and to continue attracting new audiences. “We want more and more viewers to discover the vitality and talent of these film industries and to help ensure that their growing recognition translates into a greater presence in cinemas and at festivals. We are committed to cinema that brings us closer to the cultural diversity of Asia and invites us to understand the world from other perspectives.”

articles.title: Stubb seen as most likely European candidate for talks with Russia — newspaper
articles.body:
BERLIN, October 24. /TASS/. Finnish President Alexander Stubb may become the key European mediator in negotiations with Russia on Ukraine after his talks earlier this week with US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Vladimir Zelensky in Oslo, according to Berliner Zeitung.
The story says that Stubb’s significant advantage over other European politicians is his good relations with US President Donald Trump.
Stubb’s participation in the negotiations would reduce the risk of a confrontation between Trump and Zelensky, as relations between Kiev and Washington have deteriorated sharply recently, the paper said.

Moscow has repeatedly stated its readiness to hold negotiations with European countries on the security framework on the continent, taking into account the interests of both sides. Russia will monitor the situation in the coming days, Putin added.

articles.title: AFOSI Seeks Enlisted Airmen to Train as Special Agents
articles.body:
The Air Force Office of Special Investigations is looking for a few good Airmen to swap jobs and become special agents.
No, they won’t get the 007 James Bond code—but they could learn to conduct counterintelligence and investigate procurement fraud and major crimes, OSI spokesperson Trevor Saylor told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
The office is looking to recruit agents from backgrounds other than law enforcement—it’s seeking Airmen with less than 11 years in service, with some exceptions, and is calling for applicants from other job fields in part because other areas of expertise can prove valuable in the unique types of investigations OSI conducts.
“A maintainer may understand an issue involving an aircraft or weapons system, while a contracting or acquisitions professional may recognize a process or irregularity relevant to a fraud investigation,” Special Agent Jennifer Holland, an OSI recruiter, said in a recent release. “Intelligence professionals may bring experience analyzing adversaries, identifying patterns and working with sensitive information.”
As threats to the Department of the Air Force cross traditional boundaries between criminal investigations, counterintelligence, cyber activity, and technology protection, that range of experience has become more relevant, Holland said.
Current threats and demands placed on OSI have “placed a renewed focus on defending the homeland, strengthening deterrence, protecting critical capabilities and preserving military advantages to generate combat power,” according to the release.
Skills such as foreign language proficiency, cybersecurity expertise and advanced computing skills are helpful, but not required or all that is needed.
“We’re looking for Airmen capable of exercising independent judgment, communicating with people from different backgrounds, managing competing priorities and documenting investigative activity with precision,” Holland said.
The requirements include:
- Technical sergeants who exceed the 11-year limit may be considered on a case-by-case basis and should pursue a time-in-service waiver through their local AFOSI detachment before applying.
- First-term Airmen must also meet applicable retraining window requirements.
- First-term Airmen assigned within the continental United States who are serving four-year enlistments may generally apply from the first duty day of the month in which they complete 35 months of their current enlistment through the last duty day of their 43rd month.
- For Airmen serving six-year enlistments, the corresponding window is from the 59th through the 67th month.
- First-term Airmen assigned outside the continental United States generally must apply between 12 and 15 months before their date eligible to return from overseas. They must also enter their 35th month of service, or 59th month for six-year enlistees, on or before that date.
- Applicants on a current Control Roster or with a current Unfavorable Information File are not eligible.
- Applicants must be worldwide qualified and have a current passing fitness assessment without exemptions or a profile.
- OSI does not require enlisted applicants to have a college degree.
Diverse Experience
Traditionally, law enforcement, cyber defense, healthcare, and logistics Airmen have had success translating their skills into the special agent role, Saylor wrote.
The recruitment effort isn’t from any shortage or operational gaps, Saylor said. Instead, it is part of an ongoing effort to maintain a “highly credible, robust force” of agents.
“We remain fully postured and staffed to meet all operational requirements,” Saylor wrote in an email.
OSI isn’t targeting a specific job field, and the application process is open to all Airmen who meet the criteria.
The office evaluates using the “Whole Airman” concept, Saylor wrote.
The concept focuses on evaluating Airmen as well-rounded individuals across their military and personal lives, using tools such as Enlisted Performance Reports and special duty selections, with an emphasis on leadership, job performance, self-improvement, base/community involvement, and well-being aspects tied to Airman fitness.
If an Airman submits their application package correctly and follows the USAF Personnel Center windows to secure a release from their current job, their AFSC Career Field Manager will be the final authority to approve or deny their request to move to special agent selection and training.
Application Steps:
- Apply online, complete documentation, and secure your commander’s recommendation.
- AFOSI requests your career-field release, though approval is not guaranteed.
- Approved applicants undergo suitability screening at their local unit.
- Candidates complete interviews and background investigations before final selection.
- The application process takes about three to six months.
If selected, the Airman then gets a short-term Assignment Limitation Code while they go through vetting and onboarding for special agent training, Saylor wrote.
Newly retrained Airmen-turned-agents will train at the Federal Law Enforcement Training Center in Glynco, Ga., to learn the fundamentals of federal criminal investigations before completing OSI-specific training.
They’ll then be put into specialties such as counterintelligence, procurement fraud, and major criminal investigative roles once they join their units, Saylor wrote.
Then there’s cyber.
“For roles in AFOSI’s cyber defense positions, AFOSI vectors Agents who show promise in the field into the specialized cyber fields upon the completion of probation,” Saylor wrote.
Most agents will begin their 15-month probationary period working felony-level criminal investigations and counterintelligence operations.
While some may specialize in certain areas, all special agents are expected to work interchangeably in a variety of missions and types of investigations.
Special Agents often travel more than many in the Air Force as part of their job and sometimes work high-stress cases that involve violent crime, fraud, and national security threats.
To mitigate burnout, Saylor wrote that OSI proactively supports personnel through a structured career progression plan and uses embedded wellness resources.
“Upon completing an initial probationary period of approximately 15 months focused on general criminal and counterintelligence work, agents have the opportunity to transition into specialized investigative sections,” Saylor wrote. “This structural pathway provides variety in their assignments and a deliberate break from the initial high-tempo investigative grind.”
OSI also has its own embedded chaplain corps and psychologists to provide ready access to mental health support, he wrote.
